FileUtils#touch.comment: Updates modification times (mtime) and access times (atime) of the entries given by the paths in list (a single path or an array of paths); returns list if it is an array, [list] otherwise. By default, creates an empty file for any path to a non-existent entry; use keyword argument nocreate to raise an exception instead. Argument list or its elements should be {interpretable as paths}[rdoc-ref:FileUtils@Path+Arguments]. Examples: # Single path. f = File.new('src0.txt') # Existing file. f.atime # => 2022-06-10 11:11:21.200277 -0700 f.mtime # => 2022-06-10 11:11:21.200277 -0700 FileUtils.touch('src0.txt') f = File.new('src0.txt') f.atime # => 2022-06-11 08:28:09.8185343 -0700 f.mtime # => 2022-06-11 08:28:09.8185343 -0700 # Array of paths. FileUtils.touch(['src0.txt', 'src0.dat']) Keyword arguments: * mtime: time - sets the entry's mtime to the given time, instead of the current time. * nocreate: true - raises an exception if the entry does not exist. * noop: true - does not touch entries; returns nil. * verbose: true - prints an equivalent command: FileUtils.touch('src0.txt', noop: true, verbose: true) FileUtils.touch(['src0.txt', 'src0.dat'], noop: true, verbose: true) FileUtils.touch(path, noop: true, verbose: true) Output: touch src0.txt touch src0.txt src0.dat touch src0.txt Related: FileUtils.uptodate?.

FileUtils#uptodate?.name: uptodate?
FileUtils#uptodate?.comment:
Returns <tt>true</tt> if the file at path <tt>new</tt> is newer than all the
files at paths in array <tt>old_list</tt>; <tt>false</tt> otherwise.

Argument <tt>new</tt> and the elements of <tt>old_list</tt> should be
{interpretable as paths}[rdoc-ref:FileUtils@Path+Arguments]:

  FileUtils.uptodate?('Rakefile', ['Gemfile', 'README.md']) # => true
  FileUtils.uptodate?('Gemfile', ['Rakefile', 'README.md']) # => false

A non-existent file is considered to be infinitely old.

Related: FileUtils.touch.

FileUtils::DryRun.name: FileUtils::DryRun
FileUtils::DryRun.comment:
This module has all methods of FileUtils module, but never changes
files/directories, with printing message before acting. This equates to
passing the <tt>:noop</tt> and <tt>:verbose</tt> flag to methods in FileUtils.

FileUtils::NoWrite.name: FileUtils::NoWrite
FileUtils::NoWrite.comment:
This module has all methods of FileUtils module, but never changes
files/directories.  This equates to passing the <tt>:noop</tt> flag to methods
in FileUtils.

FileUtils::Verbose.name: FileUtils::Verbose
FileUtils::Verbose.comment:
This module has all methods of FileUtils module, but it outputs messages
before acting.  This equates to passing the <tt>:verbose</tt> flag to methods
in FileUtils.

Find.name: Find
Find.comment: Module Find supports the top-down traversal of entries in the file system.

Find::find.name: find
Find::find.comment:
With a block given, performs a depth-first traversal of each given path in
<tt>paths</tt>;
calls the block with each found file or directory path:
  paths = []
Find.find('bin', 'jit') {|path| paths << path }
paths
# =>
# ["bin",
#  "bin/gem",
#  "jit",
#  "jit/Cargo.toml",
#  "jit/src",
#  "jit/src/lib.rs"]

Raises an exception if a given path cannot be read.
When keyword argument <tt>ignore_error</tt> is given as <tt>true</tt> (the
default),
certain exceptions during traversal are ignored (i.e., silently rescued):
Errno::ENOENT, Errno::EACCES, Errno::ENOTDIR, Errno::ELOOP,
Errno::ENAMETOOLONG, Errno::EINVAL;
when given as <tt>false</tt>, no exceptions are rescued.
Note that these exceptions may be ignored only in <tt>Find</tt> traversal
code;
an exception raised before traversal begins,
or raised while in the block is not ignored.
Each of the calls below raises an Errno::ENOENT exception that is not ignored:
  Find.find('nosuch') { }
Find.find('lib') {|entry| raise Errno::ENOENT }

With no block given, returns a new Enumerator.

Find::prune.name: prune
Find::prune.comment:
This method is meaningful only within a block given with Find.find.
Inside such a block,
"prunes" the traversed file tree by not descending into the current directory:
  files = []
Find.find('.') do |path|
  Find.prune if File.basename(path) == 'test'
  next unless File.file?(path) && File.extname(path) == '.rb'
  files << path
end
files.size    # => 6690
files.take(3) # => ["./KNOWNBUGS.rb", "./array.rb", "./ast.rb"]

Float.name: Float
Float.comment: A Float object stores a real number using the native architecture's double-precision floating-point representation. == Float Imprecisions Some real numbers can be represented precisely as Float objects: 37.5 # => 37.5 98.75 # => 98.75 12.3125 # => 12.3125 Others cannot; among these are the transcendental numbers, including: * Pi, π: in mathematics, a number of infinite precision: 3.1415926535897932384626433... (to 25 places); in Ruby, it is of limited precision (in this case, to 16 decimal places): Math::PI # => 3.141592653589793 * Euler's number, e: in mathematics, a number of infinite precision: 2.7182818284590452353602874... (to 25 places); in Ruby, it is of limited precision (in this case, to 15 decimal places): Math::E # => 2.718281828459045 Some floating-point computations in Ruby give precise results: 1.0/2 # => 0.5 100.0/8 # => 12.5 Others do not: * In mathematics, 2/3 as a decimal number is an infinitely-repeating decimal: 0.666... (forever); in Ruby, 2.0/3 is of limited precision (in this case, to 16 decimal places): 2.0/3 # => 0.6666666666666666 * In mathematics, the square root of 2 is an irrational number of infinite precision: 1.4142135623730950488016887... (to 25 decimal places); in Ruby, it is of limited precision (in this case, to 16 decimal places): Math.sqrt(2.0) # => 1.4142135623730951 * Even a simple computation can introduce imprecision: x = 0.1 + 0.2 # => 0.30000000000000004 y = 0.3 # => 0.3 x == y # => false See: * https://docs.oracle.com/cd/E19957-01/806-3568/ncg_goldberg.html * https://github.com/rdp/ruby_tutorials_core/wiki/Ruby-Talk-FAQ#user-content-- why-are-rubys-floats-imprecise * https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating_point#Accuracy_problems Note that precise storage and computation of rational numbers is possible using Rational objects. == Creating a Float You can create a Float object explicitly with: * A {floating-point literal}[rdoc-ref:syntax/literals.rdoc@Float+Literals]. You can convert certain objects to Floats with: * Method #Float. == What's Here First, what's elsewhere. Class Float: * Inherits from {class Numeric}[rdoc-ref:Numeric@Whats+Here] and {class Object}[rdoc-ref:Object@Whats+Here]. * Includes {module Comparable}[rdoc-ref:Comparable@Whats+Here]. Here, class Float provides methods for: * {Querying}[rdoc-ref:Float@Querying] * {Comparing}[rdoc-ref:Float@Comparing] * {Converting}[rdoc-ref:Float@Converting] === Querying * #finite?: Returns whether self is finite. * #hash: Returns the integer hash code for self. * #infinite?: Returns whether self is infinite. * #nan?: Returns whether self is a NaN (not-a-number). === Comparing * #<: Returns whether self is less than the given value. * #<=: Returns whether self is less than or equal to the given value. * #<=>: Returns a number indicating whether self is less than, equal to, or greater than the given value. * #== (aliased as #=== and #eql?): Returns whether self is equal to the given value. * #>: Returns whether self is greater than the given value. * #>=: Returns whether self is greater than or equal to the given value. === Converting * #% (aliased as #modulo): Returns self modulo the given value. * #*: Returns the product of self and the given value. * #**: Returns the value of self raised to the power of the given value. * #+: Returns the sum of self and the given value. * #-: Returns the difference of self and the given value. * #/: Returns the quotient of self and the given value. * #ceil: Returns the smallest number greater than or equal to self. * #coerce: Returns a 2-element array containing the given value converted to a Float and self * #divmod: Returns a 2-element array containing the quotient and remainder results of dividing self by the given value. * #fdiv: Returns the Float result of dividing self by the given value. * #floor: Returns the greatest number smaller than or equal to self. * #next_float: Returns the next-larger representable Float. * #prev_float: Returns the next-smaller representable Float. * #quo: Returns the quotient from dividing self by the given value. * #round: Returns self rounded to the nearest value, to a given precision. * #to_i (aliased as #to_int): Returns self truncated to an Integer. * #to_s (aliased as #inspect): Returns a string containing the place-value representation of self in the given radix. * #truncate: Returns self truncated to a given precision.

Float#%.comment:
Returns <tt>self</tt> modulo <tt>other</tt> as a Float.

For float <tt>f</tt> and real number <tt>r</tt>, these expressions are
equivalent:

  f % r
  f-r*(f/r).floor
  f.divmod(r)[1]

See Numeric#divmod.

Examples:

  10.0 % 2              # => 0.0
  10.0 % 3              # => 1.0
  10.0 % 4              # => 2.0

  10.0 % -2             # => 0.0
  10.0 % -3             # => -2.0
  10.0 % -4             # => -2.0

  10.0 % 4.0            # => 2.0
  10.0 % Rational(4, 1) # => 2.0

Float#*.comment:
Returns the numeric product of <tt>self</tt> and <tt>other</tt>:

  f = 3.14
  f * 2              # => 6.28
  f * 2.0            # => 6.28
  f * Rational(1, 2) # => 1.57
  f * Complex(2, 0)  # => (6.28+0.0i)

Float#-.comment:
Returns the difference of <tt>self</tt> and <tt>other</tt>:

  f = 3.14
  f - 1                 # => 2.14
  f - 1.0               # => 2.14
  f - Rational(1, 1)    # => 2.14
  f - Complex(1, 0)     # => (2.14+0i)

Float#/.comment:
Returns the quotient of <tt>self</tt> and <tt>other</tt>:

  f = 3.14
  f / 2              # => 1.57
  f / 2.0            # => 1.57
  f / Rational(2, 1) # => 1.57
  f / Complex(2, 0)  # => (1.57+0.0i)

Float#<.comment:
Returns whether the value of <tt>self</tt> is less than the value of
<tt>other</tt>; <tt>other</tt> must be numeric, but may not be Complex:

  2.0 < 3              # => true
  2.0 < 3.0            # => true
  2.0 < Rational(3, 1) # => true
  2.0 < 2.0            # => false

<tt>Float::NAN < Float::NAN</tt> returns an implementation-dependent value.

Float#<=.comment:
Returns whether the value of <tt>self</tt> is less than or equal to the value
of <tt>other</tt>; <tt>other</tt> must be numeric, but may not be Complex:

  2.0 <= 3              # => true
  2.0 <= 3.0            # => true
  2.0 <= Rational(3, 1) # => true
  2.0 <= 2.0            # => true
  2.0 <= 1.0            # => false

<tt>Float::NAN <= Float::NAN</tt> returns an implementation-dependent value.

Float#<=>.comment:
Compares <tt>self</tt> and <tt>other</tt>.

Returns:

* <tt>-1</tt>, if <tt>self</tt> is less than <tt>other</tt>.
* <tt>0</tt>, if <tt>self</tt> is equal to <tt>other</tt>.
* <tt>1</tt>, if <tt>self</tt> is greater than <tt>other</tt>.
* <tt>nil</tt>, if the two values are incommensurate.

Examples:

  2.0 <=> 2.1            # => -1
  2.0 <=> 2              # => 0
  2.0 <=> 2.0            # => 0
  2.0 <=> Rational(2, 1) # => 0
  2.0 <=> Complex(2, 0)  # => 0
  2.0 <=> 1.9            # => 1
  2.0 <=> 'foo'          # => nil

<tt>Float::NAN <=> Float::NAN</tt> returns an implementation-dependent value.

Class Float includes module Comparable, each of whose methods uses Float#<=>
for comparison.

Float#==.comment:
Returns whether <tt>other</tt> is numerically equal to <tt>self</tt>:

  2.0 == 2              # => true
  2.0 == 2.0            # => true
  2.0 == Rational(2, 1) # => true
  2.0 == Complex(2, 0)  # => true

<tt>Float::NAN == Float::NAN</tt> returns an implementation-dependent value.

Related: Float#eql? (requires <tt>other</tt> to be a Float).

Float#===.comment:
Returns whether <tt>other</tt> is numerically equal to <tt>self</tt>:

  2.0 == 2              # => true
  2.0 == 2.0            # => true
  2.0 == Rational(2, 1) # => true
  2.0 == Complex(2, 0)  # => true

<tt>Float::NAN == Float::NAN</tt> returns an implementation-dependent value.

Related: Float#eql? (requires <tt>other</tt> to be a Float).

Float#>.comment:
Returns whether the value of <tt>self</tt> is greater than the value of
<tt>other</tt>; <tt>other</tt> must be numeric, but may not be Complex:

  2.0 > 1              # => true
  2.0 > 1.0            # => true
  2.0 > Rational(1, 2) # => true
  2.0 > 2.0            # => false

<tt>Float::NAN > Float::NAN</tt> returns an implementation-dependent value.

Float#>=.comment:
Returns whether the value of <tt>self</tt> is greater than or equal to the
value of <tt>other</tt>; <tt>other</tt> must be numeric, but may not be
Complex:

  2.0 >= 1              # => true
  2.0 >= 1.0            # => true
  2.0 >= Rational(1, 2) # => true
  2.0 >= 2.0            # => true
  2.0 >= 2.1            # => false

<tt>Float::NAN >= Float::NAN</tt> returns an implementation-dependent value.

Float#angle.name: angle
Float#angle.comment: Returns 0 if <tt>self</tt> is positive, Math::PI otherwise.

Float#arg.name: arg
Float#arg.comment: Returns 0 if <tt>self</tt> is positive, Math::PI otherwise.

Float#ceil.name: ceil
Float#ceil.comment:
Returns a numeric that is a "ceiling" value for <tt>self</tt>,
as specified by the given <tt>ndigits</tt>,
which must be an
{integer-convertible
object}[rdoc-ref:implicit_conversion.rdoc@Integer-Convertible+Objects].
When <tt>ndigits</tt> is positive, returns a Float with <tt>ndigits</tt>
decimal digits after the decimal point
(as available, but no fewer than 1):
  f = 12345.6789
f.ceil(1) # => 12345.7
f.ceil(3) # => 12345.679
f.ceil(30) # => 12345.6789
f = -12345.6789
f.ceil(1) # => -12345.6
f.ceil(3) # => -12345.678
f.ceil(30) # => -12345.6789
f = 0.0
f.ceil(1)   # => 0.0
f.ceil(100) # => 0.0

When <tt>ndigits</tt> is non-positive,
returns an Integer based on a computed granularity:
* The granularity is <tt>10 ** ndigits.abs</tt>.
* The returned value is the smallest multiple of the granularity
   that is greater than or equal to <tt>self</tt>.
Examples with positive <tt>self</tt>:
ndigits|Granularity|12345.6789.ceil(ndigits)
-------|-----------|------------------------
      0|          1|                   12346
     -1|         10|                   12350
     -2|        100|                   12400
     -3|       1000|                   13000
     -4|      10000|                   20000
     -5|     100000|                  100000
Examples with negative <tt>self</tt>:
ndigits|Granularity|-12345.6789.ceil(ndigits)
-------|-----------|-------------------------
      0|          1|                   -12345
     -1|         10|                   -12340
     -2|        100|                   -12300
     -3|       1000|                   -12000
     -4|      10000|                   -10000
     -5|     100000|                        0
When <tt>self</tt> is zero and <tt>ndigits</tt> is non-positive,
returns Integer zero:
  0.0.ceil(0)  # => 0
0.0.ceil(-1) # => 0
0.0.ceil(-2) # => 0

Note that the limited precision of floating-point arithmetic
may lead to surprising results:
  (2.1 / 0.7).ceil  #=> 4 # Not 3 (because 2.1 / 0.7 # => 3.0000000000000004, not 3.0)

Related: Float#floor.

Float#coerce.name: coerce
Float#coerce.comment:
Returns a 2-element array containing <tt>other</tt> converted to a Float and
<tt>self</tt>:

  f = 3.14                 # => 3.14
  f.coerce(2)              # => [2.0, 3.14]
  f.coerce(2.0)            # => [2.0, 3.14]
  f.coerce(Rational(1, 2)) # => [0.5, 3.14]
  f.coerce(Complex(1, 0))  # => [1.0, 3.14]

Raises an exception if a type conversion fails.

Float#denominator.name: denominator
Float#denominator.comment:
Returns the denominator (always positive).  The result is machine dependent.

See also Float#numerator.

Float#divmod.name: divmod
Float#divmod.comment:
Returns a 2-element array <tt>[q, r]</tt>, where

  q = (self/other).floor      # Quotient
  r = self % other            # Remainder

Examples:

  11.0.divmod(4)              # => [2, 3.0]
  11.0.divmod(-4)             # => [-3, -1.0]
  -11.0.divmod(4)             # => [-3, 1.0]
  -11.0.divmod(-4)            # => [2, -3.0]

  12.0.divmod(4)              # => [3, 0.0]
  12.0.divmod(-4)             # => [-3, 0.0]
  -12.0.divmod(4)             # => [-3, -0.0]
  -12.0.divmod(-4)            # => [3, -0.0]

  13.0.divmod(4.0)            # => [3, 1.0]
  13.0.divmod(Rational(4, 1)) # => [3, 1.0]

Float#eql?.name: eql?
Float#eql?.comment:
Returns <tt>true</tt> if <tt>other</tt> is a Float with the same value as
<tt>self</tt>, <tt>false</tt> otherwise:

  2.0.eql?(2.0)            # => true
  2.0.eql?(1.0)            # => false
  2.0.eql?(1)              # => false
  2.0.eql?(Rational(2, 1)) # => false
  2.0.eql?(Complex(2, 0))  # => false

<tt>Float::NAN.eql?(Float::NAN)</tt> returns an implementation-dependent
value.

Related: Float#== (performs type conversions).

Float#fdiv.name: fdiv
Float#fdiv.comment:
Returns the quotient from dividing <tt>self</tt> by <tt>other</tt>:

  f = 3.14
  f.quo(2)              # => 1.57
  f.quo(-2)             # => -1.57
  f.quo(Rational(2, 1)) # => 1.57
  f.quo(Complex(2, 0))  # => (1.57+0.0i)

Float#finite?.name: finite?
Float#finite?.comment:
Returns <tt>true</tt> if <tt>self</tt> is not <tt>Infinity</tt>,
<tt>-Infinity</tt>, or <tt>NaN</tt>, <tt>false</tt> otherwise:

  f = 2.0      # => 2.0
  f.finite?    # => true
  f = 1.0/0.0  # => Infinity
  f.finite?    # => false
  f = -1.0/0.0 # => -Infinity
  f.finite?    # => false
  f = 0.0/0.0  # => NaN
  f.finite?    # => false

Float#floor.name: floor
Float#floor.comment:
Returns a float or integer that is a "floor" value for <tt>self</tt>,
as specified by <tt>ndigits</tt>,
which must be an
{integer-convertible
object}[rdoc-ref:implicit_conversion.rdoc@Integer-Convertible+Objects].
When <tt>self</tt> is zero,
returns a zero value:
a float if <tt>ndigits</tt> is positive,
an integer otherwise:
  f = 0.0      # => 0.0
f.floor(20)  # => 0.0
f.floor(0)   # => 0
f.floor(-20) # => 0

When <tt>self</tt> is non-zero and <tt>ndigits</tt> is positive, returns a
float with <tt>ndigits</tt>
digits after the decimal point (as available):
  f = 12345.6789
f.floor(1)  # => 12345.6
f.floor(3)  # => 12345.678
f.floor(30) # => 12345.6789
f = -12345.6789
f.floor(1)  # => -12345.7
f.floor(3)  # => -12345.679
f.floor(30) # => -12345.6789

When <tt>self</tt> is non-zero and <tt>ndigits</tt> is non-positive,
returns an integer value based on a computed granularity:
* The granularity is <tt>10 ** ndigits.abs</tt>.
* The returned value is the largest multiple of the granularity
   that is less than or equal to <tt>self</tt>.
Examples with positive <tt>self</tt>:
ndigits|Granularity|12345.6789.floor(ndigits)
-------|-----------|-------------------------
      0|          1|                    12345
     -1|         10|                    12340
     -2|        100|                    12300
     -3|       1000|                    12000
     -4|      10000|                    10000
     -5|     100000|                        0
Examples with negative <tt>self</tt>:
ndigits|Granularity|-12345.6789.floor(ndigits)
-------|-----------|--------------------------
      0|          1|                    -12346
     -1|         10|                    -12350
     -2|        100|                    -12400
     -3|       1000|                    -13000
     -4|      10000|                    -20000
     -5|     100000|                   -100000
     -6|    1000000|                  -1000000
Note that the limited precision of floating-point arithmetic
may lead to surprising results:
  (0.3 / 0.1).floor  # => 2 # Not 3, (because (0.3 / 0.1) # => 2.9999999999999996, not 3.0)

Related: Float#ceil.

Float#hash.name: hash
Float#hash.comment:
Returns the integer hash value for <tt>self</tt>.

See also Object#hash.

Float#infinite?.name: infinite?
Float#infinite?.comment:
Returns:

* 1, if <tt>self</tt> is <tt>Infinity</tt>.
* -1 if <tt>self</tt> is <tt>-Infinity</tt>.
* <tt>nil</tt>, otherwise.

Examples:

  f = 1.0/0.0  # => Infinity
  f.infinite?  # => 1
  f = -1.0/0.0 # => -Infinity
  f.infinite?  # => -1
  f = 1.0      # => 1.0
  f.infinite?  # => nil
  f = 0.0/0.0  # => NaN
  f.infinite?  # => nil

Float#inspect.name: inspect
Float#inspect.comment:
Returns a string containing a representation of <tt>self</tt>; depending of
the value of <tt>self</tt>, the string representation may contain:

* A fixed-point number.
    3.14.to_s         # => "3.14"

* A number in "scientific notation" (containing an exponent).
    (10.1**50).to_s   # => "1.644631821843879e+50"

* 'Infinity'.
    (10.1**500).to_s  # => "Infinity"

* '-Infinity'.
    (-10.1**500).to_s # => "-Infinity"

* 'NaN' (indicating not-a-number).
    (0.0/0.0).to_s    # => "NaN"

Float#modulo.name: modulo
Float#modulo.comment:
Returns <tt>self</tt> modulo <tt>other</tt> as a Float.

For float <tt>f</tt> and real number <tt>r</tt>, these expressions are
equivalent:

  f % r
  f-r*(f/r).floor
  f.divmod(r)[1]

See Numeric#divmod.

Examples:

  10.0 % 2              # => 0.0
  10.0 % 3              # => 1.0
  10.0 % 4              # => 2.0

  10.0 % -2             # => 0.0
  10.0 % -3             # => -2.0
  10.0 % -4             # => -2.0

  10.0 % 4.0            # => 2.0
  10.0 % Rational(4, 1) # => 2.0

Float#nan?.name: nan?
Float#nan?.comment:
Returns <tt>true</tt> if <tt>self</tt> is a NaN, <tt>false</tt> otherwise.

  f = -1.0     #=> -1.0
  f.nan?       #=> false
  f = 0.0/0.0  #=> NaN
  f.nan?       #=> true

Float#negative?.name: negative?
Float#negative?.comment:
Returns <tt>true</tt> if <tt>self</tt> is less than 0, <tt>false</tt>
otherwise.

Float#next_float.name: next_float
Float#next_float.comment:
Returns the next-larger representable Float.

These examples show the internally stored values (64-bit hexadecimal) for each
Float <tt>f</tt> and for the corresponding <tt>f.next_float</tt>:

  f = 0.0      # 0x0000000000000000
  f.next_float # 0x0000000000000001

  f = 0.01     # 0x3f847ae147ae147b
  f.next_float # 0x3f847ae147ae147c

In the remaining examples here, the output is shown in the usual way (result
<tt>to_s</tt>):

  0.01.next_float    # => 0.010000000000000002
  1.0.next_float     # => 1.0000000000000002
  100.0.next_float   # => 100.00000000000001

  f = 0.01
  (0..3).each_with_index {|i| printf "%2d %-20a %s\n", i, f, f.to_s; f = f.next_float }

Output:

   0 0x1.47ae147ae147bp-7 0.01
   1 0x1.47ae147ae147cp-7 0.010000000000000002
   2 0x1.47ae147ae147dp-7 0.010000000000000004
   3 0x1.47ae147ae147ep-7 0.010000000000000005

  f = 0.0; 100.times { f += 0.1 }
  f                           # => 9.99999999999998       # should be 10.0 in the ideal world.
  10-f                        # => 1.9539925233402755e-14 # the floating point error.
  10.0.next_float-10          # => 1.7763568394002505e-15 # 1 ulp (unit in the last place).
  (10-f)/(10.0.next_float-10) # => 11.0                   # the error is 11 ulp.
  (10-f)/(10*Float::EPSILON)  # => 8.8                    # approximation of the above.
  "%a" % 10                   # => "0x1.4p+3"
  "%a" % f                    # => "0x1.3fffffffffff5p+3" # the last hex digit is 5.  16 - 5 = 11 ulp.

Related: Float#prev_float

Float#numerator.name: numerator
Float#numerator.comment:
Returns the numerator.  The result is machine dependent.

  n = 0.3.numerator    #=> 5404319552844595
  d = 0.3.denominator  #=> 18014398509481984
  n.fdiv(d)            #=> 0.3

See also Float#denominator.

Float#phase.name: phase
Float#phase.comment: Returns 0 if <tt>self</tt> is positive, Math::PI otherwise.

Float#positive?.name: positive?
Float#positive?.comment:
Returns <tt>true</tt> if <tt>self</tt> is greater than 0, <tt>false</tt>
otherwise.

Float#prev_float.name: prev_float
Float#prev_float.comment:
Returns the next-smaller representable Float.

These examples show the internally stored values (64-bit hexadecimal) for each
Float <tt>f</tt> and for the corresponding <tt>f.pev_float</tt>:

  f = 5e-324   # 0x0000000000000001
  f.prev_float # 0x0000000000000000

  f = 0.01     # 0x3f847ae147ae147b
  f.prev_float # 0x3f847ae147ae147a

In the remaining examples here, the output is shown in the usual way (result
<tt>to_s</tt>):

  0.01.prev_float   # => 0.009999999999999998
  1.0.prev_float    # => 0.9999999999999999
  100.0.prev_float  # => 99.99999999999999

  f = 0.01
  (0..3).each_with_index {|i| printf "%2d %-20a %s\n", i, f, f.to_s; f = f.prev_float }

Output:

  0 0x1.47ae147ae147bp-7 0.01
  1 0x1.47ae147ae147ap-7 0.009999999999999998
  2 0x1.47ae147ae1479p-7 0.009999999999999997
  3 0x1.47ae147ae1478p-7 0.009999999999999995

Related: Float#next_float.

Float#quo.name: quo
Float#quo.comment:
Returns the quotient from dividing <tt>self</tt> by <tt>other</tt>:

  f = 3.14
  f.quo(2)              # => 1.57
  f.quo(-2)             # => -1.57
  f.quo(Rational(2, 1)) # => 1.57
  f.quo(Complex(2, 0))  # => (1.57+0.0i)

Float#rationalize.name: rationalize
Float#rationalize.comment:
Returns a simpler approximation of the value (flt-|eps| <= result <=
flt+|eps|).  If the optional argument <tt>eps</tt> is not given, it will be
chosen automatically.

  0.3.rationalize          #=> (3/10)
  1.333.rationalize        #=> (1333/1000)
  1.333.rationalize(0.01)  #=> (4/3)

See also Float#to_r.

Float#round.name: round
Float#round.comment:
Returns <tt>self</tt> rounded to the nearest value with a precision of
<tt>ndigits</tt> decimal digits.

When <tt>ndigits</tt> is non-negative, returns a float with <tt>ndigits</tt>
after the decimal point (as available):

  f = 12345.6789
  f.round(1) # => 12345.7
  f.round(3) # => 12345.679
  f = -12345.6789
  f.round(1) # => -12345.7
  f.round(3) # => -12345.679

When <tt>ndigits</tt> is negative, returns an integer with at least
<tt>ndigits.abs</tt> trailing zeros:

  f = 12345.6789
  f.round(0)  # => 12346
  f.round(-3) # => 12000
  f = -12345.6789
  f.round(0)  # => -12346
  f.round(-3) # => -12000

If keyword argument <tt>half</tt> is given, and <tt>self</tt> is equidistant
from the two candidate values, the rounding is according to the given
<tt>half</tt> value:

* <tt>:up</tt> or <tt>nil</tt>: round away from zero:

    2.5.round(half: :up)      # => 3
    3.5.round(half: :up)      # => 4
    (-2.5).round(half: :up)   # => -3

* <tt>:down</tt>: round toward zero:

    2.5.round(half: :down)    # => 2
    3.5.round(half: :down)    # => 3
    (-2.5).round(half: :down) # => -2

* <tt>:even</tt>: round toward the candidate whose last nonzero digit is even:

    2.5.round(half: :even)    # => 2
    3.5.round(half: :even)    # => 4
    (-2.5).round(half: :even) # => -2

Raises and exception if the value for <tt>half</tt> is invalid.

Related: Float#truncate.

Float#to_i.name: to_i
Float#to_i.comment:
Returns <tt>self</tt> truncated to an Integer.

  1.2.to_i    # => 1
  (-1.2).to_i # => -1

Note that the limited precision of floating-point arithmetic may lead to
surprising results:

  (0.3 / 0.1).to_i  # => 2 (!)

Float#to_int.name: to_int
Float#to_int.comment:
Returns <tt>self</tt> truncated to an Integer.

  1.2.to_i    # => 1
  (-1.2).to_i # => -1

Note that the limited precision of floating-point arithmetic may lead to
surprising results:

  (0.3 / 0.1).to_i  # => 2 (!)

Float#to_r.name: to_r
Float#to_r.comment:
Returns the value as a rational.

  2.0.to_r    #=> (2/1)
  2.5.to_r    #=> (5/2)
  -0.75.to_r  #=> (-3/4)
  0.0.to_r    #=> (0/1)
  0.3.to_r    #=> (5404319552844595/18014398509481984)

NOTE: 0.3.to_r isn't the same as "0.3".to_r.  The latter is equivalent to
"3/10".to_r, but the former isn't so.

  0.3.to_r   == 3/10r  #=> false
  "0.3".to_r == 3/10r  #=> true

See also Float#rationalize.

Float#to_s.name: to_s
Float#to_s.comment:
Returns a string containing a representation of <tt>self</tt>; depending of
the value of <tt>self</tt>, the string representation may contain:

* A fixed-point number.
    3.14.to_s         # => "3.14"

* A number in "scientific notation" (containing an exponent).
    (10.1**50).to_s   # => "1.644631821843879e+50"

* 'Infinity'.
    (10.1**500).to_s  # => "Infinity"

* '-Infinity'.
    (-10.1**500).to_s # => "-Infinity"

* 'NaN' (indicating not-a-number).
    (0.0/0.0).to_s    # => "NaN"

Float#truncate.name: truncate
Float#truncate.comment:
Returns <tt>self</tt> truncated (toward zero) to a precision of
<tt>ndigits</tt> decimal digits.

When <tt>ndigits</tt> is positive, returns a float with <tt>ndigits</tt>
digits after the decimal point (as available):

  f = 12345.6789
  f.truncate(1) # => 12345.6
  f.truncate(3) # => 12345.678
  f = -12345.6789
  f.truncate(1) # => -12345.6
  f.truncate(3) # => -12345.678

When <tt>ndigits</tt> is negative, returns an integer with at least
<tt>ndigits.abs</tt> trailing zeros:

  f = 12345.6789
  f.truncate(0)  # => 12345
  f.truncate(-3) # => 12000
  f = -12345.6789
  f.truncate(0)  # => -12345
  f.truncate(-3) # => -12000

Note that the limited precision of floating-point arithmetic may lead to
surprising results:

  (0.3 / 0.1).truncate  #=> 2 (!)

Related: Float#round.

FloatDomainError.name: FloatDomainError
FloatDomainError.comment:
Raised when attempting to convert special float values (in particular
<tt>Infinity</tt> or <tt>NaN</tt>) to numerical classes which don't support
them.

  Float::INFINITY.to_r   #=> FloatDomainError: Infinity

Forwardable.name: Forwardable
Forwardable.comment:
The Forwardable module provides delegation of specified methods to a
designated object, using the methods #def_delegator and #def_delegators.

For example, say you have a class RecordCollection which contains an array
<tt>@records</tt>.  You could provide the lookup method #record_number(),
which simply calls #[] on the <tt>@records</tt> array, like this:

  require 'forwardable'

  class RecordCollection
    attr_accessor :records
    extend Forwardable
    def_delegator :@records, :[], :record_number
  end

We can use the lookup method like so:

  r = RecordCollection.new
  r.records = [4,5,6]
  r.record_number(0)  # => 4

Further, if you wish to provide the methods #size, #<<, and #map, all of which
delegate to @records, this is how you can do it:

  class RecordCollection # re-open RecordCollection class
    def_delegators :@records, :size, :<<, :map
  end

  r = RecordCollection.new
  r.records = [1,2,3]
  r.record_number(0)   # => 1
  r.size               # => 3
  r << 4               # => [1, 2, 3, 4]
  r.map { |x| x * 2 }  # => [2, 4, 6, 8]

You can even extend regular objects with Forwardable.

  my_hash = Hash.new
  my_hash.extend Forwardable              # prepare object for delegation
  my_hash.def_delegator "STDOUT", "puts"  # add delegation for STDOUT.puts()
  my_hash.puts "Howdy!"

== Another example

You could use Forwardable as an alternative to inheritance, when you don't
want to inherit all methods from the superclass. For instance, here is how you
might add a range of <tt>Array</tt> instance methods to a new class
<tt>Queue</tt>:

  class Queue
    extend Forwardable

    def initialize
      @q = [ ]    # prepare delegate object
    end

    # setup preferred interface, enq() and deq()...
    def_delegator :@q, :push, :enq
    def_delegator :@q, :shift, :deq

    # support some general Array methods that fit Queues well
    def_delegators :@q, :clear, :first, :push, :shift, :size
  end

  q = Thread::Queue.new
  q.enq 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
  q.push 6

  q.shift    # => 1
  while q.size > 0
    puts q.deq
  end

  q.enq "Ruby", "Perl", "Python"
  puts q.first
  q.clear
  puts q.first

This should output:

  2
  3
  4
  5
  6
  Ruby
  nil

== Notes

Be advised, RDoc will not detect delegated methods.

<tt>forwardable.rb</tt> provides single-method delegation via the
def_delegator and def_delegators methods. For full-class delegation via
DelegateClass, see <tt>delegate.rb</tt>.

Forwardable#def_instance_delegator.name: def_instance_delegator
Forwardable#def_instance_delegator.comment:
Define <tt>method</tt> as delegator instance method with an optional alias
name <tt>ali</tt>. Method calls to <tt>ali</tt> will be delegated to
<tt>accessor.method</tt>.  <tt>accessor</tt> should be a method name, instance
variable name, or constant name.  Use the full path to the constant if
providing the constant name. Returns the name of the method defined.

  class MyQueue
    CONST = 1
    extend Forwardable
    attr_reader :queue
    def initialize
      @queue = []
    end

    def_delegator :@queue, :push, :mypush
    def_delegator 'MyQueue::CONST', :to_i
  end

  q = MyQueue.new
  q.mypush 42
  q.queue    #=> [42]
  q.push 23  #=> NoMethodError
  q.to_i     #=> 1

Forwardable#def_instance_delegators.name: def_instance_delegators
Forwardable#def_instance_delegators.comment:
Shortcut for defining multiple delegator methods, but with no provision for
using a different name.  The following two code samples have the same effect:

  def_delegators :@records, :size, :<<, :map

  def_delegator :@records, :size
  def_delegator :@records, :<<
  def_delegator :@records, :map

Forwardable#instance_delegate.name: instance_delegate
Forwardable#instance_delegate.comment:
Takes a hash as its argument.  The key is a symbol or an array of symbols.
These symbols correspond to method names, instance variable names, or constant
names (see def_delegator).  The value is the accessor to which the methods
will be delegated.

FrozenError.name: FrozenError
FrozenError.comment: Raised when there is an attempt to modify a frozen object. [1, 2, 3].freeze << 4 raises the exception: FrozenError: can't modify frozen Array

FrozenError::new.name: new
FrozenError::new.comment: Construct a new FrozenError exception. If given the receiver parameter may subsequently be examined using the FrozenError#receiver method. a = [].freeze raise FrozenError.new("can't modify frozen array", receiver: a)

FrozenError#receiver.name: receiver
FrozenError#receiver.comment: Return the receiver associated with this FrozenError exception.

GC.name: GC
GC.comment:
The GC module provides an interface to Ruby's mark-and-sweep garbage
collection mechanism.

Some of the underlying methods are also available via the ObjectSpace module.

You may obtain information about the operation of the GC through GC::Profiler.

GC::add_stress_to_class.name: add_stress_to_class
GC::add_stress_to_class.comment: Raises NoMemoryError when allocating an instance of the given classes.

GC::auto_compact.name: auto_compact
GC::auto_compact.comment: Returns whether or not automatic compaction has been enabled.

GC::auto_compact=.name: auto_compact=
GC::auto_compact=.comment:
Updates automatic compaction mode.

When enabled, the compactor will execute on every major collection.

Enabling compaction will degrade performance on major collections.

GC::compact.name: compact
GC::compact.comment:
This function compacts objects together in Ruby's heap. It eliminates unused
space (or fragmentation) in the heap by moving objects in to that unused
space. If there is more than 1 running Ractor, it runs a global GC compaction
(all object spaces).

The returned <tt>hash</tt> contains statistics about the objects that were
moved; see GC.latest_compact_info.

This method is only expected to work on CRuby.

To test whether GC compaction is supported, use the idiom:

  GC.respond_to?(:compact)

GC::config.name: config
GC::config.comment: This method is implementation-specific to CRuby. Sets or gets information about the current GC configuration. Configuration parameters are GC implementation-specific and may change without notice. With no argument given, returns a hash containing the configuration: GC.config # => {rgengc_allow_full_mark: true, implementation: "default"} With argument hash_to_merge given, merges that hash into the stored configuration hash; ignores unknown hash keys; returns the configuration hash: GC.config(rgengc_allow_full_mark: false) # => {rgengc_allow_full_mark: false, implementation: "default"} GC.config(foo: 'bar') # => {rgengc_allow_full_mark: false, implementation: "default"} All-Implementations Configuration The single read-only entry for all implementations is: * :implementation: the string name of the implementation; for the Ruby default implementation, 'default'. Implementation-Specific Configuration A GC implementation maintains its own implementation-specific configuration. For Ruby's default implementation the single entry is: * :rgengc_allow_full_mark: Controls whether the GC is allowed to run a full mark (young & old objects): * true (default): GC interleaves major and minor collections. A flag is set to notify GC that a full mark has been requested. This flag is accessible via GC.latest_gc_info(:need_major_by). * false: GC does not initiate a full marking cycle unless explicitly directed by user code; see GC.start. Setting this parameter to false disables young-to-old promotion. For performance reasons, we recommended warming up the application using Process.warmup before setting this parameter to false.

GC::count.name: count
GC::count.comment:
Returns the total number of times garbage collection has occurred:

With the default GC, counts the current Ractor's collections.

  GC.count # => 385
  GC.start
  GC.count # => 386

GC::disable.name: disable
GC::disable.comment:
Disables garbage collection (but GC.start remains potent): returns whether
garbage collection was already disabled.

  GC.enable
  GC.disable # => false
  GC.disable # => true

GC::enable.name: enable
GC::enable.comment:
Enables garbage collection; returns whether garbage collection was disabled:

  GC.disable
  GC.enable # => true
  GC.enable # => false

GC::latest_compact_info.name: latest_compact_info
GC::latest_compact_info.comment:
Returns information about object moved in the most recent GC compaction.

The returned <tt>hash</tt> contains the following keys:

considered:
  Hash containing the type of the object as the key and the number of objects
  of that type that were considered for movement.

moved:
  Hash containing the type of the object as the key and the number of objects
  of that type that were actually moved.

moved_up:
  Hash containing the type of the object as the key and the number of objects
  of that type that were increased in size.

moved_down:
  Hash containing the type of the object as the key and the number of objects
  of that type that were decreased in size.

Some objects can't be moved (due to pinning) so these numbers can be used to
calculate compaction efficiency.

GC::latest_gc_info.name: latest_gc_info
GC::latest_gc_info.call_seq:
GC.latest_gc_info -> new_hash
GC.latest_gc_info(key) -> value
GC.latest_gc_info(hash) -> hash
GC::latest_gc_info.comment:
With no argument given, returns information about the most recent garbage
collection:

  GC.latest_gc_info
  # =>
  {major_by: :force,
   need_major_by: nil,
   gc_by: :method,
   have_finalizer: false,
   immediate_sweep: true,
   state: :none,
   weak_references_count: 0,
   retained_weak_references_count: 0}

With symbol argument <tt>key</tt> given, returns the value for that key:

  GC.latest_gc_info(:gc_by) # => :newobj

With hash argument <tt>hash</tt> given, returns that hash with GC information
merged into its content; this form may be useful in minimizing {probe
effects}[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probe_effect]:

  h = {foo: 0, bar: 1}
  GC.latest_gc_info(h)
  # =>
  {foo: 0,
   bar: 1,
   major_by: nil,
   need_major_by: nil,
   gc_by: :newobj,
   have_finalizer: false,
   immediate_sweep: false,
   state: :sweeping,
   weak_references_count: 0,
   retained_weak_references_count: 0}

GC::malloc_allocated_size.name: malloc_allocated_size
GC::malloc_allocated_size.comment:
Returns the size of memory allocated by malloc().

Only available if ruby was built with <tt>CALC_EXACT_MALLOC_SIZE</tt>.

GC::malloc_allocations.name: malloc_allocations
GC::malloc_allocations.comment:
Returns the number of malloc() allocations.

Only available if ruby was built with <tt>CALC_EXACT_MALLOC_SIZE</tt>.

GC::measure_total_time.name: measure_total_time
GC::measure_total_time.comment:
Returns the setting for GC total time measurement in the current Ractor; the
main Ractor's initial setting is <tt>true</tt> and, with the default GC, other
Ractors inherit their creator's setting. See GC.total_time.

GC::measure_total_time=.name: measure_total_time=
GC::measure_total_time=.comment:
Enables or disables GC total time measurement; returns <tt>setting</tt>. See
GC.total_time.

When argument <tt>object</tt> is <tt>nil</tt> or <tt>false</tt>, disables
total time measurement; GC.measure_total_time then returns <tt>false</tt>:

  GC.measure_total_time = nil   # => nil
  GC.measure_total_time         # => false
  GC.measure_total_time = false # => false
  GC.measure_total_time         # => false

Otherwise, enables total time measurement; GC.measure_total_time then returns
<tt>true</tt>:

  GC.measure_total_time = true # => true
  GC.measure_total_time        # => true
  GC.measure_total_time = :foo # => :foo
  GC.measure_total_time        # => true

Note that when enabled, total time measurement affects performance.

The setting is per-Ractor: it affects only the Ractor that sets it. With the
default GC, a Ractor created by Ractor.new inherits the setting of the Ractor
that creates it; the main Ractor starts with measurement enabled.

GC::remove_stress_to_class.name: remove_stress_to_class
GC::remove_stress_to_class.comment:
No longer raises NoMemoryError when allocating an instance of the given
classes.

GC::start.name: start
GC::start.params: (full_mark: true, immediate_mark: true, immediate_sweep: true, global: true)
GC::start.comment:
Initiates garbage collection, even if explicitly disabled by GC.disable.

Keyword arguments:

* <tt>full_mark</tt>: a boolean value specifying whether to perform a major
  garbage collection cycle:

  * <tt>true</tt>: initiates a major garbage collection cycle, meaning all
    objects (old and new) are marked. When another Ractor's object space
    exists (a live Ractor, or a terminated one not yet absorbed), or one was
    absorbed since the last global collection, and <tt>global</tt> is
    <tt>true</tt> (the default), the cycle is a global collection instead; see
    <tt>global</tt>.
  * <tt>false</tt>: initiates a minor garbage collection cycle, meaning only
    young objects are marked.

* <tt>immediate_mark</tt>: a boolean value specifying whether marking is
  performed incrementally:

  * <tt>true</tt>: marking is completed before the method returns.
  * <tt>false</tt>: marking is performed in parts, interleaved with program
    execution both before the method returns and afterward; therefore marking
    may not be completed before the return. Note that if <tt>full_mark</tt> is
    <tt>false</tt>, marking is always immediate, regardless of the value of
    <tt>immediate_mark</tt>.

* <tt>immediate_sweep</tt>: a boolean value specifying whether sweeping is
  deferred (lazy sweep):

  * <tt>true</tt>: sweeping is completed before the method returns.
  * <tt>false</tt>: sweeping is performed in parts, interleaved with program
    execution both before the method returns and afterward; therefore sweeping
    may not be completed before the return.

* <tt>global</tt>: a boolean value specifying, when another Ractor's object
  space exists, whether to collect every Ractor's heap together in a single
  stop-the-world mark/sweep cycle:

  * <tt>true</tt>: with another Ractor's object space present (see
    <tt>full_mark</tt>) it runs a stop-the-world cycle and reclaims shareable
    and cross-Ractor garbage. This option, although it defaults to
    <tt>true</tt>, is ignored unless <tt>full_mark</tt>,
    <tt>immediate_mark</tt> and <tt>immediate_sweep</tt> are all
    <tt>true</tt>. With a single object space it has no effect and the other
    options apply as usual. This option is also ignored unless you're using
    the default GC.
  * <tt>false</tt>: collect only the calling Ractor's own objects. Shareable
    objects and cross-ractor garbage are not swept.

  GC.stat counts a local major collection under <tt>:major_gc_count</tt>, a
  local minor collection under <tt>:minor_gc_count</tt>, and a global
  collection under <tt>:global_gc_count</tt> for the calling Ractor.

Note that these keyword arguments are implementation- and version-dependent,
are not guaranteed to be future-compatible, and may be ignored in some
implementations.

GC::stat.name: stat
GC::stat.call_seq:
GC.stat(scope: :ractor) -> new_hash
GC.stat(key, scope: :ractor) -> value
GC.stat(hash, scope: :ractor) -> hash
GC::stat.comment:
This method is implementation-specific to CRuby.

Returns GC statistics. The particular statistics are implementation-specific
and may change in the future without notice.

With <tt>scope: :ractor</tt> (the default) or <tt>scope: :local</tt>, returns
statistics for the current Ractor's object space. With <tt>scope:
:global</tt>, returns cumulative collection counts and measured GC time across
all Ractors.

With no positional argument or <tt>nil</tt> given, returns a hash containing
the GC statistics:

  GC.stat
  # =>
  {count: 1,
   time: 0,
   marking_time: 0,
   sweeping_time: 0,
   total_malloc_bytes: 10432791,
   total_free_bytes: 6989873,
   heap_allocated_pages: 41,
   heap_empty_pages: 0,
   heap_allocatable_bytes: 228656,
   heap_eden_pages: 41,
   total_allocated_pages: 41,
   total_freed_pages: 0,
   malloc_increase_bytes: 0,
   malloc_increase_bytes_limit: 16777216,
   minor_gc_count: 0,
   major_gc_count: 1,
   global_gc_count: 0,
   compact_count: 0,
   read_barrier_faults: 0,
   total_moved_objects: 0,
   remembered_wb_unprotected_objects: 0,
   remembered_wb_unprotected_objects_limit: 7,
   old_objects: 721,
   old_objects_limit: 1442,
   oldmalloc_increase_bytes: 0,
   oldmalloc_increase_bytes_limit: 16777216,
   total_allocated_objects: 36735,
   total_freed_objects: 19527,
   heap_available_slots: 40591,
   heap_live_slots: 17208,
   heap_free_slots: 23383,
   heap_final_slots: 0,
   heap_marked_slots: 17175}

With symbol argument <tt>key</tt> given, returns the value for that key:

  GC.stat(:count) # => 30

With hash argument <tt>hash</tt> given, returns that hash with GC statistics
merged into its content; this form may be useful in minimizing {probe
effects}[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probe_effect]:

  h = {foo: 0, bar: 1}
  GC.stat(h)
  h.keys.take(5) # => [:foo, :bar, :count, :time, :marking_time]

The hash includes entries such as:

* <tt>:count</tt>: The total number of garbage collections run since
  application start (the count includes minor, major, and global garbage
  collections).
* <tt>:time</tt>: The total time spent in garbage collections (in
  milliseconds).
* <tt>:marking_time</tt>: The total time spent marking objects (in
  milliseconds).
* <tt>:sweeping_time</tt>: The total time spent sweeping objects (in
  milliseconds).
* <tt>:total_malloc_bytes</tt>: The total number of bytes allocated by malloc
  since application start.
* <tt>:total_free_bytes</tt>: The total number of bytes freed since
  application start.
* <tt>:heap_allocated_pages</tt>: The total number of allocated pages.
* <tt>:heap_empty_pages</tt>: The number of pages with no live objects, and
  that could be released to the system.
* <tt>:heap_allocatable_bytes</tt>: The number of bytes that can be allocated
  without triggering a new garbage collection cycle.
* <tt>:heap_eden_pages</tt>: The total number of pages which contain at least
  one live slot.
* <tt>:total_allocated_pages</tt>: The cumulative number of pages allocated
  since application start.
* <tt>:total_freed_pages</tt>: The cumulative number of pages freed since
  application start.
* <tt>:malloc_increase_bytes</tt>: Amount of memory allocated on the heap for
  objects. Decreased by any GC.
* <tt>:malloc_increase_bytes_limit</tt>: When <tt>:malloc_increase_bytes</tt>
  crosses this limit, GC is triggered.
* <tt>:minor_gc_count</tt>: The total number of minor garbage collections run
  since process start.
* <tt>:major_gc_count</tt>: The total number of major garbage collections run
  since process start. Global garbage collections are counted separately.
* <tt>:global_gc_count</tt>: The number of global (stop-the-world) garbage
  collections this Ractor initiated. Each global garbage collection is
  attributed to the Ractor that initiated it, so the values sum across
  Ractors. With <tt>scope: :global</tt>, the process total, including
  terminated Ractors.
* <tt>:compact_count</tt>: The total number of compactions run since process
  start.
* <tt>:read_barrier_faults</tt>: The total number of times the read barrier
  was triggered during compaction.
* <tt>:total_moved_objects</tt>: The total number of objects compaction has
  moved.
* <tt>:remembered_wb_unprotected_objects</tt>: The total number of objects
  without write barriers.
* <tt>:remembered_wb_unprotected_objects_limit</tt>: When
  <tt>:remembered_wb_unprotected_objects</tt> crosses this limit, major GC is
  triggered.
* <tt>:old_objects</tt>: Number of live, old objects which have survived at
  least 3 garbage collections.
* <tt>:old_objects_limit</tt>: When <tt>:old_objects</tt> crosses this limit,
  major GC is triggered.
* <tt>:oldmalloc_increase_bytes</tt>: Amount of memory allocated on the heap
  for objects. Decreased by major GC.
* <tt>:oldmalloc_increase_bytes_limit</tt>: When
  <tt>:oldmalloc_increase_bytes</tt> crosses this limit, major GC is
  triggered.
* <tt>:total_allocated_objects</tt>: The cumulative number of objects
  allocated since application start.
* <tt>:total_freed_objects</tt>: The cumulative number of objects freed since
  application start.
* <tt>:heap_available_slots</tt>: The total number of slots in all
  <tt>:heap_allocated_pages</tt>.
* <tt>:heap_live_slots</tt>: The total number of slots which contain live
  objects.
* <tt>:heap_free_slots</tt>: The total number of slots which do not contain
  live objects.
* <tt>:heap_final_slots</tt>: The total number of slots with pending
  finalizers to be run.
* <tt>:heap_marked_slots</tt>: The total number of objects marked in the last
  GC.

=== Global scope

With <tt>scope: :global</tt>, the default collector reports cumulative
collection counts and measured CPU time across all Ractors, retaining history
from destroyed object spaces:

  GC.stat(scope: :global)
  # => {count: 42, minor_gc_count: 32, major_gc_count: 8,
  #     global_gc_count: 2,
  #     time: 3, marking_time: 2, sweeping_time: 1}

These totals include both local and global collections, and <tt>:count</tt>
equals <tt>:minor_gc_count</tt> plus <tt>:major_gc_count</tt> plus
<tt>:global_gc_count</tt> in both scopes.

<tt>:global_gc_count</tt> attributes each global collection to the Ractor that
initiated it, and the total retains the counts of terminated Ractors.

<tt>:time</tt> may exceed <tt>:marking_time</tt> plus <tt>:sweeping_time</tt>
by one millisecond because raw nanoseconds are summed before conversion. Times
measure collector CPU work, not wall-clock pauses.

Reads combine object-space publications without requesting a stop-the-world
barrier. GC.measure_total_time controls future timing accumulation. Profiler
controls do not affect these totals. A forked child inherits its parent's
totals. MMTk and wbcheck raise NotImplementedError for this scope.

Unknown scopes and unavailable keys raise ArgumentError.

GC::stat_heap.name: stat_heap
GC::stat_heap.call_seq:
GC.stat_heap -> new_hash
GC.stat_heap(heap_id) -> new_hash
GC.stat_heap(heap_id, key) -> value
GC.stat_heap(nil, hash) -> hash
GC.stat_heap(heap_id, hash) -> hash
GC::stat_heap.comment:
This method is implementation-specific to CRuby.

Returns statistics for GC heaps. The particular statistics are
implementation-specific and may change in the future without notice.

With no argument given, returns statistics for all heaps:

  GC.stat_heap
  # =>
  {0 =>
    {slot_size: 32,
     heap_eden_pages: 24,
     heap_eden_slots: 12288,
     total_allocated_pages: 24,
     force_major_gc_count: 0,
     force_incremental_marking_finish_count: 0,
     total_allocated_objects: 8450,
     total_freed_objects: 3120},
   1 =>
    {slot_size: 64,
     heap_eden_pages: 246,
     heap_eden_slots: 402802,
     total_allocated_pages: 246,
     force_major_gc_count: 2,
     force_incremental_marking_finish_count: 1,
     total_allocated_objects: 33867152,
     total_freed_objects: 33520523},
   2 =>
    {slot_size: 128,
     heap_eden_pages: 84,
     heap_eden_slots: 68746,
     total_allocated_pages: 84,
     force_major_gc_count: 1,
     force_incremental_marking_finish_count: 4,
     total_allocated_objects: 147491,
     total_freed_objects: 90699},
   3 =>
    {slot_size: 256,
     heap_eden_pages: 157,
     heap_eden_slots: 64182,
     total_allocated_pages: 157,
     force_major_gc_count: 0,
     force_incremental_marking_finish_count: 0,
     total_allocated_objects: 211460,
     total_freed_objects: 190075},
   4 =>
    {slot_size: 512,
     heap_eden_pages: 8,
     heap_eden_slots: 1631,
     total_allocated_pages: 8,
     force_major_gc_count: 0,
     force_incremental_marking_finish_count: 0,
     total_allocated_objects: 1422,
     total_freed_objects: 700},
   5 =>
    {slot_size: 1024,
     heap_eden_pages: 16,
     heap_eden_slots: 1628,
     total_allocated_pages: 16,
     force_major_gc_count: 0,
     force_incremental_marking_finish_count: 0,
     total_allocated_objects: 1230,
     total_freed_objects: 309}}

In the example above, the keys in the outer hash are the heap identifiers:

  GC.stat_heap.keys # => [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

On CRuby, each heap identifier is an integer; on other implementations, a heap
identifier may be a string.

With only argument <tt>heap_id</tt> given, returns statistics for the given
heap identifier:

  GC.stat_heap(3)
  # =>
  {slot_size: 256,
   heap_eden_pages: 157,
   heap_eden_slots: 64182,
   total_allocated_pages: 157,
   force_major_gc_count: 0,
   force_incremental_marking_finish_count: 0,
   total_allocated_objects: 225018,
   total_freed_objects: 206647}

With arguments <tt>heap_id</tt> and <tt>key</tt> given, returns the value for
the given key in the given heap:

  GC.stat_heap(3, :slot_size) # => 256

With arguments <tt>nil</tt> and <tt>hash</tt> given, merges the statistics for
all heaps into the given hash:

  h = {foo: 0, bar: 1}
  GC.stat_heap(nil, h).keys # => [:foo, :bar, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4]

With arguments <tt>heap_id</tt> and <tt>hash</tt> given, merges the statistics
for the given heap into the given hash:

  h = {foo: 0, bar: 1}
  GC.stat_heap(2, h).keys
  # =>
  [:foo,
   :bar,
   :slot_size,
   :heap_eden_pages,
   :heap_eden_slots,
   :total_allocated_pages,
   :force_major_gc_count,
   :force_incremental_marking_finish_count,
   :total_allocated_objects,
   :total_freed_objects]

The statistics for a heap may include:

* <tt>:slot_size</tt>: The slot size of the heap in bytes.
* <tt>:heap_allocatable_pages</tt>: The number of pages that can be allocated
  without triggering a new garbage collection cycle.
* <tt>:heap_eden_pages</tt>: The number of pages in the eden heap.
* <tt>:heap_eden_slots</tt>: The total number of slots in all of the pages in
  the eden heap.
* <tt>:total_allocated_pages</tt>: The total number of pages that have been
  allocated in the heap.
* <tt>:total_freed_pages</tt>: The total number of pages that have been freed
  and released back to the system in the heap.
* <tt>:force_major_gc_count</tt>: The number of times this heap has forced
  major garbage collection cycles to start due to running out of free slots.
* <tt>:force_incremental_marking_finish_count</tt>: The number of times this
  heap has forced incremental marking to complete due to running out of pooled
  slots.

GC::stress.name: stress
GC::stress.comment:
Returns the current GC stress-mode setting, which initially is <tt>false</tt>.

The stress mode may be set by method GC.stress=.

GC::stress=.name: stress=
GC::stress=.comment:
Enables or disables stress mode. Stress mode causes GC to be invoked at every
GC opportunity (all memory and object allocations); it is intended only for
debugging and severely degrades performance.

Sets the current GC stress mode to the given value:

* If the value is <tt>nil</tt> or <tt>false</tt>, disables stress mode.
* If the value is an integer, enables stress mode with certain flags; see
  below.
* Otherwise, enables stress mode without any flags.

The flags are bits in the given integer:

* <tt>0x01</tt>: no major GC.
* <tt>0x02</tt>: no immediate sweep.
* <tt>0x04</tt>: full mark after malloc/calloc/realloc.

GC::total_time.name: total_time
GC::total_time.comment:
Returns the GC total time in nanoseconds:

With the default collector, this is the current Ractor's measured GC CPU work,
not wall-clock pause time.

  GC.total_time # => 156250

Note that total time accumulates only when total time measurement is enabled
(that is, when GC.measure_total_time is <tt>true</tt>):

  GC.measure_total_time # => true
  GC.total_time # => 625000
  GC.start
  GC.total_time # => 937500
  GC.start
  GC.total_time # => 1093750

  GC.measure_total_time = false
  GC.total_time # => 1250000
  GC.start
  GC.total_time # => 1250000
  GC.start
  GC.total_time # => 1250000

  GC.measure_total_time = true
  GC.total_time # => 1250000
  GC.start
  GC.total_time # => 1406250

GC::verify_compaction_references.name: verify_compaction_references
GC::verify_compaction_references.comment:
Verify compaction reference consistency.

This method is implementation specific.  During compaction, objects that were
moved are replaced with T_MOVED objects.  No object should have a reference to
a T_MOVED object after compaction.

This function expands the heap to ensure room to move all objects, compacts
the heap to make sure everything moves, updates all references, then performs
a full GC.  If any object contains a reference to a T_MOVED object, that
object should be pushed on the mark stack, and will make a SEGV.

GC::verify_internal_consistency.name: verify_internal_consistency
GC::verify_internal_consistency.comment:
Verifies internal consistency of the GC. This method should only be used for
debugging.

This method is only expected to work on CRuby.

GC#garbage_collect.name: garbage_collect
GC#garbage_collect.params: (full_mark: true, immediate_mark: true, immediate_sweep: true, global: true)

GC::Profiler.name: GC::Profiler
GC::Profiler.comment:
The GC profiler provides access to information on GC runs including time,
length and object space size.

Example:

  GC::Profiler.enable

  require 'rdoc/rdoc'

  GC::Profiler.report

  pp GC::Profiler.raw_data

  GC::Profiler.disable

GC::Profiler.raw_data returns one Hash per GC run, including CPU time fields
such as <tt>:GC_TIME</tt> and wall-clock fields such as
<tt>:GC_WALL_TIME</tt>, <tt>:GC_PAUSE_TIME</tt>, <tt>:GC_STOP_TIME</tt>, and
<tt>:GC_STW_TIME</tt>.  <tt>:GC_WALL_TIME</tt> is the wall-clock counterpart
to <tt>:GC_TIME</tt>, while <tt>:GC_PAUSE_TIME</tt> measures how long user
execution was blocked by the GC entry.

See also GC.count, GC.malloc_allocated_size and GC.malloc_allocations

GC::Profiler::configure.name: configure
GC::Profiler::configure.comment:
Configures how many raw profile records are retained by GC::Profiler.raw_data.

The profiler keeps at most <tt>max_records</tt> records in a bounded ring
buffer. When the buffer is full, newer GC records overwrite the oldest
retained records.  The default limit is 4096 records.

Pass <tt>nil</tt> to restore the historical unbounded behavior:

  GC::Profiler.configure(max_records: nil)

Changing <tt>max_records</tt> clears existing raw profile data.  This method
does not enable or disable the profiler; use GC::Profiler.enable and
GC::Profiler.disable for that.

GC::Profiler::enabled?.name: enabled?
GC::Profiler::enabled?.comment: The current status of GC profile mode.

GC::Profiler::raw_data.name: raw_data
GC::Profiler::raw_data.comment:
Returns an Array of retained raw profile data Hashes ordered from earliest to
latest by <tt>:GC_INVOKE_TIME</tt>.  <tt>limit:</tt> returns at most the
newest retained records.  <tt>since:</tt> returns records with
<tt>:GC_SEQUENCE</tt> greater than the given sequence.

For example:

  [
    {
       :GC_TIME=>1.3000000000000858e-05,
       :GC_INVOKE_TIME=>0.010634999999999999,
       :GC_WALL_TIME=>1.4000000000000001e-05,
       :GC_INVOKE_WALL_TIME=>0.010640000000000000,
       :GC_PAUSE_TIME=>1.5000000000000000e-05,
       :GC_STOP_TIME=>1.0000000000000000e-06,
       :GC_STW_TIME=>1.4000000000000001e-05,
       :GC_MARK_WALL_TIME=>9.0000000000000002e-06,
       :GC_SWEEP_WALL_TIME=>5.0000000000000004e-06,
       :GC_COMPACT_WALL_TIME=>0.0000000000000000e+00,
       :HEAP_USE_SIZE=>289640,
       :HEAP_TOTAL_SIZE=>588960,
       :HEAP_TOTAL_OBJECTS=>14724,
       :GC_IS_MARKED=>false
    },
    # ...
  ]

The keys mean:

<tt>:GC_SEQUENCE</tt>:
  Monotonically increasing sequence number for this profiler record.

<tt>:GC_TIME</tt>:
  CPU time elapsed in seconds for this GC run.  This is process CPU time, not
  elapsed wall-clock time.

<tt>:GC_INVOKE_TIME</tt>:
  CPU time elapsed in seconds from startup to when the GC was invoked.

<tt>:GC_WALL_TIME</tt>:
  Monotonic wall-clock counterpart to <tt>:GC_TIME</tt> for this GC record.
  This does not include time spent stopping other ractors before the VM enters
  GC.  Use the phase wall-clock fields below for mark, sweep, and compaction
  attribution.

<tt>:GC_INVOKE_WALL_TIME</tt>:
  Monotonic wall-clock time elapsed in seconds from startup to when the GC was
  invoked.

<tt>:GC_PAUSE_TIME</tt>:
  Monotonic wall-clock time elapsed in seconds while user execution was
  blocked by this GC entry, including time to stop other ractors.  This may
  include time from incremental marking or lazy sweeping continuation charged
  to this record.

<tt>:GC_STOP_TIME</tt>:
  Monotonic wall-clock time elapsed in seconds stopping other ractors.

<tt>:GC_STW_TIME</tt>:
  Monotonic wall-clock time elapsed in seconds after other ractors have
  stopped and before the VM exits GC.

<tt>:GC_MARK_WALL_TIME</tt>:
  Monotonic wall-clock time elapsed in seconds spent marking for this GC
  record, accumulated across incremental marking continuations.

<tt>:GC_SWEEP_WALL_TIME</tt>:
  Monotonic wall-clock time elapsed in seconds spent sweeping for this GC
  record, accumulated across lazy sweeping continuations.  This does not
  include compaction time, which is reported separately as
  <tt>:GC_COMPACT_WALL_TIME</tt>.

<tt>:GC_COMPACT_WALL_TIME</tt>:
  Monotonic wall-clock time elapsed in seconds spent compacting for this GC
  record, or <tt>0.0</tt> if this GC did not compact.

<tt>:HEAP_USE_SIZE</tt>:
  Total bytes of heap used

<tt>:HEAP_TOTAL_SIZE</tt>:
  Total size of heap in bytes

<tt>:HEAP_TOTAL_OBJECTS</tt>:
  Total number of objects

<tt>:GC_IS_MARKED</tt>:
  Returns <tt>true</tt> if the GC is in mark phase

The wall-clock timing fields relate to each other as follows:

  GC_PAUSE_TIME == GC_STOP_TIME + GC_STW_TIME

<tt>:GC_MARK_WALL_TIME</tt>, <tt>:GC_SWEEP_WALL_TIME</tt>, and
<tt>:GC_COMPACT_WALL_TIME</tt> report separate phase timings and must not be
added to <tt>:GC_WALL_TIME</tt>.

<tt>:GC_WALL_TIME</tt> is the wall-clock counterpart to <tt>:GC_TIME</tt> and
is nested inside <tt>:GC_STW_TIME</tt>, so it must not be added to
<tt>:GC_STW_TIME</tt>.  The difference +GC_STW_TIME - GC_WALL_TIME+ is VM
overhead inside the stopped interval (GC event hooks, bookkeeping, consistency
checks, and continuation work).

If ruby was built with <tt>GC_PROFILE_MORE_DETAIL</tt>, you will also have
access to the following hash keys:

<tt>:GC_MARK_TIME</tt>
<tt>:GC_SWEEP_TIME</tt>
<tt>:ALLOCATE_INCREASE</tt>
<tt>:ALLOCATE_LIMIT</tt>
<tt>:HEAP_USE_PAGES</tt>
<tt>:HEAP_LIVE_OBJECTS</tt>
<tt>:HEAP_FREE_OBJECTS</tt>
<tt>:HAVE_FINALIZE</tt>:

GC::Profiler::report.name: report
GC::Profiler::report.comment: Writes the GC::Profiler.result to <tt>$stdout</tt> or the given IO object.

GC::Profiler::result.name: result
GC::Profiler::result.comment:
Returns a profile data report such as:

  GC 1 invokes.
  Index    Invoke Time(sec)       Use Size(byte)     Total Size(byte)         Total Object                    GC time(ms)
      1               0.012               159240               212940                10647         0.00000000000001530000

GC::Profiler::total_time.name: total_time
GC::Profiler::total_time.comment: The total time used for garbage collection in seconds

Gem.name: Gem
Gem.comment:
RubyGems is the Ruby standard for publishing and managing third party
libraries.

For user documentation, see:

* <tt>gem help</tt> and <tt>gem help [command]</tt>
* {RubyGems User Guide}[https://guides.rubygems.org/]
* {Frequently Asked Questions}[https://guides.rubygems.org/faqs]

For gem developer documentation see:

* {Creating Gems}[https://guides.rubygems.org/make-your-own-gem]
* Gem::Specification
* Gem::Version for version dependency notes

Further RubyGems documentation can be found at:

* {RubyGems Guides}[https://guides.rubygems.org]
* {RubyGems API}[https://guides.rubygems.org/rubygems-org-api/] (also
  available from <tt>gem server</tt>)

== RubyGems Plugins

RubyGems will load plugins in the latest version of each installed gem or
$LOAD_PATH.  Plugins must be named 'rubygems_plugin' (.rb, .so, etc) and
placed at the root of your gem's #require_path.  Plugins are installed at a
special location and loaded on boot.

For an example plugin, see the {Graph gem}[https://github.com/seattlerb/graph]
which adds a <tt>gem graph</tt> command.

== RubyGems Defaults, Packaging

RubyGems defaults are stored in lib/rubygems/defaults.rb.  If you're packaging
RubyGems or implementing Ruby you can change RubyGems' defaults.

For RubyGems packagers, provide lib/rubygems/defaults/operating_system.rb and
override any defaults from lib/rubygems/defaults.rb.

For Ruby implementers, provide lib/rubygems/defaults/#{RUBY_ENGINE}.rb and
override any defaults from lib/rubygems/defaults.rb.

If you need RubyGems to perform extra work on install or uninstall, your
defaults override file can set pre/post install and uninstall hooks. See
Gem::pre_install, Gem::pre_uninstall, Gem::post_install, Gem::post_uninstall.

Gem::activate_and_load_bin_path.name: activate_and_load_bin_path
Gem::activate_and_load_bin_path.comment: Find and load the full path to the executable for gem name. If the exec_name is not given, an exception will be raised, otherwise the specified executable's path is returned. requirements allows you to specify specific gem versions. A side effect of this method is that it will activate the gem that contains the executable. This method should only be used in bin stub files.

Gem::activated_gem_paths.name: activated_gem_paths
Gem::activated_gem_paths.comment:
The number of paths in the +$LOAD_PATH+ from activated gems. Used to
prioritize <tt>-I</tt> and <tt>ENV['RUBYLIB']</tt> entries during
<tt>require</tt>.

Gem::add_to_load_path.name: add_to_load_path
Gem::add_to_load_path.comment: Add a list of paths to the $LOAD_PATH at the proper place.

Gem::bin_path.name: bin_path
Gem::bin_path.comment:
Find the full path to the executable for gem <tt>name</tt>.  If the
<tt>exec_name</tt> is not given, an exception will be raised, otherwise the
specified executable's path is returned.  <tt>requirements</tt> allows you to
specify specific gem versions.

Gem::binary_mode.name: binary_mode
Gem::binary_mode.comment: The mode needed to read a file as straight binary.

Gem::bindir.name: bindir
Gem::bindir.comment: The path where gem executables are to be installed.

Gem::cache_home.name: cache_home
Gem::cache_home.comment: The path to standard location of the user's cache directory.

Gem::clear_default_specs.name: clear_default_specs
Gem::clear_default_specs.comment: Clear default gem related variables. It is for test

Gem::clear_paths.name: clear_paths
Gem::clear_paths.comment:
Reset the <tt>dir</tt> and <tt>path</tt> values.  The next time <tt>dir</tt>
or <tt>path</tt> is requested, the values will be calculated from scratch.
This is mainly used by the unit tests to provide test isolation.

Gem::config_file.name: config_file
Gem::config_file.comment: The path to standard location of the user's .gemrc file.

Gem::config_home.name: config_home
Gem::config_home.comment: The path to standard location of the user's configuration directory.

Gem::configuration.name: configuration
Gem::configuration.comment: The standard configuration object for gems.

Gem::configuration=.name: configuration=
Gem::configuration=.comment:
Use the given configuration object (which implements the ConfigFile protocol)
as the standard configuration object.

Gem::data_home.name: data_home
Gem::data_home.comment: The path to standard location of the user's data directory.

Gem::default_cert_path.name: default_cert_path
Gem::default_cert_path.comment: The default signing certificate chain path

Gem::default_dir.name: default_dir
Gem::default_dir.comment:
Default home directory path to be used if an alternate value is not specified
in the environment

Gem::default_exec_format.name: default_exec_format
Gem::default_exec_format.comment: Deduce Ruby's --program-prefix and --program-suffix from its install name

Gem::default_ext_dir_for.name: default_ext_dir_for
Gem::default_ext_dir_for.comment:
Returns binary extensions dir for specified RubyGems base dir or nil if such
directory cannot be determined.

By default, the binary extensions are located side by side with their Ruby
counterparts, therefore nil is returned

Gem::default_rubygems_dirs.name: default_rubygems_dirs
Gem::default_rubygems_dirs.comment: Paths where RubyGems' .rb files and bin files are installed

Gem::default_sources.name: default_sources
Gem::default_sources.comment: An Array of the default sources that come with RubyGems

Gem::default_spec_cache_dir.name: default_spec_cache_dir
Gem::default_spec_cache_dir.comment:
Default spec directory path to be used if an alternate value is not specified
in the environment

Gem::default_specifications_dir.name: default_specifications_dir
Gem::default_specifications_dir.comment: Path to specification files of default gems.

Gem::dir.name: dir
Gem::dir.comment: The path where gems are to be installed.

Gem::done_installing.name: done_installing
Gem::done_installing.comment:
Adds a post-installs hook that will be passed a Gem::DependencyInstaller and a
list of installed specifications when Gem::DependencyInstaller#install is
complete

Gem::dynamic_library_suffixes.name: dynamic_library_suffixes
Gem::dynamic_library_suffixes.comment: Suffixes for dynamic library require-able paths.

Gem::ensure_default_gem_subdirectories.name: ensure_default_gem_subdirectories
Gem::ensure_default_gem_subdirectories.comment:
Quietly ensure the Gem directory <tt>dir</tt> contains all the proper
subdirectories for handling default gems.  If we can't create a directory due
to a permission problem, then we will silently continue.

If <tt>mode</tt> is given, missing directories are created with this mode.

World-writable directories will never be created.

Gem::ensure_gem_subdirectories.name: ensure_gem_subdirectories
Gem::ensure_gem_subdirectories.comment:
Quietly ensure the Gem directory <tt>dir</tt> contains all the proper
subdirectories.  If we can't create a directory due to a permission problem,
then we will silently continue.

If <tt>mode</tt> is given, missing directories are created with this mode.

World-writable directories will never be created.

Gem::find_default_spec.name: find_default_spec
Gem::find_default_spec.comment: Find a Gem::Specification of default gem from <tt>path</tt>

Gem::find_files.name: find_files
Gem::find_files.comment:
Returns a list of paths matching <tt>glob</tt> that can be used by a gem to
pick up features from other gems.  For example:

  Gem.find_files('rdoc/discover').each do |path| load path end

if <tt>check_load_path</tt> is true (the default), then find_files also
searches $LOAD_PATH for files as well as gems.

Note that find_files will return all files even if they are from different
versions of the same gem.  See also find_latest_files

Gem::find_latest_files.name: find_latest_files
Gem::find_latest_files.comment:
Returns a list of paths matching <tt>glob</tt> from the latest gems that can
be used by a gem to pick up features from other gems.  For example:

  Gem.find_latest_files('rdoc/discover').each do |path| load path end

if <tt>check_load_path</tt> is true (the default), then find_latest_files also
searches $LOAD_PATH for files as well as gems.

Unlike find_files, find_latest_files will return only files from the latest
version of a gem.

Gem::find_unresolved_default_spec.name: find_unresolved_default_spec
Gem::find_unresolved_default_spec.comment: Find an unresolved Gem::Specification of default gem from <tt>path</tt>

Gem::global_gem_cache_path.name: global_gem_cache_path
Gem::global_gem_cache_path.comment:
The path to the global gem cache directory. This is used when global_gem_cache
is enabled to share .gem files across all Ruby installations.

Gem::host.name: host
Gem::host.comment:
Get the default RubyGems API host. This is normally
<tt>https://rubygems.org</tt>.

Gem::host=.name: host=
Gem::host=.comment: Set the default RubyGems API host.

Gem::install.name: install
Gem::install.comment:
Top level install helper method. Allows you to install gems interactively:

  % irb
  >> Gem.install "minitest"
  Fetching: minitest-5.14.0.gem (100%)
  => [#<Gem::Specification:0x1013b4528 @name="minitest", ...>]

Gem::latest_rubygems_version.name: latest_rubygems_version
Gem::latest_rubygems_version.comment: Returns the latest release version of RubyGems.

Gem::latest_spec_for.name: latest_spec_for
Gem::latest_spec_for.comment: Returns the latest release-version specification for the gem <tt>name</tt>.

Gem::latest_version_for.name: latest_version_for
Gem::latest_version_for.comment: Returns the version of the latest release-version of gem <tt>name</tt>

Gem::load_bundler_extensions.name: load_bundler_extensions
Gem::load_bundler_extensions.comment:
Load Bundler extensions to RubyGems, making sure to avoid redefinition
warnings in platform constants

Gem::load_env_plugins.name: load_env_plugins
Gem::load_env_plugins.comment: Find all 'rubygems_plugin' files in $LOAD_PATH and load them

Gem::load_path_insert_index.name: load_path_insert_index
Gem::load_path_insert_index.comment:
The index to insert activated gem paths into the $LOAD_PATH. The activated
gem's paths are inserted before site lib directory by default.

Gem::load_plugins.name: load_plugins
Gem::load_plugins.comment:
Find rubygems plugin files in the standard location and load them. At most one
stub is loaded per gem: a stub in the running Ruby's ABI directory wins over a
root stub of the same name, since it was installed specifically for this Ruby.

Gem::location_of_caller.name: location_of_caller
Gem::location_of_caller.comment:
The file name and line number of the caller of the caller of this method.

<tt>depth</tt> is how many layers up the call stack it should go.

e.g.,

def a; Gem.location_of_caller; end a #=> ["x.rb", 2]  # (it'll vary depending
on file name and line number)

def b; c; end def c; Gem.location_of_caller(2); end b #=> ["x.rb", 6]  #
(it'll vary depending on file name and line number)

Gem::marshal_version.name: marshal_version
Gem::marshal_version.comment: The version of the Marshal format for your Ruby.

Gem::open_file.name: open_file
Gem::open_file.comment: Open a file with given flags

Gem::open_file_with_flock.name: open_file_with_flock
Gem::open_file_with_flock.comment: Open a file with given flags, and protect access with flock

Gem::open_file_with_lock.name: open_file_with_lock
Gem::open_file_with_lock.comment: Open a file with given flags, and protect access with a file lock

Gem::operating_system_defaults.name: operating_system_defaults
Gem::operating_system_defaults.comment:
Default options for gem commands for Ruby packagers.

The options here should be structured as an array of string "gem" command
names as keys and a string of the default options as values.

Example:

def self.operating_system_defaults
  {
      'install' => '--no-rdoc --no-ri --env-shebang',
      'update' => '--no-rdoc --no-ri --env-shebang'
  }

end

Gem::path_separator.name: path_separator
Gem::path_separator.comment: How String Gem paths should be split.  Overridable for esoteric platforms.

Gem::paths.name: paths
Gem::paths.comment: Retrieve the PathSupport object that RubyGems uses to lookup files.

Gem::paths=.name: paths=
Gem::paths=.comment:
Initialize the filesystem paths to use from <tt>env</tt>. <tt>env</tt> is a
hash-like object (typically ENV) that is queried for 'GEM_HOME', 'GEM_PATH',
and 'GEM_SPEC_CACHE' Keys for the <tt>env</tt> hash should be Strings, and
values of the hash should be Strings or <tt>nil</tt>.

Gem::platform_defaults.name: platform_defaults
Gem::platform_defaults.comment:
Default options for gem commands for Ruby implementers.

The options here should be structured as an array of string "gem" command
names as keys and a string of the default options as values.

Example:

def self.platform_defaults
  {
      'install' => '--no-rdoc --no-ri --env-shebang',
      'update' => '--no-rdoc --no-ri --env-shebang'
  }

end

Gem::platforms.name: platforms
Gem::platforms.comment: Array of platforms this RubyGems supports.

Gem::platforms=.name: platforms=
Gem::platforms=.comment: Set array of platforms this RubyGems supports (primarily for testing).

Gem::plugin_suffix_pattern.name: plugin_suffix_pattern
Gem::plugin_suffix_pattern.comment: Glob pattern for require-able plugin suffixes.

Gem::plugindir.name: plugindir
Gem::plugindir.comment: The path were rubygems plugins are to be installed.

Gem::post_build.name: post_build
Gem::post_build.comment:
Adds a post-build hook that will be passed an Gem::Installer instance when
Gem::Installer#install is called.  The hook is called after the gem has been
extracted and extensions have been built but before the executables or gemspec
has been written.  If the hook returns <tt>false</tt> then the gem's files
will be removed and the install will be aborted.

Gem::post_install.name: post_install
Gem::post_install.comment:
Adds a post-install hook that will be passed an Gem::Installer instance when
Gem::Installer#install is called

Gem::post_reset.name: post_reset
Gem::post_reset.comment: Adds a hook that will get run after Gem::Specification.reset is run.

Gem::post_uninstall.name: post_uninstall
Gem::post_uninstall.comment:
Adds a post-uninstall hook that will be passed a Gem::Uninstaller instance and
the spec that was uninstalled when Gem::Uninstaller#uninstall is called

Gem::pre_install.name: pre_install
Gem::pre_install.comment:
Adds a pre-install hook that will be passed an Gem::Installer instance when
Gem::Installer#install is called.  If the hook returns <tt>false</tt> then the
install will be aborted.

Gem::pre_reset.name: pre_reset
Gem::pre_reset.comment: Adds a hook that will get run before Gem::Specification.reset is run.

Gem::pre_uninstall.name: pre_uninstall
Gem::pre_uninstall.comment:
Adds a pre-uninstall hook that will be passed an Gem::Uninstaller instance and
the spec that will be uninstalled when Gem::Uninstaller#uninstall is called

Gem::prefix.name: prefix
Gem::prefix.comment:
The directory prefix this RubyGems was installed at. If your prefix is in a
standard location (ie, rubygems is installed where you'd expect it to be),
then prefix returns nil.

Gem::rdoc_hooks_defined_via_plugin?.name: rdoc_hooks_defined_via_plugin?
Gem::rdoc_hooks_defined_via_plugin?.comment:
Returns whether RDoc defines its own install hooks through a RubyGems plugin.
This and whatever is guarded by it can be removed once no supported Ruby ships
with RDoc older than 6.9.0.
