Gem::Package.name: Gem::Package
Gem::Package.comment:
Example using a Gem::Package

Builds a .gem file given a Gem::Specification. A .gem file is a tarball which
contains a data.tar.gz, metadata.gz, checksums.yaml.gz and possibly
signatures.

  require 'rubygems'
  require 'rubygems/package'

  spec = Gem::Specification.new do |s|
    s.summary = "Ruby based make-like utility."
    s.name = 'rake'
    s.version = PKG_VERSION
    s.requirements << 'none'
    s.files = PKG_FILES
    s.description = <<-EOF
  Rake is a Make-like program implemented in Ruby. Tasks
  and dependencies are specified in standard Ruby syntax.
    EOF
  end

  Gem::Package.build spec

Reads a .gem file.

  require 'rubygems'
  require 'rubygems/package'

  the_gem = Gem::Package.new(path_to_dot_gem)
  the_gem.contents # get the files in the gem
  the_gem.extract_files destination_directory # extract the gem into a directory
  the_gem.spec # get the spec out of the gem
  the_gem.verify # check the gem is OK (contains valid gem specification, contains a not corrupt contents archive)

#files are the files in the .gem tar file, not the Ruby files in the gem
#extract_files and #contents automatically call #verify

Gem::Package::build.name: build
Gem::Package::build.params: (spec, skip_validation = false, strict_validation = false, file_name = nil, content_addressable: false)
Gem::Package::build.comment:
Builds the gem described by <tt>spec</tt> and returns the built file name.

When <tt>content_addressable</tt> is true, builds a gem named by the SHA-256
digest of its contents. The spec must declare a non-Ruby platform and a
<tt>required_ruby_version</tt> identifying a single Ruby ABI. Its
<tt>required_rubygems_version</tt> is constrained to at least
MINIMUM_RUBYGEMS_VERSION. Content-addressable builds are incompatible with
<tt>file_name</tt>.

Gem::Package::new.name: new
Gem::Package::new.comment:
Creates a new Gem::Package for the file at <tt>gem</tt>. <tt>gem</tt> can also
be provided as an IO object.

If <tt>gem</tt> is an existing file in the old format a Gem::Package::Old will
be returned.

Gem::Package::raw_spec.name: raw_spec
Gem::Package::raw_spec.comment:
Extracts the Gem::Specification and raw metadata from the .gem file at
<tt>path</tt>.

Gem::Package#add_checksums.name: add_checksums
Gem::Package#add_checksums.comment: Adds a checksum for each entry in the gem to checksums.yaml.gz.

Gem::Package#build.name: build
Gem::Package#build.comment: Builds this package based on the specification set by #spec=

Gem::Package#build_content_addressable_f.name: build_content_addressable_file
Gem::Package#build_content_addressable_f.comment:
Builds this package and writes it to a content-addressable file name derived
from the SHA-256 digest of the gem contents, for example
"example-1.0-01234567.gem". Returns the written file name.

The spec is validated for content addressing. Its
<tt>required_ruby_version</tt> determines the Ruby ABI, while its
<tt>required_rubygems_version</tt> is constrained before building.

Gem::Package#content_address.name: content_address
Gem::Package#content_address.comment:
Derives the content address from the gem's file name and verifies it against
the SHA256 digest of the file contents.

Gem::Package#contents.name: contents
Gem::Package#contents.comment: A list of file names contained in this gem

Gem::Package#extract_files.name: extract_files
Gem::Package#extract_files.comment:
Extracts the files in this package into <tt>destination_dir</tt>

If <tt>pattern</tt> is specified, only entries matching that glob will be
extracted.

Gem::Package#read_checksums.name: read_checksums
Gem::Package#read_checksums.comment: Reads and loads checksums.yaml.gz from the tar file <tt>gem</tt>

Gem::Package#setup_signer.name: setup_signer
Gem::Package#setup_signer.comment:
Prepares the gem for signing and checksum generation.  If a signing
certificate and key are not present only checksum generation is set up.

Gem::Package#spec.name: spec
Gem::Package#spec.comment: Sets the Gem::Specification to use to build this package.

Gem::Package#verify.name: verify
Gem::Package#verify.comment:
Verifies that this gem:

* Contains a valid gem specification
* Contains a contents archive
* The contents archive is not corrupt

After verification the gem specification from the gem is available from #spec

Gem::Package#initialize.name: initialize
Gem::Package#initialize.comment: Creates a new package that will read or write to the file <tt>gem</tt>.

Gem::Package#create_symlink.name: create_symlink
Gem::Package#create_symlink.comment:
Create a symlink and fallback to copy the file or directory on Windows, where
symlink creation needs special privileges in form of the Developer Mode. JRuby
on Windows raises TypeError from the wincode path-conversion helper when it
cannot create the symlink, so fall back to copy in that case too.

Gem::Package#excludes_rubygems_floor?.name: excludes_rubygems_floor?
Gem::Package#excludes_rubygems_floor?.comment:
Whether <tt>requirement</tt> excludes every RubyGems version satisfying the
<tt>floor</tt>, so that no RubyGems could install the built gem.

Gem::Package#normalized_required_rubygem.name: normalized_required_rubygems_version
Gem::Package#normalized_required_rubygem.comment:
The <tt>required_rubygems_version</tt> for a content-addressable build: the
spec's requirement raised to at least MINIMUM_RUBYGEMS_VERSION, warning if it
had to be changed. Raises if the requirement excludes every version satisfying
that floor, since no RubyGems could install the built gem.

Gem::Package#satisfies_rubygems_floor?.name: satisfies_rubygems_floor?
Gem::Package#satisfies_rubygems_floor?.comment:
Whether one of the lower bounds of <tt>requirement</tt> already guarantees the
<tt>floor</tt>.

Gem::Package::DigestIO.name: Gem::Package::DigestIO
Gem::Package::DigestIO.comment: IO wrapper that creates digests of contents written to the IO it wraps.

Gem::Package::DigestIO::new.name: new
Gem::Package::DigestIO::new.comment:
Creates a new DigestIO instance.  Using ::wrap is recommended, see the ::wrap
documentation for documentation of <tt>io</tt> and <tt>digests</tt>.

Gem::Package::DigestIO::wrap.name: wrap
Gem::Package::DigestIO::wrap.comment:
Wraps <tt>io</tt> and updates digest for each of the digest algorithms in the
<tt>digests</tt> Hash.  Returns the digests hash.  Example:

  io = StringIO.new
  digests = {
    'SHA1'   => OpenSSL::Digest.new('SHA1'),
    'SHA512' => OpenSSL::Digest.new('SHA512'),
  }

  Gem::Package::DigestIO.wrap io, digests do |digest_io|
    digest_io.write "hello"
  end

  digests['SHA1'].hexdigest   #=> "aaf4c61d[...]"
  digests['SHA512'].hexdigest #=> "9b71d224[...]"

Gem::Package::DigestIO#write.name: write
Gem::Package::DigestIO#write.comment: Writes <tt>data</tt> to the underlying IO and updates the digests

Gem::Package::InvalidWindowsFileNameErro.name: Gem::Package::InvalidWindowsFileNameError
Gem::Package::InvalidWindowsFileNameErro.comment: Raised when a filename contains characters that are invalid on Windows

Gem::Package::Old.name: Gem::Package::Old
Gem::Package::Old.comment:
The format class knows the guts of the ancient .gem file format and provides
the capability to read such ancient gems.

Please pretend this doesn't exist.

Gem::Package::Old::new.name: new
Gem::Package::Old::new.comment:
Creates a new old-format package reader for <tt>gem</tt>.  Old-format packages
cannot be written.

Gem::Package::Old#contents.name: contents
Gem::Package::Old#contents.comment: A list of file names contained in this gem

Gem::Package::Old#extract_files.name: extract_files
Gem::Package::Old#extract_files.comment: Extracts the files in this package into <tt>destination_dir</tt>

Gem::Package::Old#verify.name: verify
Gem::Package::Old#verify.comment:
Raises an exception if a security policy that verifies data is active. Old
format gems cannot be verified as signed.

Gem::Package::TarHeader.name: Gem::Package::TarHeader
Gem::Package::TarHeader.comment: A header for a tar file

Gem::Package::TarHeader::from.name: from
Gem::Package::TarHeader::from.comment: Creates a tar header from IO <tt>stream</tt>

Gem::Package::TarInvalidError.name: Gem::Package::TarInvalidError
Gem::Package::TarInvalidError.comment: Raised when a tar file is corrupt

Gem::Package::TarReader.name: Gem::Package::TarReader
Gem::Package::TarReader.comment: TarReader reads tar files and allows iteration over their items

Gem::Package::TarReader::new.name: new
Gem::Package::TarReader::new.comment:
Creates a new tar file reader on <tt>io</tt> which needs to respond to #pos,
#eof?, #read, #getc and #pos=

Gem::Package::TarReader#each.name: each
Gem::Package::TarReader#each.comment: Iterates over files in the tarball yielding each entry

Gem::Package::TarReader#seek.name: seek

<tt>name</tt> and yields it.  Rewinds the tar file to the beginning when the
block terminates.

Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry.name: Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry
Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry.comment: Class for reading entries out of a tar file

Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry::new.name: new
Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry::new.comment: Creates a new tar entry for <tt>header</tt> that will be read from <tt>io</tt>

Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry::open.name: open
Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry::open.comment:
Creates a new tar entry for <tt>header</tt> that will be read from <tt>io</tt>
If a block is given, the entry is yielded and then closed.

Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#bytes_rea.name: bytes_read
Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#bytes_rea.comment: Number of bytes read out of the tar entry

Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#directory.name: directory?
Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#directory.comment: Is this tar entry a directory?

Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#eof?.name: eof?
Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#eof?.comment: Are we at the end of the tar entry?

Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#file?.name: file?
Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#file?.comment: Is this tar entry a file?

Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#full_name.name: full_name
Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#full_name.comment: Full name of the tar entry

Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#getc.name: getc
Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#getc.comment: Read one byte from the tar entry

Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#pos.name: pos
Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#pos.comment: The position in the tar entry

Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#pos=.name: pos=
Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#pos=.comment: Seek to the position in the tar entry

Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#read.name: read
Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#read.comment:
Reads <tt>maxlen</tt> bytes from the tar file entry, or the rest of the entry
if nil

Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#rewind.name: rewind
Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#rewind.comment: Rewinds to the beginning of the tar file entry

Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#seek.name: seek
Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#seek.comment:
Seeks to <tt>offset</tt> bytes into the tar file entry <tt>whence</tt> can be
IO::SEEK_SET, IO::SEEK_CUR, or IO::SEEK_END

Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#symlink?.name: symlink?
Gem::Package::TarReader::Entry#symlink?.comment: Is this tar entry a symlink?

Gem::Package::TarWriter::new.name: new
Gem::Package::TarWriter::new.comment: Creates a new TarWriter that will write to <tt>io</tt>

Gem::Package::TarWriter#add_file.name: add_file
Gem::Package::TarWriter#add_file.comment:
Adds file <tt>name</tt> with permissions <tt>mode</tt> and mtime
<tt>mtime</tt> (sets Gem.source_date_epoch if not specified), and yields an IO
for writing the file to

Gem::Package::TarWriter#add_file_digest.name: add_file_digest
Gem::Package::TarWriter#add_file_digest.comment:
Adds <tt>name</tt> with permissions <tt>mode</tt> to the tar, yielding
<tt>io</tt> for writing the file.  The <tt>digest_algorithm</tt> is written to
a read-only <tt>name</tt>.sum file following the given file contents

The created digest object is returned.

Gem::Package::TarWriter#add_file_signed.name: add_file_signed
Gem::Package::TarWriter#add_file_signed.comment:
Adds <tt>name</tt> with permissions <tt>mode</tt> to the tar, yielding
<tt>io</tt> for writing the file.  The <tt>signer</tt> is used to add a digest
file using its digest_algorithm per add_file_digest and a cryptographic

Returns the digest.

Gem::Package::TarWriter#add_file_simple.name: add_file_simple
Gem::Package::TarWriter#add_file_simple.comment:
Add file <tt>name</tt> with permissions <tt>mode</tt> <tt>size</tt> bytes
long.  Yields an IO to write the file to.

Gem::Package::TarWriter#add_symlink.name: add_symlink
Gem::Package::TarWriter#add_symlink.comment:
Adds symlink <tt>name</tt> with permissions <tt>mode</tt>, linking to
<tt>target</tt>.

Gem::Package::TarWriter#check_closed.name: check_closed
Gem::Package::TarWriter#check_closed.comment: Raises IOError if the TarWriter is closed

Gem::Package::TarWriter#mkdir.name: mkdir
Gem::Package::TarWriter#mkdir.comment: Creates a new directory in the tar file <tt>name</tt> with <tt>mode</tt>

Gem::Package::TarWriter::BoundedStream.name: Gem::Package::TarWriter::BoundedStream
Gem::Package::TarWriter::BoundedStream.comment: IO wrapper that allows writing a limited amount of data

Gem::Package::TarWriter::BoundedStream::.name: new

Gem::Package::TarWriter::BoundedStream#w.name: write
Gem::Package::TarWriter::BoundedStream#w.comment:
Writes <tt>data</tt> onto the IO, raising a FileOverflow exception if the
number of bytes will be more than #limit

Gem::PackageTask.name: Gem::PackageTask
Gem::PackageTask.comment: Create a package based upon a Gem::Specification. Gem packages, as well as zip files and tar/gzipped packages can be produced by this task. In addition to the Rake targets generated by Rake::PackageTask, a Gem::PackageTask will also generate the following tasks: "package_dir/name-version.gem": Create a RubyGems package with the given name and version. Example using a Gem::Specification: require 'rubygems' require 'rubygems/package_task' spec = Gem::Specification.new do |s| s.summary = "Ruby based make-like utility." s.name = 'rake' s.version = PKG_VERSION s.requirements << 'none' s.files = PKG_FILES s.description = <<-EOF Rake is a Make-like program implemented in Ruby. Tasks and dependencies are specified in standard Ruby syntax. EOF end Gem::PackageTask.new(spec) do |pkg| pkg.need_zip = true pkg.need_tar = true end

Gem::PackageTask::new.name: new
Gem::PackageTask::new.comment:
Create a Gem Package task library.  Automatically define the gem if a block is
given.  If no block is supplied, then #define needs to be called to define the
task.

Gem::PackageTask#define.name: define
Gem::PackageTask#define.comment:
Create the Rake tasks and actions specified by this Gem::PackageTask.
(<tt>define</tt> is automatically called if a block is given to <tt>new</tt>).

Gem::PackageTask#init.name: init
Gem::PackageTask#init.comment: Initialization tasks without the "yield self" or define operations.

Gem::PackageTask#package_name.name: package_name
Gem::PackageTask#package_name.comment:
The name of this package. Content-addressable builds append the Ruby ABI so
per-ABI builds of the same <tt>full_name</tt> do not share a staging
directory.

Gem::PathSupport.name: Gem::PathSupport
Gem::PathSupport.comment:
Gem::PathSupport facilitates the GEM_HOME and GEM_PATH environment settings to
the rest of RubyGems.

Gem::PathSupport::new.name: new
Gem::PathSupport::new.comment:
Constructor. Takes a single argument which is to be treated like a hashtable,
or defaults to ENV, the system environment.

Gem::PathSupport#split_gem_path.name: split_gem_path
Gem::PathSupport#split_gem_path.comment: Split the Gem search path (as reported by Gem.path).

Gem::Platform.name: Gem::Platform
Gem::Platform.comment:
Available list of platforms for targeting Gem installations.

See `gem help platform` for information on platform matching.

Gem::Platform::generic.name: generic
Gem::Platform::generic.comment: Returns the generic platform for the given platform.

Gem::Platform::platform_specificity_matc.name: platform_specificity_match
Gem::Platform::platform_specificity_matc.comment:
Returns the platform specificity match for the given spec platform and user
platform.

Gem::Platform::sort_and_filter_best_plat.name: sort_and_filter_best_platform_match
Gem::Platform::sort_and_filter_best_plat.comment:
Sorts and filters the best platform match for the given matching specs and
platform.

Gem::Platform::sort_best_platform_match.name: sort_best_platform_match
Gem::Platform::sort_best_platform_match.comment: Sorts the best platform match for the given matching specs and platform.

Gem::Platform#==.comment:
Is <tt>other</tt> equal to this platform?  Two platforms are equal if they
have the same CPU, OS and version.

Gem::Platform#===.comment:
Does <tt>other</tt> match this platform?  Two platforms match if they have the
same CPU, or either has a CPU of 'universal', they have the same OS, and they
have the same version, or either one has no version

Additionally, the platform will match if the local CPU is 'arm' and the other
CPU starts with "armv" (for generic 32-bit ARM family support).

Of note, this method is not commutative. Indeed the OS 'linux' has a special
case: the version is the libc name, yet while "no version" stands as a
wildcard for a binary gem platform (as for other OSes), for the runtime
platform "no version" stands for 'gnu'. To be able to distinguish these, the
method receiver is the gem platform, while the argument is the runtime
platform.

Gem::Platform#=~.comment:
Does <tt>other</tt> match this platform?  If <tt>other</tt> is a String it
will be converted to a Gem::Platform first.  See #=== for matching rules.

Gem::Platform#deconstruct.name: deconstruct
Gem::Platform#deconstruct.comment:
Deconstructs the platform into an array for pattern matching. Returns [cpu,
os, version].

  Gem::Platform.new("x86_64-linux").deconstruct  #=> ["x86_64", "linux", nil]

This enables array pattern matching:

  case Gem::Platform.new("arm64-darwin-21")
  in ["arm64", "darwin", version]
    # version => "21"
  end

Gem::Platform#deconstruct_keys.name: deconstruct_keys
Gem::Platform#deconstruct_keys.comment:
Deconstructs the platform into a hash for pattern matching. Returns a hash
with keys <tt>:cpu</tt>, <tt>:os</tt>, and <tt>:version</tt>.

  Gem::Platform.new("x86_64-darwin-20").deconstruct_keys(nil)
  #=> { cpu: "x86_64", os: "darwin", version: "20" }

This enables hash pattern matching:

  case Gem::Platform.new("x86_64-linux")
  in cpu: "x86_64", os: "linux"
    # Matches Linux on x86_64
  end

Gem::PlatformMismatch.name: Gem::PlatformMismatch
Gem::PlatformMismatch.comment:
Generated when trying to lookup a gem to indicate that the gem was found, but
that it isn't usable on the current platform.

fetch and install read these and report them to the user to aid in figuring
out why a gem couldn't be installed.

Gem::PlatformMismatch#add_platform.name: add_platform
Gem::PlatformMismatch#add_platform.comment:
append a platform to the list of mismatched platforms.

Platforms are added via this instead of injected via the constructor so that
we can loop over a list of mismatches and just add them rather than perform
some kind of calculation mismatch summary before creation.

Gem::PlatformMismatch#wordy.name: wordy
Gem::PlatformMismatch#wordy.comment: A wordy description of the error.

Gem::QueryUtils#installed?.name: installed?
Gem::QueryUtils#installed?.comment: Check if gem <tt>name</tt> version <tt>version</tt> is installed.

Gem::RemoteError.name: Gem::RemoteError
Gem::RemoteError.comment:
Signals that a remote operation cannot be conducted, probably due to not being
connected (or just not finding host).

Gem::RemoteFetcher.name: Gem::RemoteFetcher
Gem::RemoteFetcher.comment:
RemoteFetcher handles the details of fetching gems and gem information from a
remote source.

Gem::RemoteFetcher::new.name: new
Gem::RemoteFetcher::new.comment:
Initialize a remote fetcher using the source URI and possible proxy
information.

<tt>proxy</tt>
* [String]: explicit specification of proxy; overrides any environment
    variable setting

* nil: respect environment variables (HTTP_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY_USER,
    HTTP_PROXY_PASS)

* <tt>:no_proxy</tt>: ignore environment variables and _don't_ use a proxy

<tt>headers</tt>: A set of additional HTTP headers to be sent to the server
when
  fetching the gem.

Gem::RemoteFetcher#cache_update_path.name: cache_update_path
Gem::RemoteFetcher#cache_update_path.comment:
Downloads <tt>uri</tt> to <tt>path</tt> if necessary. If no path is given, it
just passes the data.

Gem::RemoteFetcher#download.name: download
Gem::RemoteFetcher#download.comment:
Moves the gem <tt>spec</tt> from <tt>source_uri</tt> to the cache dir unless
it is already there.  If the source_uri is local the gem cache dir copy is
always replaced.

Gem::RemoteFetcher#download_to_cache.name: download_to_cache
Gem::RemoteFetcher#download_to_cache.comment:
Given a name and requirement, downloads this gem into cache and returns the
filename. Returns nil if the gem cannot be located.

Gem::RemoteFetcher#fetch_file.name: fetch_file
Gem::RemoteFetcher#fetch_file.comment: File Fetcher. Dispatched by <tt>fetch_path</tt>. Use it instead.

Gem::RemoteFetcher#fetch_http.name: fetch_http
Gem::RemoteFetcher#fetch_http.params: (uri, last_modified = nil, head = false, depth = 0, headers = self.headers)
Gem::RemoteFetcher#fetch_http.comment: HTTP Fetcher. Dispatched by <tt>fetch_path</tt>. Use it instead.

Gem::RemoteFetcher#fetch_https.name: fetch_https
Gem::RemoteFetcher#fetch_https.params: (uri, last_modified = nil, head = false, depth = 0, headers = self.headers)

Gem::RemoteFetcher#fetch_path.name: fetch_path
Gem::RemoteFetcher#fetch_path.comment: Downloads <tt>uri</tt> and returns it as a String.

Gem::RemoteFetcher#request.name: request
Gem::RemoteFetcher#request.comment:
Performs a Gem::Net::HTTP request of type <tt>request_class</tt> on
<tt>uri</tt> returning a Gem::Net::HTTP response object.  request maintains a
table of persistent connections to reduce connect overhead.

Gem::RemoteFetcher#s3_uri_signer.name: s3_uri_signer
Gem::RemoteFetcher#s3_uri_signer.comment: we have our own signing code here to avoid a dependency on the aws-sdk gem

Gem::RemoteFetcher#ensure_writable_cache.name: ensure_writable_cache_dir
Gem::RemoteFetcher#ensure_writable_cache.comment:
Creates <tt>cache_dir</tt> so its writability can be probed, since
File.writable? is false for a path that does not exist yet.

Gem::RemoteFetcher::FetchError.name: Gem::RemoteFetcher::FetchError
Gem::RemoteFetcher::FetchError.comment:
A FetchError exception wraps up the various possible IO and HTTP failures that
could happen while downloading from the internet.

Gem::RemoteFetcher::UnknownHostError.name: Gem::RemoteFetcher::UnknownHostError
Gem::RemoteFetcher::UnknownHostError.comment:
A FetchError that indicates that the reason for not being able to fetch data
was that the host could not be contacted

Gem::RemoteSourceException.name: Gem::RemoteSourceException
Gem::RemoteSourceException.comment: Represents an error communicating via HTTP.

Gem::Request::get_proxy_from_env.name: get_proxy_from_env
Gem::Request::get_proxy_from_env.comment:
Returns a proxy URI for the given <tt>scheme</tt> if one is set in the
environment variables.

Gem::Request#connection_for.name: connection_for
Gem::Request#connection_for.comment:
Creates or an HTTP connection based on <tt>uri</tt>, or retrieves an existing
connection, using a proxy if needed.

Gem::RequestSet.name: Gem::RequestSet
Gem::RequestSet.comment:
A RequestSet groups a request to activate a set of dependencies.

  nokogiri = Gem::Dependency.new 'nokogiri', '>= 1.6'
  pg = Gem::Dependency.new 'pg', '>= 0.14'

  set = Gem::RequestSet.new nokogiri, pg

  requests = set.resolve

  p requests.map { |r| r.full_name }
  #=> ["nokogiri-1.6.0", "mini_portile-0.5.1", "pg-0.17.0"]

Gem::RequestSet::new.name: new
Gem::RequestSet::new.comment:
Creates a RequestSet for a list of Gem::Dependency objects, <tt>deps</tt>.
You can then #resolve and #install the resolved list of dependencies.

  nokogiri = Gem::Dependency.new 'nokogiri', '>= 1.6'
  pg = Gem::Dependency.new 'pg', '>= 0.14'

  set = Gem::RequestSet.new nokogiri, pg

Gem::RequestSet#gem.name: gem
Gem::RequestSet#gem.comment:
Declare that a gem of name <tt>name</tt> with <tt>reqs</tt> requirements is
needed.

Gem::RequestSet#import.name: import
Gem::RequestSet#import.comment: Add <tt>deps</tt> Gem::Dependency objects to the set.

Gem::RequestSet#install.name: install
Gem::RequestSet#install.comment:
Installs gems for this RequestSet using the Gem::Installer <tt>options</tt>.

If a <tt>block</tt> is given an activation <tt>request</tt> and
<tt>installer</tt> are yielded. The <tt>installer</tt> will be <tt>nil</tt> if
a gem matching the request was already installed.

Gem::RequestSet#install_from_gemdeps.name: install_from_gemdeps
Gem::RequestSet#install_from_gemdeps.comment:
Installs from the gem dependencies files in the <tt>:gemdeps</tt> option in
<tt>options</tt>, yielding to the <tt>block</tt> as in #install.

If <tt>:without_groups</tt> is given in the <tt>options</tt>, those groups in
the gem dependencies file are not used.  See Gem::Installer for other
<tt>options</tt>.

Gem::RequestSet#resolve.name: resolve
Gem::RequestSet#resolve.comment:
Resolve the requested dependencies and return an Array of Specification
objects to be activated.

Gem::RequestSet#resolve_current.name: resolve_current
Gem::RequestSet#resolve_current.comment:
Resolve the requested dependencies against the gems available via Gem.path and
return an Array of Specification objects to be activated.

Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI.name: Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI
Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI.comment:
A semi-compatible DSL for the Bundler Gemfile and Isolate gem dependencies
files.

To work with both the Bundler Gemfile and Isolate formats this implementation
takes some liberties to allow compatibility with each, most notably in
#source.

A basic gem dependencies file will look like the following:

  source 'https://rubygems.org'

  gem 'rails', '3.2.14a
  gem 'devise', '>= 2.1.3', '< 3'
  gem 'cancan'
  gem 'airbrake'
  gem 'pg'

RubyGems recommends saving this as gem.deps.rb over Gemfile or Isolate.

To install the gems in this Gemfile use `gem install -g` to install it and
create a lockfile.  The lockfile will ensure that when you make changes to
your gem dependencies file a minimum amount of change is made to the
dependencies of your gems.

RubyGems can activate all the gems in your dependencies file at startup using
the RUBYGEMS_GEMDEPS environment variable or through Gem.use_gemdeps. See
Gem.use_gemdeps for details and warnings.

See `gem help install` and `gem help gem_dependencies` for further details.

Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI::new.name: new
Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI::new.comment:
Creates a new GemDependencyAPI that will add dependencies to the
Gem::RequestSet <tt>set</tt> based on the dependency API description in
<tt>path</tt>.

Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI#gem.name: gem
Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI#gem.comment:
Specifies a gem dependency with the given <tt>name</tt> and
<tt>requirements</tt>.  You may also supply <tt>options</tt> following the
<tt>requirements</tt>

<tt>options</tt> include:

require::
  RubyGems does not provide any autorequire features so requires in a gem
  dependencies file are recorded but ignored.

  In bundler the require: option overrides the file to require during
  Bundler.require.  By default the name of the dependency is required in
  Bundler.  A single file or an Array of files may be given.

  To disable requiring any file give <tt>false</tt>:

    gem 'rake', require: false

group::
  Place the dependencies in the given dependency group.  A single group or an
  Array of groups may be given.

  See also #group

platform::
  Only install the dependency on the given platform.  A single platform or an
  Array of platforms may be given.

  See #platform for a list of platforms available.

path::
  Install this dependency from an unpacked gem in the given directory.

    gem 'modified_gem', path: 'vendor/modified_gem'

git::
  Install this dependency from a git repository:

    gem 'private_gem', git: 'git@my.company.example:private_gem.git'

gist::
  Install this dependency from the gist ID:

    gem 'bang', gist: '1232884'

github::
  Install this dependency from a github git repository:

    gem 'private_gem', github: 'my_company/private_gem'

submodules::
  Set to <tt>true</tt> to include submodules when fetching the git repository
  for git:, gist: and github: dependencies.

ref::
  Use the given commit name or SHA for git:, gist: and github: dependencies.

branch::
  Use the given branch for git:, gist: and github: dependencies.

tag::
  Use the given tag for git:, gist: and github: dependencies.

Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI#gemspe.name: gemspec
Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI#gemspe.comment:
Loads dependencies from a gemspec file.

<tt>options</tt> include:

name::
  The name portion of the gemspec file.  Defaults to searching for any gemspec
  file in the current directory.

    gemspec name: 'my_gem'

path::
  The path the gemspec lives in.  Defaults to the current directory:

    gemspec 'my_gem', path: 'gemspecs', name: 'my_gem'

development_group::
  The group to add development dependencies to.  By default this is
  :development.  Only one group may be specified.

Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI#git.name: git
Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI#git.comment:
Block form for specifying gems from a git <tt>repository</tt>.

  git 'https://github.com/rails/rails.git' do
    gem 'activesupport'
    gem 'activerecord'
  end

Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI#git_so.name: git_source
Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI#git_so.comment:
Defines a custom git source that uses <tt>name</tt> to expand git repositories
for use in gems built from git repositories.  You must provide a block that
accepts a git repository name for expansion.

Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI#group.name: group
Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI#group.comment:
Block form for placing a dependency in the given <tt>groups</tt>.

  group :development do
    gem 'debugger'
  end

  group :development, :test do
    gem 'minitest'
  end

Groups can be excluded at install time using `gem install -g --without
development`.  See `gem help install` and `gem help gem_dependencies` for
further details.

Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI#load.name: load
Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI#load.comment: Loads the gem dependency file and returns self.

Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI#platfo.name: platform
Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI#platfo.comment:
Block form for restricting gems to a set of platforms.

The gem dependencies platform is different from Gem::Platform.  A platform
gem.deps.rb platform matches on the ruby engine, the ruby version and whether
or not windows is allowed.

:ruby, :ruby_XY:
  Matches non-windows, non-jruby implementations where X and Y can be used to
  match releases in the 1.8, 1.9, 2.0 or 2.1 series.

:mri, :mri_XY:
  Matches non-windows C Ruby (Matz Ruby) or only the 1.8, 1.9, 2.0 or 2.1
  series.

:mingw, :mingw_XY:
  Matches 32 bit C Ruby on MinGW or only the 1.8, 1.9, 2.0 or 2.1 series.

:x64_mingw, :x64_mingw_XY:
  Matches 64 bit C Ruby on MinGW or only the 1.8, 1.9, 2.0 or 2.1 series.

:mswin, :mswin_XY:
  Matches 32 bit C Ruby on Microsoft Windows or only the 1.8, 1.9, 2.0 or 2.1
  series.

:mswin64, :mswin64_XY:
  Matches 64 bit C Ruby on Microsoft Windows or only the 1.8, 1.9, 2.0 or 2.1
  series.

:jruby, :jruby_XY:
  Matches JRuby or JRuby in 1.8 or 1.9 mode.

:maglev:
  Matches Maglev

:rbx:
  Matches non-windows Rubinius

NOTE:  There is inconsistency in what environment a platform matches.  You may
need to read the source to know the exact details.

Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI#platfo.name: platforms
Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI#platfo.comment:
Block form for restricting gems to a particular set of platforms.  See
#platform.

Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI#ruby.name: ruby
Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI#ruby.comment:
Restricts this gem dependencies file to the given ruby <tt>version</tt>.

You may also provide <tt>engine:</tt> and <tt>engine_version:</tt> options to
restrict this gem dependencies file to a particular ruby engine and its engine
version.  This matching is performed by using the RUBY_ENGINE and
RUBY_ENGINE_VERSION constants.

Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI#source.name: source
Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI#source.comment:
Sets <tt>url</tt> as a source for gems for this dependency API.  RubyGems uses
the default configured sources if no source was given.  If a source is set
only that source is used.

This method differs in behavior from Bundler:

* The <tt>:gemcutter</tt>, # <tt>:rubygems</tt> and <tt>:rubyforge</tt>
  sources are not supported as they are deprecated in bundler.
* The <tt>prepend:</tt> option is not supported.  If you wish to order sources
  then list them in your preferred order.

Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI#pin_ge.name: pin_gem_source
Gem::RequestSet::GemDependencyAPI#pin_ge.comment:
Pins the gem <tt>name</tt> to the given <tt>source</tt>.  Adding a gem with
the same name from a different <tt>source</tt> will raise an exception.

Gem::RequestSet::Lockfile.name: Gem::RequestSet::Lockfile
Gem::RequestSet::Lockfile.comment:
Parses a gem.deps.rb.lock file and constructs a LockSet containing the
dependencies found inside.  If the lock file is missing no LockSet is
constructed.

Gem::RequestSet::Lockfile::build.name: build
Gem::RequestSet::Lockfile::build.comment:
Creates a new Lockfile for the given Gem::RequestSet and
<tt>gem_deps_file</tt> location.

Gem::RequestSet::Lockfile#to_s.name: to_s
Gem::RequestSet::Lockfile#to_s.comment: The contents of the lock file.

Gem::RequestSet::Lockfile#write.name: write
Gem::RequestSet::Lockfile#write.comment: Writes the lock file alongside the gem dependencies file

Gem::RequestSet::Lockfile::ParseError.name: Gem::RequestSet::Lockfile::ParseError
Gem::RequestSet::Lockfile::ParseError.comment: Raised when a lockfile cannot be parsed

Gem::RequestSet::Lockfile::ParseError::n.name: new
Gem::RequestSet::Lockfile::ParseError::n.comment:
Raises a ParseError with the given <tt>message</tt> which was encountered at a
<tt>line</tt> and <tt>column</tt> while parsing.

Gem::Requirement.name: Gem::Requirement
Gem::Requirement.comment:
A Requirement is a set of one or more version restrictions. It supports a few
(<tt>=, !=, >, <, >=, <=, ~></tt>) different restriction operators.

See Gem::Version for a description on how versions and requirements work
together in RubyGems.

Gem::Requirement::create.name: create
Gem::Requirement::create.comment:
Factory method to create a Gem::Requirement object.  Input may be a Version, a
String, or nil.  Intended to simplify client code.

If the input is "weird", the default version requirement is returned.

Gem::Requirement::new.name: new
Gem::Requirement::new.comment:
Constructs a requirement from <tt>requirements</tt>. Requirements can be
Strings, Gem::Versions, or Arrays of those. <tt>nil</tt> and duplicate
requirements are ignored. An empty set of <tt>requirements</tt> is the same as
<tt>">= 0"</tt>.

Gem::Requirement::parse.name: parse
Gem::Requirement::parse.comment:
Parse <tt>obj</tt>, returning an <tt>[op, version]</tt> pair. <tt>obj</tt> can
be a String or a Gem::Version.

If <tt>obj</tt> is a String, it can be either a full requirement
specification, like <tt>">= 1.2"</tt>, or a simple version number, like
<tt>"1.2"</tt>.

  parse("> 1.0")                 # => [">", Gem::Version.new("1.0")]
  parse("1.0")                   # => ["=", Gem::Version.new("1.0")]
  parse(Gem::Version.new("1.0")) # => ["=,  Gem::Version.new("1.0")]

Gem::Requirement#concat.name: concat
Gem::Requirement#concat.comment: Concatenates the <tt>new</tt> requirements onto this requirement.

Gem::Requirement#exact?.name: exact?
Gem::Requirement#exact?.comment: true if the requirement is for only an exact version

Gem::Requirement#none?.name: none?
Gem::Requirement#none?.comment: true if this gem has no requirements.

Gem::Requirement#prerelease?.name: prerelease?
Gem::Requirement#prerelease?.comment:
A requirement is a prerelease if any of the versions inside of it are
prereleases

Gem::Requirement#specific?.name: specific?
Gem::Requirement#specific?.comment: True if the requirement will not always match the latest version.

Gem::Requirement::BadRequirementError.name: Gem::Requirement::BadRequirementError
Gem::Requirement::BadRequirementError.comment: Raised when a bad requirement is encountered

Gem::Resolver.name: Gem::Resolver
Gem::Resolver.comment:
Given a set of Gem::Dependency objects as <tt>needed</tt> and a way to query
the set of available specs via <tt>set</tt>, calculates a set of
ActivationRequest objects which indicate all the specs that should be
activated to meet the all the requirements.

Gem::Resolver::compose_sets.name: compose_sets
Gem::Resolver::compose_sets.comment:
Combines <tt>sets</tt> into a ComposedSet that allows specification lookup in
a uniform manner.  If one of the <tt>sets</tt> is itself a ComposedSet its
sets are flattened into the result ComposedSet.

Gem::Resolver::for_current_gems.name: for_current_gems
Gem::Resolver::for_current_gems.comment:
Creates a Resolver that queries only against the already installed gems for
the <tt>needed</tt> dependencies.

Gem::Resolver::new.name: new
Gem::Resolver::new.comment:
Create Resolver object which will resolve the tree starting with
<tt>needed</tt> Dependency objects.

<tt>set</tt> is an object that provides where to look for specifications to
satisfy the Dependencies. This defaults to IndexSet, which will query
rubygems.org.

Gem::Resolver#cooldown_skipped.name: cooldown_skipped
Gem::Resolver#cooldown_skipped.comment:
Per-gem summary entries for the newest versions the cooldown kept out of a
successful resolution.  See Gem::Cooldown.output_skipped_summary.

Gem::Resolver#resolve.name: resolve
Gem::Resolver#resolve.comment: Proceed with resolution! Returns an array of ActivationRequest objects.

Gem::Resolver#cooldown_skipped_summary.name: cooldown_skipped_summary
Gem::Resolver#cooldown_skipped_summary.comment:
Reports, per gem, the newest version that the cooldown kept out of a
successful resolution.  A skipped version is only worth reporting when it is
newer than the resolved version and satisfies every requirement the final
resolution places on that gem, so we don't claim a version the resolver could
never have picked anyway.

Gem::Resolver#filter_cooldown_specs.name: filter_cooldown_specs
Gem::Resolver#filter_cooldown_specs.comment:
Rejects specs published within the cooldown period.  Specs with an unknown
publish time (installed gems, lockfiles, sources without timestamps) are kept,
so the cooldown fails open.

Gem::Resolver#range_admits_prerelease?.name: range_admits_prerelease?
Gem::Resolver#range_admits_prerelease?.comment:
Only the min bound is inspected: `~>` synthesises a max like `X.A` whose
suffix looks prerelease to Gem::Version but is not the user's intent, so
checking max would mis-admit prereleases for every `~>`.

Gem::Resolver::APISet.name: Gem::Resolver::APISet
Gem::Resolver::APISet.comment:
The global rubygems pool, available via the Compact Index API. Returns
instances of APISpecification.

Gem::Resolver::APISet::new.name: new
Gem::Resolver::APISet::new.comment:
Creates a new APISet that will retrieve gems from <tt>uri</tt> using the
Compact Index API URL <tt>dep_uri</tt> which is described at
https://guides.rubygems.org/rubygems-org-compact-index-api

Gem::Resolver::APISet#find_all.name: find_all
Gem::Resolver::APISet#find_all.comment:
Return an array of APISpecification objects matching DependencyRequest
<tt>req</tt>.

Gem::Resolver::APISet#prefetch.name: prefetch
Gem::Resolver::APISet#prefetch.comment:
A hint run by the resolver to allow the Set to fetch data for
DependencyRequests <tt>reqs</tt>.

Gem::Resolver::APISpecification.name: Gem::Resolver::APISpecification
Gem::Resolver::APISpecification.comment:
Represents a specification retrieved via the Compact Index API.

This is used to avoid loading the full Specification object when all we need
is the name, version, and dependencies.

Gem::Resolver::APISpecification::new.name: new
Gem::Resolver::APISpecification::new.comment:
Creates an APISpecification for the given <tt>set</tt> from the Compact Index
API <tt>api_data</tt>.

See https://guides.rubygems.org/rubygems-org-compact-index-api for the format
of the <tt>api_data</tt>.

Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest.name: Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest
Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest.comment:
Specifies a Specification object that should be activated.  Also contains a
dependency that was used to introduce this activation.

Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest::new.name: new
Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest::new.comment:
Creates a new ActivationRequest that will activate <tt>spec</tt>.  The parent
<tt>request</tt> is used to provide diagnostics in case of conflicts.

Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest#develop.name: development?
Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest#develop.comment: Is this activation request for a development dependency?

Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest#downloa.name: download
Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest#downloa.comment: Downloads a gem at <tt>path</tt> and returns the file path.

Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest#full_na.name: full_name
Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest#full_na.comment: The full name of the specification to be activated.

Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest#full_sp.name: full_spec
Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest#full_sp.comment: The Gem::Specification for this activation request.

Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest#install.name: installed?
Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest#install.comment: True if the requested gem has already been installed.

Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest#name.name: name
Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest#name.comment: The name of this activation request's specification

Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest#parent.name: parent
Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest#parent.comment:
Return the ActivationRequest that contained the dependency that we were
activated for.

Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest#platfor.name: platform
Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest#platfor.comment: The platform of this activation request's specification

Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest#version.name: version
Gem::Resolver::ActivationRequest#version.comment: The version of this activation request's specification

Gem::Resolver::BestSet.name: Gem::Resolver::BestSet
Gem::Resolver::BestSet.comment:
The BestSet chooses the best available method to query a remote index.

It combines IndexSet and APISet

Gem::Resolver::BestSet::new.name: new
Gem::Resolver::BestSet::new.comment:
Creates a BestSet for the given <tt>sources</tt> or Gem::sources if none are
specified.  <tt>sources</tt> must be a Gem::SourceList.

Gem::Resolver::ComposedSet.name: Gem::Resolver::ComposedSet
Gem::Resolver::ComposedSet.comment:
A ComposedSet allows multiple sets to be queried like a single set.

To create a composed set with any number of sets use:

  Gem::Resolver.compose_sets set1, set2

This method will eliminate nesting of composed sets.

Gem::Resolver::ComposedSet::new.name: new
Gem::Resolver::ComposedSet::new.comment:
Creates a new ComposedSet containing <tt>sets</tt>.  Use
Gem::Resolver::compose_sets instead.

Gem::Resolver::ComposedSet#find_all.name: find_all
Gem::Resolver::ComposedSet#find_all.comment: Finds all specs matching <tt>req</tt> in all sets.

Gem::Resolver::ComposedSet#prerelease=.name: prerelease=
Gem::Resolver::ComposedSet#prerelease=.comment:
When <tt>allow_prerelease</tt> is set to <tt>true</tt> prereleases gems are
allowed to match dependencies.

Gem::Resolver::ComposedSet#remote=.name: remote=
Gem::Resolver::ComposedSet#remote=.comment: Sets the remote network access for all composed sets.

Gem::Resolver::CurrentSet.name: Gem::Resolver::CurrentSet
Gem::Resolver::CurrentSet.comment:
A set which represents the installed gems. Respects all the normal settings
that control where to look for installed gems.

Gem::Resolver::DependencyRequest.name: Gem::Resolver::DependencyRequest
Gem::Resolver::DependencyRequest.comment:
Used Internally. Wraps a Dependency object to also track which spec contained
the Dependency.

Gem::Resolver::DependencyRequest::new.name: new
Gem::Resolver::DependencyRequest::new.comment:
Creates a new DependencyRequest for <tt>dependency</tt> from
<tt>requester</tt>. +requester may be nil if the request came from a user.

Gem::Resolver::DependencyRequest#develop.name: development?
Gem::Resolver::DependencyRequest#develop.comment: Is this dependency a development dependency?

Gem::Resolver::DependencyRequest#explici.name: explicit?
Gem::Resolver::DependencyRequest#explici.comment: Indicate that the request is for a gem explicitly requested by the user

Gem::Resolver::DependencyRequest#implici.name: implicit?
Gem::Resolver::DependencyRequest#implici.comment:
Indicate that the request is for a gem requested as a dependency of another
gem

Gem::Resolver::DependencyRequest#match?.name: match?
Gem::Resolver::DependencyRequest#match?.comment:
Does this dependency request match <tt>spec</tt>?

NOTE:  #match? only matches prerelease versions when #dependency is a
prerelease dependency.

Gem::Resolver::DependencyRequest#matches.name: matches_spec?
Gem::Resolver::DependencyRequest#matches.comment:
Does this dependency request match <tt>spec</tt>?

NOTE:  #matches_spec? matches prerelease versions.  See also #match?

Gem::Resolver::DependencyRequest#name.name: name
Gem::Resolver::DependencyRequest#name.comment: The name of the gem this dependency request is requesting.

Gem::Resolver::DependencyRequest#request.name: request_context
Gem::Resolver::DependencyRequest#request.comment:
Return a String indicating who caused this request to be added (only valid for
implicit requests)

Gem::Resolver::DependencyRequest#require.name: requirement
Gem::Resolver::DependencyRequest#require.comment: The version requirement for this dependency request

Gem::Resolver::GitSet.name: Gem::Resolver::GitSet
Gem::Resolver::GitSet.comment:
A GitSet represents gems that are sourced from git repositories.

This is used for gem dependency file support.

Example:

  set = Gem::Resolver::GitSet.new
  set.add_git_gem 'rake', 'git://example/rake.git', tag: 'rake-10.1.0'

Gem::Resolver::GitSet#prefetch.name: prefetch
Gem::Resolver::GitSet#prefetch.comment: Prefetches specifications from the git repositories in this set.

Gem::Resolver::GitSpecification.name: Gem::Resolver::GitSpecification
Gem::Resolver::GitSpecification.comment:
A GitSpecification represents a gem that is sourced from a git repository and
is being loaded through a gem dependencies file through the <tt>git:</tt>
option.

Gem::Resolver::GitSpecification#install.name: install
Gem::Resolver::GitSpecification#install.comment:
Installing a git gem only involves building the extensions and generating the
executables.

Gem::Resolver::IndexSet.name: Gem::Resolver::IndexSet
Gem::Resolver::IndexSet.comment: The global rubygems pool represented via the traditional source index.

Gem::Resolver::IndexSet#find_all.name: find_all
Gem::Resolver::IndexSet#find_all.comment:
Return an array of IndexSpecification objects matching DependencyRequest
<tt>req</tt>.

Gem::Resolver::IndexSpecification.name: Gem::Resolver::IndexSpecification
Gem::Resolver::IndexSpecification.comment:
Represents a possible Specification object returned from IndexSet.  Used to
delay needed to download full Specification objects when only the
<tt>name</tt> and <tt>version</tt> are needed.

Gem::Resolver::IndexSpecification::new.name: new
Gem::Resolver::IndexSpecification::new.params: (set, name, version, source, platform, content_address: nil)
Gem::Resolver::IndexSpecification::new.comment:
An IndexSpecification is created from the index format described in `gem help
generate_index`.

The <tt>set</tt> contains other specifications for this (URL) <tt>source</tt>.

The <tt>name</tt>, <tt>version</tt> and <tt>platform</tt> are the name,
version and platform of the gem.

Gem::Resolver::IndexSpecification#depend.name: dependencies
Gem::Resolver::IndexSpecification#depend.comment: The dependencies of the gem for this specification

Gem::Resolver::IndexSpecification#requir.name: required_ruby_version
Gem::Resolver::IndexSpecification#requir.comment:
The required_ruby_version constraint for this specification

A fallback is included because when generated, some marshalled specs have it
set to <tt>nil</tt>.

Gem::Resolver::IndexSpecification#requir.name: required_rubygems_version
Gem::Resolver::IndexSpecification#requir.comment:
The required_rubygems_version constraint for this specification

A fallback is included because the original version of the specification API
didn't include that field, so some marshalled specs in the index have it set
to <tt>nil</tt>.

Gem::Resolver::InstalledSpecification.name: Gem::Resolver::InstalledSpecification
Gem::Resolver::InstalledSpecification.comment: An InstalledSpecification represents a gem that is already installed locally.

Gem::Resolver::InstalledSpecification#in.name: install
Gem::Resolver::InstalledSpecification#in.comment:
This is a null install as this specification is already installed.
<tt>options</tt> are ignored.

Gem::Resolver::InstalledSpecification#in.name: installable_platform?
Gem::Resolver::InstalledSpecification#in.comment: Returns <tt>true</tt> if this gem is installable for the current platform.

Gem::Resolver::InstallerSet.name: Gem::Resolver::InstallerSet
Gem::Resolver::InstallerSet.comment:
A set of gems for installation sourced from remote sources and local .gem
files

Gem::Resolver::InstallerSet::new.name: new
Gem::Resolver::InstallerSet::new.comment: Creates a new InstallerSet that will look for gems in <tt>domain</tt>.

Gem::Resolver::InstallerSet#add_always_i.name: add_always_install
Gem::Resolver::InstallerSet#add_always_i.comment:
Looks up the latest specification for <tt>dependency</tt> and adds it to the
always_install list.

Gem::Resolver::InstallerSet#add_local.name: add_local
Gem::Resolver::InstallerSet#add_local.comment:
Adds a local gem requested using <tt>dep_name</tt> with the given
<tt>spec</tt> that can be loaded and installed using the <tt>source</tt>.

Gem::Resolver::InstallerSet#find_all.name: find_all
Gem::Resolver::InstallerSet#find_all.comment:
Returns an array of IndexSpecification objects matching DependencyRequest
<tt>req</tt>.

Gem::Resolver::LocalSpecification.name: Gem::Resolver::LocalSpecification
Gem::Resolver::LocalSpecification.comment: A LocalSpecification comes from a .gem file on the local filesystem.

Gem::Resolver::LocalSpecification#instal.name: installable_platform?
Gem::Resolver::LocalSpecification#instal.comment: Returns <tt>true</tt> if this gem is installable for the current platform.

Gem::Resolver::LockSet.name: Gem::Resolver::LockSet
Gem::Resolver::LockSet.comment: A set of gems from a gem dependencies lockfile.

Gem::Resolver::LockSet::new.name: new
Gem::Resolver::LockSet::new.comment: Creates a new LockSet from the given <tt>sources</tt>

Gem::Resolver::LockSet#find_all.name: find_all
Gem::Resolver::LockSet#find_all.comment:
Returns an Array of IndexSpecification objects matching the DependencyRequest
<tt>req</tt>.

Gem::Resolver::LockSpecification.name: Gem::Resolver::LockSpecification
Gem::Resolver::LockSpecification.comment:
The LockSpecification comes from a lockfile (Gem::RequestSet::Lockfile).

Gem::Resolver::RequirementList.name: Gem::Resolver::RequirementList

The RequirementList is used to hold the requirements being considered while
resolving a set of gems.

The RequirementList acts like a queue where the oldest items are removed
first.

Gem::Resolver::RequirementList#add.name: add
Gem::Resolver::RequirementList#add.comment: Adds Resolver::DependencyRequest <tt>req</tt> to this requirements list.

Gem::Resolver::RequirementList#next5.name: next5

Gem::Resolver::RequirementList#remove.name: remove

Gem::Resolver::RequirementList#size.name: size

Gem::Resolver::RootPackage.name: Gem::Resolver::RootPackage

Custom root package so error messages say "your request depends on..." instead
of PubGrub's default "root depends on...".

Gem::Resolver::Set.name: Gem::Resolver::Set

Resolver sets are used to look up specifications (and their dependencies) used
in resolution.  This set is abstract.

The #prefetch method may be overridden, but this is not necessary.  This
default implementation does nothing, which is suitable for sets where looking
up a specification is cheap (such as installed gems).

<tt>reqs</tt>.

Gem::Resolver::SourceSet.name: Gem::Resolver::SourceSet

Kind off like BestSet but filters the sources for gems

Installs this specification using the Gem::Installer <tt>options</tt>.  The

Gem::Resolver::VendorSet.name: Gem::Resolver::VendorSet

and is being loaded through a gem dependencies file through the <tt>path:</tt>

Gem::RubyVersionMismatch.name: Gem::RubyVersionMismatch

Gem::SafeYAML.name: Gem::SafeYAML

specifications.  For loading other YAML safely, please see Psych.safe_load

Gem::Security.name: Gem::Security
Gem::Security.comment:
= Signing gems

The Gem::Security implements cryptographic signatures for gems.  The section
below is a step-by-step guide to using signed gems and generating your own.

== Walkthrough

=== Building your certificate

In order to start signing your gems, you'll need to build a private key and a
self-signed certificate.  Here's how:

  # build a private key and certificate for yourself:
  $ gem cert --build you@example.com

This could take anywhere from a few seconds to a minute or two, depending on
the speed of your computer (public key algorithms aren't exactly the speediest
crypto algorithms in the world).  When it's finished, you'll see the files
"gem-private_key.pem" and "gem-public_cert.pem" in the current directory.

First things first: Move both files to ~/.gem if you don't already have a key
and certificate in that directory.  Ensure the file permissions make the key
unreadable by others (by default the file is saved securely).

Keep your private key hidden; if it's compromised, someone can sign packages
as you (note: PKI has ways of mitigating the risk of stolen keys; more on that
later).

=== Signing Gems

In RubyGems 2 and newer there is no extra work to sign a gem.  RubyGems will
automatically find your key and certificate in your home directory and use
them to sign newly packaged gems.

If your certificate is not self-signed (signed by a third party) RubyGems will
attempt to load the certificate chain from the trusted certificates. Use
<tt>gem cert --add signing_cert.pem</tt> to add your signers as trusted
certificates.  See below for further information on certificate chains.

If you build your gem it will automatically be signed.  If you peek inside
your gem file, you'll see a couple of new files have been added:

  $ tar tf your-gem-1.0.gem
  metadata.gz
  metadata.gz.sig # metadata signature
  data.tar.gz
  data.tar.gz.sig # data signature
  checksums.yaml.gz
  checksums.yaml.gz.sig # checksums signature

=== Manually signing gems

If you wish to store your key in a separate secure location you'll need to set
your gems up for signing by hand.  To do this, set the <tt>signing_key</tt>
and <tt>cert_chain</tt> in the gemspec before packaging your gem:

  s.signing_key = '/secure/path/to/gem-private_key.pem'
  s.cert_chain = %w[/secure/path/to/gem-public_cert.pem]

When you package your gem with these options set RubyGems will automatically
load your key and certificate from the secure paths.

=== Signed gems and security policies

Now let's verify the signature.  Go ahead and install the gem, but add the
following options: <tt>-P HighSecurity</tt>, like this:

  # install the gem with using the security policy "HighSecurity"
  $ sudo gem install your.gem -P HighSecurity

The <tt>-P</tt> option sets your security policy -- we'll talk about that in
just a minute.  Eh, what's this?

  $ gem install -P HighSecurity your-gem-1.0.gem
  ERROR:  While executing gem ... (Gem::Security::Exception)
      root cert /CN=you/DC=example is not trusted

The culprit here is the security policy.  RubyGems has several different
security policies.  Let's take a short break and go over the security
policies.  Here's a list of the available security policies, and a brief
description of each one:

* NoSecurity - Well, no security at all.  Signed packages are treated like
  unsigned packages.
* LowSecurity - Pretty much no security.  If a package is signed then RubyGems
  will make sure the signature matches the signing certificate, and that the
  signing certificate hasn't expired, but that's it.  A malicious user could
  easily circumvent this kind of security.
* MediumSecurity - Better than LowSecurity and NoSecurity, but still fallible.
   Package contents are verified against the signing certificate, and the
  signing certificate is checked for validity, and checked against the rest of
  the certificate chain (if you don't know what a certificate chain is, stay
  tuned, we'll get to that). The biggest improvement over LowSecurity is that
  MediumSecurity won't install packages that are signed by untrusted sources.
  Unfortunately, MediumSecurity still isn't totally secure -- a malicious user
  can still unpack the gem, strip the signatures, and distribute the gem
  unsigned.
* HighSecurity - Here's the bugger that got us into this mess. The
  HighSecurity policy is identical to the MediumSecurity policy, except that
  it does not allow unsigned gems.  A malicious user doesn't have a whole lot
  of options here; they can't modify the package contents without invalidating
  the signature, and they can't modify or remove signature or the signing
  certificate chain, or RubyGems will simply refuse to install the package.
  Oh well, maybe they'll have better luck causing problems for CPAN users
  instead :).

The reason RubyGems refused to install your shiny new signed gem was because
it was from an untrusted source.  Well, your code is infallible (naturally),
so you need to add yourself as a trusted source:

  # add trusted certificate
  gem cert --add ~/.gem/gem-public_cert.pem

You've now added your public certificate as a trusted source.  Now you can
install packages signed by your private key without any hassle.  Let's try the
install command above again:

  # install the gem with using the HighSecurity policy (and this time
  # without any shenanigans)
  $ gem install -P HighSecurity your-gem-1.0.gem
  Successfully installed your-gem-1.0
  1 gem installed

This time RubyGems will accept your signed package and begin installing.

While you're waiting for RubyGems to work it's magic, have a look at some of
the other security commands by running <tt>gem help cert</tt>:

  Options:
    -a, --add CERT                   Add a trusted certificate.
    -l, --list [FILTER]              List trusted certificates where the
                                     subject contains FILTER
    -r, --remove FILTER              Remove trusted certificates where the
                                     subject contains FILTER
    -b, --build EMAIL_ADDR           Build private key and self-signed
                                     certificate for EMAIL_ADDR
    -C, --certificate CERT           Signing certificate for --sign
    -K, --private-key KEY            Key for --sign or --build
    -A, --key-algorithm ALGORITHM    Select key algorithm for --build from
                                     RSA, DSA, EC, ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65,
                                     or ML-DSA-87. Defaults to RSA.
    -s, --sign CERT                  Signs CERT with the key from -K
                                     and the certificate from -C
    -d, --days NUMBER_OF_DAYS        Days before the certificate expires
    -R, --re-sign                    Re-signs the certificate from -C with the key from -K

We've already covered the <tt>--build</tt> option, and the <tt>--add</tt>,
<tt>--list</tt>, and <tt>--remove</tt> commands seem fairly straightforward;
they allow you to add, list, and remove the certificates in your trusted
certificate list.  But what's with this <tt>--sign</tt> option?

=== Certificate chains

To answer that question, let's take a look at "certificate chains", a concept
I mentioned earlier.  There are a couple of problems with self-signed
certificates: first of all, self-signed certificates don't offer a whole lot
of security.  Sure, the certificate says Yukihiro Matsumoto, but how do I know
it was actually generated and signed by matz himself unless he gave me the
certificate in person?

The second problem is scalability.  Sure, if there are 50 gem authors, then I
have 50 trusted certificates, no problem.  What if there are 500 gem authors?
1000?  Having to constantly add new trusted certificates is a pain, and it
actually makes the trust system less secure by encouraging RubyGems users to
blindly trust new certificates.

Here's where certificate chains come in.  A certificate chain establishes an
arbitrarily long chain of trust between an issuing certificate and a child
certificate.  So instead of trusting certificates on a per-developer basis, we
use the PKI concept of certificate chains to build a logical hierarchy of
trust.  Here's a hypothetical example of a trust hierarchy based (roughly) on
geography:

                      --------------------------
                      | rubygems@rubygems.org |
                      --------------------------
                                  |
                -----------------------------------
                |                                 |
    ----------------------------    -----------------------------
    |  seattlerb@seattlerb.org |    | dcrubyists@richkilmer.com |
    ----------------------------    -----------------------------
         |                |                 |             |
  ---------------   ----------------   -----------   --------------
  |   drbrain   |   |   zenspider  |   | pabs@dc |   | tomcope@dc |
  ---------------   ----------------   -----------   --------------

Now, rather than having 4 trusted certificates (one for drbrain, zenspider,
pabs@dc, and tomecope@dc), a user could actually get by with one certificate,
the "rubygems@rubygems.org" certificate.

Here's how it works:

I install "rdoc-3.12.gem", a package signed by "drbrain".  I've never heard of
"drbrain", but his certificate has a valid signature from the
"seattle.rb@seattlerb.org" certificate, which in turn has a valid signature
from the "rubygems@rubygems.org" certificate.  Voila!  At this point, it's
much more reasonable for me to trust a package signed by "drbrain", because I
can establish a chain to "rubygems@rubygems.org", which I do trust.

=== Signing certificates

The <tt>--sign</tt> option allows all this to happen.  A developer creates
their build certificate with the <tt>--build</tt> option, then has their
certificate signed by taking it with them to their next regional Ruby meetup
(in our hypothetical example), and it's signed there by the person holding the
regional RubyGems signing certificate, which is signed at the next RubyConf by
the holder of the top-level RubyGems certificate.  At each point the issuer
runs the same command:

  # sign a certificate with the specified key and certificate
  # (note that this modifies client_cert.pem!)
  $ gem cert -K /mnt/floppy/issuer-priv_key.pem -C issuer-pub_cert.pem
     --sign client_cert.pem

Then the holder of issued certificate (in this case, your buddy "drbrain"),
can start using this signed certificate to sign RubyGems.  By the way, in
order to let everyone else know about his new fancy signed certificate,
"drbrain" would save his newly signed certificate as
<tt>~/.gem/gem-public_cert.pem</tt>

Obviously this RubyGems trust infrastructure doesn't exist yet.  Also, in the
"real world", issuers actually generate the child certificate from a
certificate request, rather than sign an existing certificate.  And our
hypothetical infrastructure is missing a certificate revocation system. These
are that can be fixed in the future...

At this point you should know how to do all of these new and interesting
things:

* build a gem signing key and certificate
* adjust your security policy
* modify your trusted certificate list
* sign a certificate

== Manually verifying signatures

In case you don't trust RubyGems you can verify gem signatures manually:

1. Fetch and unpack the gem

     gem fetch some_signed_gem
     tar -xf some_signed_gem-1.0.gem

2. Grab the public key from the gemspec

     gem spec some_signed_gem-1.0.gem cert_chain | \
       ruby -rpsych -e 'puts Psych.load($stdin)' > public_key.crt

3. Generate a SHA1 hash of the data.tar.gz

     openssl dgst -sha1 < data.tar.gz > my.hash

4. Verify the signature

     openssl rsautl -verify -inkey public_key.crt -certin \
       -in data.tar.gz.sig > verified.hash

5. Compare your hash to the verified hash

     diff -s verified.hash my.hash

6. Repeat 5 and 6 with metadata.gz

== OpenSSL Reference

The .pem files generated by --build and --sign are PEM files.  Here's a couple
of useful OpenSSL commands for manipulating them:

  # convert a PEM format X509 certificate into DER format:
  # (note: Windows .cer files are X509 certificates in DER format)
  $ openssl x509 -in input.pem -outform der -out output.der

  # print out the certificate in a human-readable format:
  $ openssl x509 -in input.pem -noout -text

And you can do the same thing with the private key file as well:

  # convert a PEM format RSA key into DER format:
  $ openssl rsa -in input_key.pem -outform der -out output_key.der

  # print out the key in a human readable format:
  $ openssl rsa -in input_key.pem -noout -text

== Bugs/TODO

* There's no way to define a system-wide trust list.
* custom security policies (from a YAML file, etc)
* Simple method to generate a signed certificate request
* Support for OCSP, SCVP, CRLs, or some other form of cert status check (list
  is in order of preference)
* Support for encrypted private keys
* Some sort of semi-formal trust hierarchy (see long-winded explanation above)
* Path discovery (for gem certificate chains that don't have a self-signed
  root) -- by the way, since we don't have this, THE ROOT OF THE CERTIFICATE
  CHAIN MUST BE SELF SIGNED if Policy#verify_root is true (and it is for the
  MediumSecurity and HighSecurity policies)
* Better explanation of X509 naming (ie, we don't have to use email addresses)
* Honor AIA field (see note about OCSP above)
* Honor extension restrictions
* Might be better to store the certificate chain as a PKCS#7 or PKCS#12 file,
  instead of an array embedded in the metadata.
