Gem::Security::create_cert.name: create_cert
Gem::Security::create_cert.params: (subject, key, age = ONE_YEAR, extensions = EXTENSIONS, serial = 1)
Gem::Security::create_cert.comment:
Creates an unsigned certificate for <tt>subject</tt> and <tt>key</tt>.  The
lifetime of the key is from the current time to <tt>age</tt> which defaults to
one year.

The <tt>extensions</tt> restrict the key to the indicated uses.

Gem::Security::create_cert_email.name: create_cert_email
Gem::Security::create_cert_email.comment:
Creates a self-signed certificate with an issuer and subject from
<tt>email</tt>, a subject alternative name of <tt>email</tt> and the given
<tt>extensions</tt> for the <tt>key</tt>.

Gem::Security::create_cert_self_signed.name: create_cert_self_signed
Gem::Security::create_cert_self_signed.params: (subject, key, age = ONE_YEAR, extensions = EXTENSIONS, serial = 1)
Gem::Security::create_cert_self_signed.comment:
Creates a self-signed certificate with an issuer and subject of
<tt>subject</tt> and the given <tt>extensions</tt> for the <tt>key</tt>.

Gem::Security::create_digest.name: create_digest
Gem::Security::create_digest.comment:
Creates a new digest instance using the specified <tt>algorithm</tt>. The
default is SHA256.

Gem::Security::create_key.name: create_key
Gem::Security::create_key.comment:
Creates a new key pair of the specified <tt>algorithm</tt>. RSA, DSA, EC,
ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, and ML-DSA-87 are supported.

Gem::Security::digest_required?.name: digest_required?
Gem::Security::digest_required?.comment:
Returns whether the <tt>key</tt> requires an explicit digest algorithm for
signing and verification. ML-DSA has a built-in digest and does not accept
one. Any other algorithm raises, since a gem carries no record of how its
signature was produced and RubyGems must not guess.

Gem::Security::get_public_key.name: get_public_key
Gem::Security::get_public_key.comment: Gets the right public key from a PKey instance

Gem::Security::re_sign.name: re_sign
Gem::Security::re_sign.comment:
Signs <tt>expired_certificate</tt> with <tt>private_key</tt> if the keys match
and the expired certificate was self-signed.

Gem::Security::reset.name: reset
Gem::Security::reset.comment: Resets the trust directory for verifying gems.

Gem::Security::sign.name: sign
Gem::Security::sign.params: (certificate, signing_key, signing_cert, age = ONE_YEAR, extensions = EXTENSIONS, serial = 1)
Gem::Security::sign.comment:
Sign the public key from <tt>certificate</tt> with the <tt>signing_key</tt>
and <tt>signing_cert</tt>, using the Gem::Security::DIGEST_NAME.  Uses the
default certificate validity range and extensions.

Returns the newly signed certificate.

Gem::Security::trust_dir.name: trust_dir
Gem::Security::trust_dir.comment:
Returns a Gem::Security::TrustDir which wraps the directory where trusted
certificates live.

Gem::Security::trusted_certificates.name: trusted_certificates
Gem::Security::trusted_certificates.comment: Enumerates the trusted certificates via Gem::Security::TrustDir.

Gem::Security::write_certificate.name: write_certificate
Gem::Security::write_certificate.comment:
Writes the <tt>certificate</tt> to <tt>path</tt> with the given
<tt>permissions</tt>.

Gem::Security::write_private_key.name: write_private_key
Gem::Security::write_private_key.params: (key, path, permissions = 0o600, passphrase = nil, cipher = KEY_CIPHER)
Gem::Security::write_private_key.comment:
Writes the private <tt>key</tt> to <tt>path</tt> with the given
<tt>permissions</tt>. If passed <tt>passphrase</tt> and <tt>cipher</tt>, the
key is encrypted.

Gem::Security::create_ml_dsa_key.name: create_ml_dsa_key
Gem::Security::create_ml_dsa_key.comment:
Creates an ML-DSA key pair of the <tt>algorithm</tt> such as ML-DSA-65. ML-DSA
requires OpenSSL >= 3.5 or an SSL library supporting ML-DSA.

Gem::Security::ml_dsa_key?.name: ml_dsa_key?
Gem::Security::ml_dsa_key?.comment:
Returns whether <tt>key</tt> uses ML-DSA. OpenSSL::PKey::PKey#oid raises for
the provider-backed keys ML-DSA uses, so the algorithm is read from the
SubjectPublicKeyInfo instead.

Gem::Security::Policy.name: Gem::Security::Policy
Gem::Security::Policy.comment:
A Gem::Security::Policy object encapsulates the settings for verifying signed
gem files.  This is the base class.  You can either declare an instance of
this or use one of the preset security policies in Gem::Security::Policies.

Gem::Security::Policy::new.name: new
Gem::Security::Policy::new.comment: Create a new Gem::Security::Policy object with the given mode and options.

Gem::Security::Policy#check_cert.name: check_cert
Gem::Security::Policy#check_cert.comment:
Ensures that <tt>signer</tt> is valid for <tt>time</tt> and was signed by the
<tt>issuer</tt>. If the <tt>issuer</tt> is <tt>nil</tt> no verification is
performed.

Gem::Security::Policy#check_chain.name: check_chain
Gem::Security::Policy#check_chain.comment:
Verifies each certificate in <tt>chain</tt> has signed the following
certificate and is valid for the given <tt>time</tt>.

Gem::Security::Policy#check_data.name: check_data
Gem::Security::Policy#check_data.comment:
Verifies that <tt>data</tt> matches the <tt>signature</tt> created by
<tt>public_key</tt> and the <tt>digest</tt> algorithm.

Gem::Security::Policy#check_key.name: check_key
Gem::Security::Policy#check_key.comment:
Ensures the public key of <tt>key</tt> matches the public key in
<tt>signer</tt>

Gem::Security::Policy#check_root.name: check_root
Gem::Security::Policy#check_root.comment:
Ensures the root certificate in <tt>chain</tt> is self-signed and valid for
<tt>time</tt>.

Gem::Security::Policy#check_trust.name: check_trust
Gem::Security::Policy#check_trust.comment:
Ensures the root of <tt>chain</tt> has a trusted certificate in
Gem::Security.trust_dir and the digests of the two certificates match
according to <tt>digester</tt>

Gem::Security::Policy#verify.name: verify
Gem::Security::Policy#verify.comment:
For <tt>full_name</tt>, verifies the certificate <tt>chain</tt> is valid, the
<tt>digests</tt> match the signatures <tt>signatures</tt> created by the
signer depending on the <tt>policy</tt> settings.

If <tt>key</tt> is given it is used to validate the signing certificate.

Gem::Security::Policy#verify_signatures.name: verify_signatures
Gem::Security::Policy#verify_signatures.comment:
Extracts the certificate chain from the <tt>spec</tt> and calls #verify to
ensure the signatures and certificate chain is valid according to the policy..

Gem::Security::Signer::new.name: new
Gem::Security::Signer::new.comment:
Creates a new signer with an RSA <tt>key</tt> or path to a key, and a
certificate <tt>chain</tt> containing X509 certificates, encoding certificates
or paths to certificates.

Gem::Security::Signer::re_sign_cert.name: re_sign_cert
Gem::Security::Signer::re_sign_cert.comment: Attempts to re-sign an expired cert with a given private key

Gem::Security::Signer#sign.name: sign
Gem::Security::Signer#sign.comment: Sign data with given digest algorithm

Gem::Security::TrustDir.name: Gem::Security::TrustDir
Gem::Security::TrustDir.comment: The TrustDir manages the trusted certificates for gem signature verification.

Gem::Security::TrustDir::new.name: new
Gem::Security::TrustDir::new.comment:
Creates a new TrustDir using <tt>dir</tt> where the directory and file
permissions will be checked according to <tt>permissions</tt>

Gem::Security::TrustDir#cert_path.name: cert_path
Gem::Security::TrustDir#cert_path.comment: Returns the path to the trusted <tt>certificate</tt>

Gem::Security::TrustDir#issuer_of.name: issuer_of
Gem::Security::TrustDir#issuer_of.comment:
Returns the issuer certificate of the given <tt>certificate</tt> if it exists
in the trust directory.

Gem::Security::TrustDir#name_path.name: name_path
Gem::Security::TrustDir#name_path.comment: Returns the path to the trusted certificate with the given ASN.1 <tt>name</tt>

Gem::Security::TrustDir#trust_cert.name: trust_cert
Gem::Security::TrustDir#trust_cert.comment: Add a certificate to trusted certificate list.

Gem::Security::TrustDir#verify.name: verify
Gem::Security::TrustDir#verify.comment:
Make sure the trust directory exists.  If it does exist, make sure it's
actually a directory.  If not, then create it with the appropriate
permissions.

Gem::SecurityOption.name: Gem::SecurityOption
Gem::SecurityOption.comment: Mixin methods for security option for Gem::Commands

Gem::SilentUI.name: Gem::SilentUI
Gem::SilentUI.comment: SilentUI is a UI choice that is absolutely silent.

Gem::SilentUI::new.name: new
Gem::SilentUI::new.comment: The SilentUI has no arguments as it does not use any stream.

Gem::Source.name: Gem::Source
Gem::Source.comment:
A Source knows how to list and fetch gems from a RubyGems marshal index.

There are other Source subclasses for installed gems, local gems, the Compact
Index API and so-forth.

Gem::Source::new.name: new
Gem::Source::new.comment: Creates a new Source which will use the index located at <tt>uri</tt>.

Gem::Source#<=>.comment: Sources are ordered by installation preference.

Gem::Source#cache_dir.name: cache_dir
Gem::Source#cache_dir.comment: Returns the local directory to write <tt>uri</tt> to.

Gem::Source#created_at.name: created_at
Gem::Source#created_at.comment:
The publish time of gem <tt>name</tt> at <tt>version</tt> for <tt>suffix</tt>,
when this source provides it through the compact index created_at metadata.
Returns nil when the source, the gem or the version has no known publish time.

Gem::Source#created_at_for_tuple.name: created_at_for_tuple
Gem::Source#created_at_for_tuple.comment:
The publish time for <tt>tuple</tt>. Content-addressable tuples are looked up
by content address; all other tuples are looked up by platform.

Gem::Source#decode_content_addressable_t.name: decode_content_addressable_tuples
Gem::Source#decode_content_addressable_t.comment:
Decodes content-addressable <tt>tuples</tt> (whose platform field holds the
content address) into tuples carrying their real platform and Ruby ABI from
the compact index /info metadata.

Gem::Source#dependency_resolver_set.name: dependency_resolver_set
Gem::Source#dependency_resolver_set.comment:
Returns a Set that can fetch specifications from this source.

The set will optionally fetch prereleases if requested.

Gem::Source#download.name: download
Gem::Source#download.comment:
Downloads <tt>spec</tt> and writes it to <tt>dir</tt>.  See also
Gem::RemoteFetcher#download.

Gem::Source#fetch_spec.name: fetch_spec
Gem::Source#fetch_spec.comment: Fetches a specification for the given Gem::NameTuple.

Gem::Source#load_specs.name: load_specs
Gem::Source#load_specs.comment:
Loads <tt>type</tt> kind of specs fetching from +@uri+ if the on-disk cache is
out of date.

<tt>type</tt> is one of the following:

:released   => Return the list of all released specs :latest     => Return the
list of only the highest version of each gem :prerelease => Return the list of
all prerelease only specs

The compact index is used when the source provides it, falling back to the
Marshal spec indexes.

Gem::Source#update_cache?.name: update_cache?
Gem::Source#update_cache?.comment: Returns true when it is possible and safe to update the cache directory.

Gem::Source#load_compact_index_specs.name: load_compact_index_specs
Gem::Source#load_compact_index_specs.comment:
Builds the name tuple list for <tt>type</tt> from the compact index versions
file. Returns nil when the source does not provide a usable compact index, so
the caller can fall back to the Marshal spec indexes.

Gem::Source::Git.name: Gem::Source::Git
Gem::Source::Git.comment:
A git gem for use in a gem dependencies file.

Example:

  source =
    Gem::Source::Git.new 'rake', 'git@example:rake.git', 'rake-10.1.0', false

  source.specs

Gem::Source::Git::new.name: new
Gem::Source::Git::new.comment:
Creates a new git gem source for a gems from loaded from <tt>repository</tt>
at the given <tt>reference</tt>.  The <tt>name</tt> is only used to track the
repository back to a gem dependencies file, it has no real significance as a
git repository may contain multiple gems.  If <tt>submodules</tt> is true,
submodules will be checked out when the gem is installed.

Gem::Source::Git#specs.name: specs
Gem::Source::Git#specs.comment: Loads all gemspecs in the repository

Gem::Source::Installed.name: Gem::Source::Installed
Gem::Source::Installed.comment: Represents an installed gem.  This is used for dependency resolution.

Gem::Source::Installed#<=>.comment: Installed sources sort before all other sources

Gem::Source::Installed#download.name: download
Gem::Source::Installed#download.comment: We don't need to download an installed gem

Gem::Source::Local.name: Gem::Source::Local
Gem::Source::Local.comment:
The local source finds gems in the current directory for fulfilling
dependencies.

Gem::Source::Local#<=>.comment: Local sorts before Gem::Source and after Gem::Source::Installed

Gem::Source::Lock.name: Gem::Source::Lock
Gem::Source::Lock.comment:
A Lock source wraps an installed gem's source and sorts before other sources
during dependency resolution.  This allows RubyGems to prefer gems from
dependency lock files.

Gem::Source::Lock::new.name: new
Gem::Source::Lock::new.comment:
Creates a new Lock source that wraps <tt>source</tt> and moves it earlier in
the sort list.

Gem::Source::Lock#fetch_spec.name: fetch_spec
Gem::Source::Lock#fetch_spec.comment: Delegates to the wrapped source's fetch_spec method.

Gem::Source::SpecificFile.name: Gem::Source::SpecificFile
Gem::Source::SpecificFile.comment:
A source representing a single .gem file.  This is used for installation of
local gems.

Gem::Source::SpecificFile::new.name: new
Gem::Source::SpecificFile::new.comment: Creates a new SpecificFile for the gem in <tt>file</tt>

Gem::Source::SpecificFile#<=>.comment:
Orders this source against <tt>other</tt>.

If <tt>other</tt> is a SpecificFile from a different gem name <tt>nil</tt> is
returned.

If <tt>other</tt> is a SpecificFile from the same gem name the versions are
compared using Gem::Version#<=>

Otherwise Gem::Source#<=> is used.

Gem::Source::Vendor.name: Gem::Source::Vendor
Gem::Source::Vendor.comment: This represents a vendored source that is similar to an installed gem.

Gem::Source::Vendor::new.name: new
Gem::Source::Vendor::new.comment: Creates a new Vendor source for a gem that was unpacked at <tt>path</tt>.

Gem::SourceFetchProblem.name: Gem::SourceFetchProblem
Gem::SourceFetchProblem.comment: An error that indicates we weren't able to fetch some data from a source

Gem::SourceFetchProblem::new.name: new
Gem::SourceFetchProblem::new.comment:
Creates a new SourceFetchProblem for the given <tt>source</tt> and
<tt>error</tt>.

Gem::SourceFetchProblem#wordy.name: wordy
Gem::SourceFetchProblem#wordy.comment: An English description of the error.

Gem::SourceList.name: Gem::SourceList
Gem::SourceList.comment:
The SourceList represents the sources rubygems has been configured to use. A
source may be created from an array of sources:

  Gem::SourceList.from %w[https://rubygems.example https://internal.example]

Or by adding them:

  sources = Gem::SourceList.new
  sources << 'https://rubygems.example'

The most common way to get a SourceList is Gem.sources.

Gem::SourceList::from.name: from
Gem::SourceList::from.comment: Creates a new SourceList from an array of sources.

Gem::SourceList#<<.comment:
Appends <tt>obj</tt> to the source list which may be a Gem::Source, Gem::URI
or URI String.

Gem::SourceList#append.name: append
Gem::SourceList#append.comment:
Appends <tt>obj</tt> to the end of the source list, moving it if already
present. <tt>obj</tt> may be a Gem::Source, Gem::URI or URI String. Moves
<tt>obj</tt> to the end of the list if already present.

Gem::SourceList#clear.name: clear
Gem::SourceList#clear.comment: Removes all sources from the SourceList.

Gem::SourceList#delete.name: delete
Gem::SourceList#delete.comment:
Deletes <tt>source</tt> from the source list which may be a Gem::Source or a
URI.

Gem::SourceList#each.name: each
Gem::SourceList#each.comment: Yields each source URI in the list.

Gem::SourceList#each_source.name: each_source
Gem::SourceList#each_source.comment: Yields each source in the list.

Gem::SourceList#empty?.name: empty?
Gem::SourceList#empty?.comment: Returns true if there are no sources in this SourceList.

Gem::SourceList#first.name: first
Gem::SourceList#first.comment: Returns the first source in the list.

Gem::SourceList#include?.name: include?
Gem::SourceList#include?.comment:
Returns true if this source list includes <tt>other</tt> which may be a
Gem::Source or a source URI.

Gem::SourceList#prepend.name: prepend
Gem::SourceList#prepend.comment:
Prepends <tt>obj</tt> to the beginning of the source list which may be a
Gem::Source, Gem::URI or URI Moves <tt>obj</tt> to the beginning of the list
if already present. String.

Gem::SourceList#replace.name: replace
Gem::SourceList#replace.comment:
Replaces this SourceList with the sources in <tt>other</tt>  See #<< for
acceptable items in <tt>other</tt>.

Gem::SourceList#to_a.name: to_a
Gem::SourceList#to_a.comment: Returns an Array of source URI Strings.

Gem::SpecFetcher.name: Gem::SpecFetcher
Gem::SpecFetcher.comment: SpecFetcher handles metadata updates from remote gem repositories.

Gem::SpecFetcher::fetcher.name: fetcher
Gem::SpecFetcher::fetcher.comment:
Default fetcher instance.  Use this instead of ::new to reduce object
allocation.

Gem::SpecFetcher::new.name: new
Gem::SpecFetcher::new.comment:
Creates a new SpecFetcher.  Ordinarily you want to use the default fetcher
from Gem::SpecFetcher::fetcher which uses the Gem.sources.

If you need to retrieve specifications from a different <tt>source</tt>, you
can send it as an argument.

Gem::SpecFetcher#available_specs.name: available_specs
Gem::SpecFetcher#available_specs.comment:
Returns a list of gems available for each source in Gem::sources.

<tt>type</tt> can be one of 3 values: :released   => Return the list of all
released specs :complete   => Return the list of all specs :latest     =>
Return the list of only the highest version of each gem :prerelease => Return
the list of all prerelease only specs

Gem::SpecFetcher#decode_content_addressa.name: decode_content_addressable_tuples
Gem::SpecFetcher#decode_content_addressa.comment:
Decodes the content-addressable tuples in <tt>spec_tuples</tt> ([tuple,
source] pairs) to carry their real platform and Ruby ABI via each source.

Gem::SpecFetcher#detect.name: detect
Gem::SpecFetcher#detect.comment: Return all gem name tuples who's names match <tt>obj</tt>

Gem::SpecFetcher#search_for_dependency.name: search_for_dependency
Gem::SpecFetcher#search_for_dependency.comment:
Find and fetch gem name tuples that match <tt>dependency</tt>.

If <tt>matching_platform</tt> is false, gems for all platforms are returned.

<tt>type</tt> overrides the index type derived from <tt>dependency</tt>.  See
#available_specs for the list of types.

Gem::SpecFetcher#spec_for_dependency.name: spec_for_dependency
Gem::SpecFetcher#spec_for_dependency.comment:
Find and fetch specs that match <tt>dependency</tt>.

If <tt>matching_platform</tt> is false, gems for all platforms are returned.

Gem::SpecFetcher#suggest_gems_from_name.name: suggest_gems_from_name
Gem::SpecFetcher#suggest_gems_from_name.comment:
Suggests gems based on the supplied <tt>gem_name</tt>. Returns an array of
alternative gem names.

Gem::SpecificGemNotFoundException::new.name: new
Gem::SpecificGemNotFoundException::new.comment:
Creates a new SpecificGemNotFoundException for a gem with the given
<tt>name</tt> and <tt>version</tt>.  Any <tt>errors</tt> encountered when
attempting to find the gem are also stored.

Gem::Specification.name: Gem::Specification
Gem::Specification.comment:
The Specification class contains the information for a gem.  Typically defined
in a .gemspec file or a Rakefile, and looks like this:

  Gem::Specification.new do |s|
    s.name        = 'example'
    s.version     = '0.1.0'
    s.licenses    = ['MIT']
    s.summary     = "This is an example!"
    s.description = "Much longer explanation of the example!"
    s.authors     = ["Ruby Coder"]
    s.email       = 'rubycoder@example.com'
    s.files       = ["lib/example.rb"]
    s.homepage    = 'https://rubygems.org/gems/example'
    s.metadata    = { "source_code_uri" => "https://github.com/example/example" }
  end

Starting in RubyGems 2.0, a Specification can hold arbitrary metadata.  See
#metadata for restrictions on the format and size of metadata items you may
add to a specification.

Specifications must be deterministic, as in the example above. For instance,
you cannot define attributes conditionally:

  # INVALID: do not do this.
  unless RUBY_ENGINE == "jruby"
    s.extensions << "ext/example/extconf.rb"
  end

Gem::Specification::_load.name: _load
Gem::Specification::_load.comment: Load custom marshal format, re-initializing defaults as needed

Gem::Specification::add_spec.name: add_spec
Gem::Specification::add_spec.comment:
Adds <tt>spec</tt> to the known specifications, keeping the collection
properly sorted.

Gem::Specification::all.name: all
Gem::Specification::all.comment:
Returns all specifications. This method is discouraged from use. You probably
want to use one of the Enumerable methods instead.

Gem::Specification::all_names.name: all_names
Gem::Specification::all_names.comment: Return full names of all specs in sorted order.

Gem::Specification::array_attributes.name: array_attributes
Gem::Specification::array_attributes.comment: Return the list of all array-oriented instance variables.

Gem::Specification::attribute_names.name: attribute_names
Gem::Specification::attribute_names.comment: Return the list of all instance variables.

Gem::Specification::default_stubs.name: default_stubs
Gem::Specification::default_stubs.comment: Returns a Gem::StubSpecification for default gems

Gem::Specification::dirs.name: dirs
Gem::Specification::dirs.comment: Return the directories that Specification uses to find specs.

Gem::Specification::dirs=.name: dirs=
Gem::Specification::dirs=.comment:
Set the directories that Specification uses to find specs. Setting this resets
the list of known specs.

Gem::Specification::each.name: each
Gem::Specification::each.comment:
Enumerate every known spec.  See ::dirs= and ::add_spec to set the list of
specs.

Gem::Specification::find_active_stub_by_.name: find_active_stub_by_path
Gem::Specification::find_active_stub_by_.comment:
Return the best specification that contains the file matching <tt>path</tt>,
among those already activated.

Gem::Specification::find_all_by_full_nam.name: find_all_by_full_name
Gem::Specification::find_all_by_full_nam.comment: Returns every spec that has the given <tt>full_name</tt>

Gem::Specification::find_all_by_name.name: find_all_by_name
Gem::Specification::find_all_by_name.comment:
Returns every spec that matches <tt>name</tt> and optional
<tt>requirements</tt>.

Gem::Specification::find_by_full_name.name: find_by_full_name
Gem::Specification::find_by_full_name.comment: Find the best specification matching a <tt>full_name</tt>.

Gem::Specification::find_by_name.name: find_by_name
Gem::Specification::find_by_name.comment:
Find the best specification matching a <tt>name</tt> and
<tt>requirements</tt>. Raises if the dependency doesn't resolve to a valid
specification.

Gem::Specification::find_by_path.name: find_by_path
Gem::Specification::find_by_path.comment: Return the best specification that contains the file matching <tt>path</tt>.

Gem::Specification::find_in_unresolved.name: find_in_unresolved
Gem::Specification::find_in_unresolved.comment:
Return currently unresolved specs that contain the file matching
<tt>path</tt>.

Gem::Specification::find_in_unresolved_t.name: find_in_unresolved_tree
Gem::Specification::find_in_unresolved_t.comment:
Search through all unresolved deps and sub-dependencies and return specs that
contain the file matching <tt>path</tt>.

Gem::Specification::find_inactive_by_pat.name: find_inactive_by_path
Gem::Specification::find_inactive_by_pat.comment:
Return the best specification that contains the file matching <tt>path</tt>
amongst the specs that are not activated.

Gem::Specification::find_unloaded_by_pat.name: find_unloaded_by_path
Gem::Specification::find_unloaded_by_pat.comment:
Return the best specification that contains the file matching <tt>path</tt>
amongst the specs that are not loaded. This method is different than
<tt>find_inactive_by_path</tt> as it will filter out loaded specs by their
name.

Gem::Specification::from_yaml.name: from_yaml
Gem::Specification::from_yaml.comment:
Special loader for YAML files.  When a Specification object is loaded from a
YAML file, it bypasses the normal Ruby object initialization routine
(#initialize).  This method makes up for that and deals with gems of different
ages.

<tt>input</tt> can be anything that YAML.load() accepts: String or IO.

Gem::Specification::latest_spec_for.name: latest_spec_for
Gem::Specification::latest_spec_for.comment: Return the latest installed spec for gem <tt>name</tt>.

Gem::Specification::latest_specs.name: latest_specs
Gem::Specification::latest_specs.comment:
Return the latest specs, optionally including prerelease specs if
<tt>prerelease</tt> is true.

Gem::Specification::load_defaults.name: load_defaults
Gem::Specification::load_defaults.comment: Loads the default specifications. It should be called only once.

Gem::Specification::new.name: new
Gem::Specification::new.comment:
Specification constructor. Assigns the default values to the attributes and
yields itself for further initialization.  Optionally takes <tt>name</tt> and
<tt>version</tt>.

Gem::Specification::non_nil_attributes.name: non_nil_attributes
Gem::Specification::non_nil_attributes.comment: Specification attributes that must be non-nil

Gem::Specification::normalize_yaml_input.name: normalize_yaml_input
Gem::Specification::normalize_yaml_input.comment: Make sure the YAML specification is properly formatted with dashes

Gem::Specification::outdated.name: outdated
Gem::Specification::outdated.comment:
Return a list of all outdated local gem names.  This method is HEAVY as it
must go fetch specifications from the server.

Use outdated_and_latest_version if you wish to retrieve the latest remote
version as well.

Gem::Specification::outdated_and_latest_.name: outdated_and_latest_version
Gem::Specification::outdated_and_latest_.comment:
Enumerates the outdated local gems yielding the local specification and the
latest remote version.

This method may take some time to return as it must check each local gem
against the server's index.

Gem::Specification::reset.name: reset
Gem::Specification::reset.comment:
Reset the list of known specs, running pre and post reset hooks registered in
Gem.

Gem::Specification::specification_record.name: specification_record
Gem::Specification::specification_record.comment: Keeps track of all currently known specifications

Gem::Specification::stubs.name: stubs
Gem::Specification::stubs.comment: Returns a Gem::StubSpecification for every installed gem

Gem::Specification::stubs_for.name: stubs_for
Gem::Specification::stubs_for.comment:
Returns a Gem::StubSpecification for installed gem named <tt>name</tt> only
returns stubs that match Gem.platforms

Gem::Specification::unresolved_deps.name: unresolved_deps
Gem::Specification::unresolved_deps.comment: DOC: This method needs documented or nodoc'd

Gem::Specification#abbreviate.name: abbreviate
Gem::Specification#abbreviate.comment:
Abbreviate the spec for downloading.  Abbreviated specs are only used for
searching, downloading and related activities and do not need deployment
specific information (e.g. list of files).  So we abbreviate the spec, making
it much smaller for quicker downloads.

Gem::Specification#activate.name: activate
Gem::Specification#activate.comment:
Activate this spec, registering it as a loaded spec and adding it's lib paths
to $LOAD_PATH. Returns true if the spec was activated, false if it was
previously activated. Freaks out if there are conflicts upon activation.

Gem::Specification#activate_dependencies.name: activate_dependencies
Gem::Specification#activate_dependencies.comment:
Activate all unambiguously resolved runtime dependencies of this spec. Add any
ambiguous dependencies to the unresolved list to be resolved later, as needed.

Gem::Specification#add_bindir.name: add_bindir
Gem::Specification#add_bindir.comment:
Returns an array with bindir attached to each executable in the
<tt>executables</tt> list

Gem::Specification#add_dependency.name: add_dependency
Gem::Specification#add_dependency.comment:
Adds a runtime dependency named <tt>gem</tt> with <tt>requirements</tt> to
this gem.

Usage:

  spec.add_dependency 'example', '>= 1.1.4', '< 2'

Gem::Specification#add_development_depen.name: add_development_dependency
Gem::Specification#add_development_depen.comment:
Adds a development dependency named <tt>gem</tt> with <tt>requirements</tt> to
this gem.

Usage:

  spec.add_development_dependency 'example', '>= 1.1.4', '< 2'

Development dependencies aren't installed by default and aren't activated when
a gem is required.

Gem::Specification#add_self_to_load_path.name: add_self_to_load_path
Gem::Specification#add_self_to_load_path.comment: Adds this spec's require paths to LOAD_PATH, in the proper location.

Gem::Specification#author.name: author
Gem::Specification#author.comment: Singular reader for #authors.  Returns the first author in the list

Gem::Specification#author=.name: author=
Gem::Specification#author=.comment:
Singular (alternative) writer for #authors

Usage:

  spec.author = 'John Jones'

Gem::Specification#authors.name: authors
Gem::Specification#authors.comment:
The list of author names who wrote this gem.

  spec.authors = ['Chad Fowler', 'Jim Weirich', 'Rich Kilmer']

Gem::Specification#authors=.name: authors=
Gem::Specification#authors=.comment:
A list of authors for this gem.

Alternatively, a single author can be specified by assigning a string to
<tt>spec.author</tt>

Usage:

  spec.authors = ['John Jones', 'Mary Smith']

Gem::Specification#bin_dir.name: bin_dir
Gem::Specification#bin_dir.comment:
Returns the full path to installed gem's bin directory.

NOTE: do not confuse this with <tt>bindir</tt>, which is just 'bin', not a
full path.

Gem::Specification#bin_file.name: bin_file
Gem::Specification#bin_file.comment: Returns the full path to an executable named <tt>name</tt> in this gem.

Gem::Specification#build_args.name: build_args
Gem::Specification#build_args.comment: Returns the build_args used to install the gem

Gem::Specification#build_info_dir.name: build_info_dir
Gem::Specification#build_info_dir.comment: Returns the full path to the build info directory

Gem::Specification#build_info_file.name: build_info_file
Gem::Specification#build_info_file.comment:
Returns the full path to the file containing the build information generated
when the gem was installed

Gem::Specification#cache_dir.name: cache_dir
Gem::Specification#cache_dir.comment:
Returns the full path to the cache directory containing this spec's cached
gem.

Gem::Specification#cache_file.name: cache_file
Gem::Specification#cache_file.comment: Returns the full path to the cached gem for this spec.

Gem::Specification#conflicts.name: conflicts
Gem::Specification#conflicts.comment: Return any possible conflicts against the currently loaded specs.

Gem::Specification#date.name: date
Gem::Specification#date.comment:
The date this gem was created.

If SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH is set as an environment variable, use that to support
reproducible builds; otherwise, default to the current UTC date.

Details on SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH:
https://reproducible-builds.org/specs/source-date-epoch/

Gem::Specification#date=.name: date=
Gem::Specification#date=.comment:
The date this gem was created

DO NOT set this, it is set automatically when the gem is packaged.

Gem::Specification#default_value.name: default_value
Gem::Specification#default_value.comment: The default value for specification attribute <tt>name</tt>

Gem::Specification#dependencies.name: dependencies
Gem::Specification#dependencies.comment:
A list of Gem::Dependency objects this gem depends on.

Use #add_dependency or #add_development_dependency to add dependencies to a
gem.

Gem::Specification#dependent_gems.name: dependent_gems
Gem::Specification#dependent_gems.comment:
Return a list of all gems that have a dependency on this gemspec.  The list is
structured with entries that conform to:

  [depending_gem, dependency, [list_of_gems_that_satisfy_dependency]]

Gem::Specification#dependent_specs.name: dependent_specs
Gem::Specification#dependent_specs.comment: Returns all specs that matches this spec's runtime dependencies.

Gem::Specification#description=.name: description=
Gem::Specification#description=.comment: A detailed description of this gem.  See also #summary

Gem::Specification#development_dependenc.name: development_dependencies
Gem::Specification#development_dependenc.comment: List of dependencies that are used for development

Gem::Specification#doc_dir.name: doc_dir
Gem::Specification#doc_dir.comment:
Returns the full path to this spec's documentation directory.  If
<tt>type</tt> is given it will be appended to the end.  For example:

  spec.doc_dir      # => "/path/to/gem_repo/doc/a-1"

  spec.doc_dir 'ri' # => "/path/to/gem_repo/doc/a-1/ri"

Gem::Specification#executables.name: executables
Gem::Specification#executables.comment:
Executables included in the gem.

For example, the rake gem has rake as an executable. You don't specify the
full path (as in bin/rake); all application-style files are expected to be
found in bindir.  These files must be executable Ruby files.  Files that use
bash or other interpreters will not work.

Executables included may only be ruby scripts, not scripts for other languages
or compiled binaries.

Usage:

  spec.executables << 'rake'

Gem::Specification#executables=.name: executables=
Gem::Specification#executables=.comment: Sets executables to <tt>value</tt>, ensuring it is an array.

Gem::Specification#extensions.name: extensions
Gem::Specification#extensions.comment:
Extensions to build when installing the gem, specifically the paths to
extconf.rb-style files used to compile extensions.

These files will be run when the gem is installed, causing the C (or whatever)
code to be compiled on the user's machine.

Usage:

  spec.extensions << 'ext/rmagic/extconf.rb'

See Gem::Ext::Builder for information about writing extensions for gems.

Gem::Specification#extensions=.name: extensions=
Gem::Specification#extensions=.comment: Sets extensions to <tt>extensions</tt>, ensuring it is an array.

Gem::Specification#extensions_dir.name: extensions_dir
Gem::Specification#extensions_dir.comment: The path where this gem installs its extensions.

Gem::Specification#extra_rdoc_files.name: extra_rdoc_files
Gem::Specification#extra_rdoc_files.comment:
Extra files to add to RDoc such as README or doc/examples.txt

When the user elects to generate the RDoc documentation for a gem (typically
at install time), all the library files are sent to RDoc for processing. This
option allows you to have some non-code files included for a more complete set
of documentation.

Usage:

  spec.extra_rdoc_files = ['README', 'doc/user-guide.txt']

Gem::Specification#extra_rdoc_files=.name: extra_rdoc_files=
Gem::Specification#extra_rdoc_files=.comment: Sets extra_rdoc_files to <tt>files</tt>, ensuring it is an array.

Gem::Specification#file_name.name: file_name
Gem::Specification#file_name.comment:
The default (generated) file name of the gem.  See also #spec_name.

  spec.file_name # => "example-1.0.gem"

Gem::Specification#files.name: files
Gem::Specification#files.comment:
Files included in this gem.  You cannot append to this accessor, you must
assign to it.

Only add files you can require to this list, not directories, etc.

Directories are automatically stripped from this list when building a gem,
other non-files cause an error.

Usage:

  require 'rake'
  spec.files = FileList['lib/**/*.rb',
                        'bin/*',
                        '[A-Z]*'].to_a

  # or without Rake...
  spec.files = Dir['lib/**/*.rb'] + Dir['bin/*']
  spec.files += Dir['[A-Z]*']
  spec.files.reject! { |fn| fn.include? "CVS" }

Gem::Specification#files=.name: files=
Gem::Specification#files=.comment: Sets files to <tt>files</tt>, ensuring it is an array.

Gem::Specification#for_cache.name: for_cache
Gem::Specification#for_cache.comment: Creates a duplicate spec without large blobs that aren't used at runtime.

Gem::Specification#has_conflicts?.name: has_conflicts?
Gem::Specification#has_conflicts?.comment:
Return true if there are possible conflicts against the currently loaded
specs.

Gem::Specification#initialize_copy.name: initialize_copy
Gem::Specification#initialize_copy.comment:
Duplicates Array and Gem::Requirement attributes from <tt>other_spec</tt> so
state isn't shared.

Gem::Specification#lib_files.name: lib_files
Gem::Specification#lib_files.comment: Files in the Gem under one of the require_paths

Gem::Specification#license=.name: license=
Gem::Specification#license=.comment:
The license for this gem.

The license must be no more than 64 characters, and should be a single SPDX
license identifier from https://spdx.org/licenses/. Ideally, you should pick
one that is OSI (Open Source Initiative) https://opensource.org/licenses/
approved.

The most commonly used OSI-approved licenses are MIT and Apache-2.0. GitHub
also provides a license picker at https://choosealicense.com/.

The full text of the license should be inside of the gem (at the top level)
when you build it.

RubyGems validates the license against the SPDX license list when you run
<tt>gem build</tt> and warns about unknown or deprecated identifiers. An
identifier may carry a trailing <tt>+</tt> (this version or any later version)
and a license exception joined with WITH, for example <tt>Apache-2.0 WITH
LLVM-exception</tt>.

Compound SPDX license expressions such as <tt>MIT OR Apache-2.0</tt> are not
currently supported. RubyGems treats the whole string as a single identifier
and warns that it is invalid. For a gem available under more than one license,
set each license as a separate entry with #licenses=.

For a license that has no SPDX identifier, use Nonstandard, or
LicenseRef-<idstring> where idstring is the name of the file containing the
license text.

You should specify a license for your gem so that people know how they are
permitted to use it and any restrictions you're placing on it.  Not specifying
a license means all rights are reserved; others have no right to use the code
for any purpose.

Usage:
  spec.license = 'MIT'

Gem::Specification#licenses.name: licenses
Gem::Specification#licenses.comment:
Plural accessor for setting licenses

See #license= for details

Gem::Specification#licenses=.name: licenses=
Gem::Specification#licenses=.comment:
The license(s) for the library.

Each entry must be a single SPDX license identifier, no more than 64
characters. Entries are validated independently, so a compound expression such
as <tt>MIT OR Apache-2.0</tt> is not valid as an entry. Listing the
identifiers as separate array elements is currently the only way RubyGems
supports declaring a dual- or multi-licensed gem.

Note that the array itself does not state how the licenses combine. Include
the full text of each license in the gem and describe the exact terms there.

See #license= for more discussion

Usage:
  spec.licenses = ['MIT', 'GPL-2.0-only']

Gem::Specification#missing_extensions?.name: missing_extensions?
Gem::Specification#missing_extensions?.comment:
Is this specification missing its extensions?  When this returns true you
probably want to build_extensions

Gem::Specification#name_tuple.name: name_tuple
Gem::Specification#name_tuple.comment: Return a NameTuple that represents this Specification

Gem::Specification#normalize.name: normalize
Gem::Specification#normalize.comment:
Normalize the list of files so that:
* All file lists have redundancies removed.
* Files referenced in the extra_rdoc_files are included in the package file
  list.

Gem::Specification#platform.name: platform
Gem::Specification#platform.comment: The platform this gem runs on.  See Gem::Platform for details.

Gem::Specification#platform=.name: platform=
Gem::Specification#platform=.comment:
The platform this gem runs on.

This is usually Gem::Platform::RUBY or Gem::Platform::CURRENT.

Most gems contain pure Ruby code; they should simply leave the default value
in place.  Some gems contain C (or other) code to be compiled into a Ruby
"extension".  The gem should leave the default value in place unless the code
will only compile on a certain type of system.  Some gems consist of
pre-compiled code ("binary gems").  It's especially important that they set
the platform attribute appropriately.  A shortcut is to set the platform to
Gem::Platform::CURRENT, which will cause the gem builder to set the platform
to the appropriate value for the system on which the build is being performed.

If this attribute is set to a non-default value, it will be included in the
filename of the gem when it is built such as: nokogiri-1.6.0-x86-mingw32.gem

Usage:

  spec.platform = Gem::Platform.local

Gem::Specification#rdoc_options.name: rdoc_options
Gem::Specification#rdoc_options.comment:
Specifies the rdoc options to be used when generating API documentation.

Usage:

  spec.rdoc_options << '--title' << 'Rake -- Ruby Make' <<
    '--main' << 'README' <<
    '--line-numbers'

Gem::Specification#rdoc_options=.name: rdoc_options=
Gem::Specification#rdoc_options=.comment:
Sets rdoc_options to <tt>value</tt>, ensuring it is a flat array of strings.
Handles malformed gemspecs where rdoc_options may be a Hash or contain Hashes.

Gem::Specification#require_paths=.name: require_paths=
Gem::Specification#require_paths=.comment:
Paths in the gem to add to <tt>$LOAD_PATH</tt> when this gem is activated. If
you have an extension you do not need to add <tt>"ext"</tt> to the require
path, the extension build process will copy the extension files into "lib" for
you.

The default value is <tt>"lib"</tt>

Usage:

  # If all library files are in the root directory...
  spec.require_paths = ['.']

Gem::Specification#required_ruby_version.name: required_ruby_version=
Gem::Specification#required_ruby_version.comment:
The version of Ruby required by this gem.  The ruby version can be specified
to the patch-level:

  $ ruby -v -e 'p Gem.ruby_version'
  ruby 2.0.0p247 (2013-06-27 revision 41674) [x86_64-darwin12.4.0]
  #<Gem::Version "2.0.0.247">

Prereleases can also be specified.

Usage:

  # This gem will work with 1.8.6 or greater...
  spec.required_ruby_version = '>= 1.8.6'

  # Only with final releases of major version 2 where minor version is at least 3
  spec.required_ruby_version = '~> 2.3'

  # Only prereleases or final releases after 2.6.0.preview2
  spec.required_ruby_version = '> 2.6.0.preview2'

  # This gem will work with 2.3.0 or greater, including major version 3, but lesser than 4.0.0
  spec.required_ruby_version = '>= 2.3', '< 4'

Gem::Specification#required_rubygems_ver.name: required_rubygems_version=
Gem::Specification#required_rubygems_ver.comment: The RubyGems version required by this gem

Gem::Specification#requirements.name: requirements
Gem::Specification#requirements.comment:
Lists the external (to RubyGems) requirements that must be met for this gem to
work.  It's simply information for the user.

Usage:

  spec.requirements << 'libmagick, v6.0'
  spec.requirements << 'A good graphics card'

Gem::Specification#requirements=.name: requirements=
Gem::Specification#requirements=.comment: Set requirements to <tt>req</tt>, ensuring it is an array.

Gem::Specification#reset_nil_attributes_.name: reset_nil_attributes_to_default
Gem::Specification#reset_nil_attributes_.comment: Reset nil attributes to their default values to make the spec valid

Gem::Specification#ri_dir.name: ri_dir
Gem::Specification#ri_dir.comment: Returns the full path to this spec's ri directory.

Gem::Specification#ruby_abi.name: ruby_abi
Gem::Specification#ruby_abi.comment:
Ruby ABI of the gem derived from required_ruby_version Only supports
required_ruby_version in "~> X.Y.0" format (single pessimistic requirement
with 3 segments) Returns nil if the required_ruby_version does not specify a
single Ruby ABI

Gem::Specification#runtime_dependencies.name: runtime_dependencies
Gem::Specification#runtime_dependencies.comment: List of dependencies that will automatically be activated at runtime.

Gem::Specification#sanitize.name: sanitize
Gem::Specification#sanitize.comment:
Sanitize the descriptive fields in the spec.  Sometimes non-ASCII characters
will garble the site index.  Non-ASCII characters will be replaced by their
XML entity equivalent.

Gem::Specification#satisfies_requirement.name: satisfies_requirement?
Gem::Specification#satisfies_requirement.comment: Checks if this specification meets the requirement of <tt>dependency</tt>.

Gem::Specification#sort_obj.name: sort_obj
Gem::Specification#sort_obj.comment: Returns an object you can use to sort specifications in #sort_by.

Gem::Specification#spec_dir.name: spec_dir
Gem::Specification#spec_dir.comment:
Full path to the directory containing this spec's gemspec file. ABI-scoped for
content-addressed specs.

Gem::Specification#spec_file.name: spec_file
Gem::Specification#spec_file.comment:
Returns the full path to this spec's gemspec file. eg:
/usr/local/lib/ruby/gems/1.8/specifications/mygem-1.0.gemspec

Gem::Specification#spec_name.name: spec_name
Gem::Specification#spec_name.comment:
The default name of the gemspec.  See also #file_name

  spec.spec_name # => "example-1.0.gemspec"

Gem::Specification#summary=.name: summary=
Gem::Specification#summary=.comment: A short summary of this gem's description.

Gem::Specification#to_ruby.name: to_ruby
Gem::Specification#to_ruby.comment:
Returns a Ruby code representation of this specification, such that it can be
eval'ed and reconstruct the same specification later.  Attributes that still
have their default values are omitted.

Gem::Specification#to_ruby_for_cache.name: to_ruby_for_cache
Gem::Specification#to_ruby_for_cache.comment:
Returns a Ruby lighter-weight code representation of this specification, used
for indexing only.

See #to_ruby.

Gem::Specification#traverse.name: traverse
Gem::Specification#traverse.comment:
Recursively walk dependencies of this spec, executing the <tt>block</tt> for
each hop.

Gem::Specification#validate.name: validate
Gem::Specification#validate.comment:
Checks that the specification contains all required fields, and does a very
basic sanity check.

Raises InvalidSpecificationException if the spec does not pass the checks..

Gem::Specification#add_dependency_with_t.name: add_dependency_with_type
Gem::Specification#add_dependency_with_t.comment:
Adds a dependency on gem <tt>dependency</tt> with type <tt>type</tt> that
requires <tt>requirements</tt>.  Valid types are currently <tt>:runtime</tt>
and <tt>:development</tt>.

Gem::Specification#ruby_code.name: ruby_code
Gem::Specification#ruby_code.comment: Return a string containing a Ruby code representation of the given object.

Gem::Specification#same_attributes?.name: same_attributes?
Gem::Specification#same_attributes?.comment: True if this gem has the same attributes as <tt>other</tt>.

Gem::SpecificationPolicy#validate.name: validate
Gem::SpecificationPolicy#validate.comment:
Does a sanity check on the specification.

Raises InvalidSpecificationException if the spec does not pass the checks.

It also performs some validations that do not raise but print warning messages
instead.

Gem::SpecificationPolicy#validate_permis.name: validate_permissions
Gem::SpecificationPolicy#validate_permis.comment:
Issues a warning for each file to be packaged which is world-readable.

Implementation for Specification#validate_permissions

Gem::SpecificationPolicy#validate_requir.name: validate_required!
Gem::SpecificationPolicy#validate_requir.comment:
Does a sanity check on the specification.

Raises InvalidSpecificationException if the spec does not pass the checks.

Only runs checks that are considered necessary for the specification to be
functional.

Gem::SpecificationRecord::abi_scoped_spe.name: abi_scoped_spec_dir?
Gem::SpecificationRecord::abi_scoped_spe.comment:
Whether <tt>dir</tt> is an ABI-scoped spec dir
(<tt>.../specifications/<ruby_abi></tt>). Requires the parent to be named
<tt>specifications</tt> to avoid false positives.

Gem::SpecificationRecord::dirs_from.name: dirs_from
Gem::SpecificationRecord::dirs_from.comment:
Specification directories for each path: the flat <tt>specifications</tt> dir
and the ABI-scoped +specifications/<ruby_abi>+ subdir.

Gem::SpecificationRecord::dirs_with_abi.name: dirs_with_abi
Gem::SpecificationRecord::dirs_with_abi.comment:
Ensure ABI-scoped subdirectories are present in <tt>dirs</tt>.  No-op when
<tt>dirs</tt> already includes them (e.g. MRI); expands flat-only
<tt>dirs</tt>

Gem::SpecificationRecord::specification_.name: specification_dir_for
Gem::SpecificationRecord::specification_.comment:
The spec dir for <tt>spec</tt> under <tt>base_dir</tt>: the ABI-scoped subdir
for content-addressed specs, the flat <tt>specifications</tt> dir otherwise.

Gem::SpecificationRecord#add_spec.name: add_spec
Gem::SpecificationRecord#add_spec.comment: Adds <tt>spec</tt> to the record, keeping the collection properly sorted.

Gem::SpecificationRecord#all.name: all
Gem::SpecificationRecord#all.comment: Returns the list of all specifications in the record

Gem::SpecificationRecord#all=.name: all=
Gem::SpecificationRecord#all=.comment: Sets the specs known by the record to <tt>specs</tt>.

Gem::SpecificationRecord#all_names.name: all_names
Gem::SpecificationRecord#all_names.comment: Return full names of all specs in the record in sorted order.

Gem::SpecificationRecord#find_active_stu.name: find_active_stub_by_path
Gem::SpecificationRecord#find_active_stu.comment:
Return the best specification in the record that contains the file matching
<tt>path</tt>, among those already activated.

Gem::SpecificationRecord#find_all_by_nam.name: find_all_by_name
Gem::SpecificationRecord#find_all_by_nam.comment:
Returns every spec in the record that matches <tt>name</tt> and optional
<tt>requirements</tt>.

Gem::SpecificationRecord#find_by_path.name: find_by_path
Gem::SpecificationRecord#find_by_path.comment:
Return the best specification in the record that contains the file matching
<tt>path</tt>.

Gem::SpecificationRecord#find_inactive_b.name: find_inactive_by_path
Gem::SpecificationRecord#find_inactive_b.comment:
Return the best specification in the record that contains the file matching
<tt>path</tt> amongst the specs that are not activated.

Gem::SpecificationRecord#find_unloaded_b.name: find_unloaded_by_path
Gem::SpecificationRecord#find_unloaded_b.comment:
Return the best specification that contains the file matching <tt>path</tt>
amongst the specs that are not loaded. This method is different than
<tt>find_inactive_by_path</tt> as it will filter out loaded specs by their
name.

Gem::SpecificationRecord#latest_spec_for.name: latest_spec_for
Gem::SpecificationRecord#latest_spec_for.comment: Return the latest installed spec in the record for gem <tt>name</tt>.

Gem::SpecificationRecord#latest_specs.name: latest_specs
Gem::SpecificationRecord#latest_specs.comment:
Return the latest specs in the record, optionally including prerelease specs
if <tt>prerelease</tt> is true.

Gem::SpecificationRecord#stubs.name: stubs
Gem::SpecificationRecord#stubs.comment: Returns a Gem::StubSpecification for every specification in the record

Gem::SpecificationRecord#stubs_for.name: stubs_for
Gem::SpecificationRecord#stubs_for.comment:
Returns a Gem::StubSpecification for every specification in the record named
<tt>name</tt> only returns stubs that match Gem.platforms

Gem::SpecificationRecord#stubs_for_patte.name: stubs_for_pattern
Gem::SpecificationRecord#stubs_for_patte.comment:
Finds stub specifications matching a pattern in the record, optionally
filtering out specs not matching the current platform

Gem::StreamUI.name: Gem::StreamUI
Gem::StreamUI.comment: Gem::StreamUI implements a simple stream based user interface.

Gem::StreamUI::new.name: new
Gem::StreamUI::new.comment:
Creates a new StreamUI wrapping <tt>in_stream</tt> for user input,
<tt>out_stream</tt> for standard output, <tt>err_stream</tt> for error output.
 If <tt>usetty</tt> is true then special operations (like asking for
passwords) will use the TTY commands to disable character echo.

Gem::StreamUI#alert.name: alert
Gem::StreamUI#alert.comment: Display an informational alert.  Will ask <tt>question</tt> if it is not nil.

Gem::StreamUI#alert_error.name: alert_error
Gem::StreamUI#alert_error.comment:
Display an error message in a location expected to get error messages. Will
ask <tt>question</tt> if it is not nil.

Gem::StreamUI#alert_warning.name: alert_warning
Gem::StreamUI#alert_warning.comment: Display a warning on stderr.  Will ask <tt>question</tt> if it is not nil.

Gem::StreamUI#ask.name: ask
Gem::StreamUI#ask.comment: Ask a question.  Returns an answer if connected to a tty, nil otherwise.

Gem::StreamUI#ask_for_password.name: ask_for_password
Gem::StreamUI#ask_for_password.comment: Ask for a password. Does not echo response to terminal.

Gem::StreamUI#ask_yes_no.name: ask_yes_no
Gem::StreamUI#ask_yes_no.comment:
Ask a question.  Returns a true for yes, false for no.  If not connected to a
tty, raises an exception if default is nil, otherwise returns default.

Gem::StreamUI#backtrace.name: backtrace
Gem::StreamUI#backtrace.comment: Prints a formatted backtrace to the errors stream if backtraces are enabled.

Gem::StreamUI#choose_from_list.name: choose_from_list
Gem::StreamUI#choose_from_list.comment:
Choose from a list of options.  <tt>question</tt> is a prompt displayed above
the list.  <tt>list</tt> is a list of option strings.  Returns the pair
[option_name, option_index].

Gem::StreamUI#download_reporter.name: download_reporter
Gem::StreamUI#download_reporter.comment: Return a download reporter object chosen from the current verbosity

Gem::StreamUI#progress_reporter.name: progress_reporter
Gem::StreamUI#progress_reporter.comment: Return a progress reporter object chosen from the current verbosity.

Gem::StreamUI#terminate_interaction.name: terminate_interaction
Gem::StreamUI#terminate_interaction.comment:
Terminate the application with exit code <tt>status</tt>, running any exit
handlers that might have been defined.

Gem::StreamUI#tty?.name: tty?
Gem::StreamUI#tty?.comment: Returns true if TTY methods should be used on this StreamUI.

Gem::StreamUI::SilentDownloadReporter::n.name: new
Gem::StreamUI::SilentDownloadReporter::n.comment: The silent download reporter ignores all arguments

Gem::StreamUI::SilentDownloadReporter#do.name: done
Gem::StreamUI::SilentDownloadReporter#do.comment:
The silent download reporter won't tell you when the download is done. Because
it is silent.

Gem::StreamUI::SilentDownloadReporter#fe.name: fetch
Gem::StreamUI::SilentDownloadReporter#fe.comment:
The silent download reporter does not display <tt>filename</tt> or care about
<tt>filesize</tt> because it is silent.

Gem::StreamUI::SilentDownloadReporter#up.name: update
Gem::StreamUI::SilentDownloadReporter#up.comment: Nothing can update the silent download reporter.

Gem::StreamUI::SilentProgressReporter::n.name: new
Gem::StreamUI::SilentProgressReporter::n.comment: Creates a silent progress reporter that ignores all input arguments.

Gem::StreamUI::SilentProgressReporter#do.name: done
Gem::StreamUI::SilentProgressReporter#do.comment:
Does not print anything when complete as this object has taken a vow of
silence.

Gem::StreamUI::SilentProgressReporter#up.name: updated
Gem::StreamUI::SilentProgressReporter#up.comment:
Does not print <tt>message</tt> when updated as this object has taken a vow of
silence.

Gem::StreamUI::SimpleProgressReporter::n.name: new
Gem::StreamUI::SimpleProgressReporter::n.comment:
Creates a new progress reporter that will write to <tt>out_stream</tt> for
<tt>size</tt> items.  Shows the given <tt>initial_message</tt> when progress
starts and the <tt>terminal_message</tt> when it is complete.

Gem::StreamUI::SimpleProgressReporter#up.name: updated
Gem::StreamUI::SimpleProgressReporter#up.comment: Prints out a dot and ignores <tt>message</tt>.

Gem::StreamUI::ThreadedDownloadReporter.name: Gem::StreamUI::ThreadedDownloadReporter
Gem::StreamUI::ThreadedDownloadReporter.comment: A progress reporter that behaves nicely with threaded downloading.

Gem::StreamUI::ThreadedDownloadReporter:.name: new
Gem::StreamUI::ThreadedDownloadReporter:.comment:
Creates a new threaded download reporter that will display on
<tt>out_stream</tt>.  The other arguments are ignored.

Gem::StreamUI::ThreadedDownloadReporter#.name: fetch
Gem::StreamUI::ThreadedDownloadReporter#.comment:
Tells the download reporter that the <tt>file_name</tt> is being fetched. The
other arguments are ignored.

Gem::StreamUI::ThreadedDownloadReporter#.name: update
Gem::StreamUI::ThreadedDownloadReporter#.comment: Updates the threaded download reporter for the given number of <tt>bytes</tt>.

Gem::StreamUI::VerboseProgressReporter.name: Gem::StreamUI::VerboseProgressReporter
Gem::StreamUI::VerboseProgressReporter.comment: A progress reporter that prints out messages about the current progress.

Gem::StreamUI::VerboseProgressReporter::.name: new
Gem::StreamUI::VerboseProgressReporter::.comment:
Creates a new progress reporter that will write to <tt>out_stream</tt> for
<tt>size</tt> items.  Shows the given <tt>initial_message</tt> when progress
starts and the <tt>terminal_message</tt> when it is complete.

Gem::StreamUI::VerboseProgressReporter#u.name: updated
Gem::StreamUI::VerboseProgressReporter#u.comment: Prints out the position relative to the total and the <tt>message</tt>.

Gem::StubSpecification.name: Gem::StubSpecification
Gem::StubSpecification.comment:
Gem::StubSpecification reads the stub: line from the gemspec.  This prevents
us having to eval the entire gemspec in order to find out certain information.

Gem::SystemExitException.name: Gem::SystemExitException
Gem::SystemExitException.comment:
Raised to indicate that a system exit should occur with the specified
exit_code

Gem::SystemExitException::new.name: new

The uninstaller fires pre and post uninstall hooks.  Hooks can be added either
through a rubygems_plugin.rb file in an installed gem or via a
rubygems/defaults/#{RUBY_ENGINE}.rb or rubygems/defaults/operating_system.rb

Gem::Uninstaller::new.name: new
Gem::Uninstaller::new.comment:
Constructs an uninstaller that will uninstall gem named <tt>gem</tt>.
<tt>options</tt> is a Hash with the following keys:

:version:
  Version requirement for the gem to uninstall. If not specified, uses
  Gem::Requirement.default.

:install_dir:
  The directory where the gem is installed. If not specified, uses Gem.dir.

:executables:
  Whether executables should be removed without confirmation or not. If nil,
  asks the user explicitly.

:all:
  If more than one version matches the requirement, whether to forcefully
  remove all matching versions or ask the user to select specific matching
  versions that should be removed.

:ignore:
  Ignore broken dependency checks when uninstalling.

:bin_dir:
  Directory containing executables to remove. If not specified, uses
  Gem.bindir.

:format_executable:
  In order to find executables to be removed, format executable names using
  Gem::Installer.exec_format.

:abort_on_dependent:
  Directly abort uninstallation if dependencies would be broken, rather than
  asking the user for confirmation.

:check_dev:
  When checking if uninstalling gem would leave broken dependencies around,
  also consider development dependencies.

:force:
  Set both :all and :ignore to true for forced uninstallation.

:user_install:
  Uninstall from user gem directory instead of system directory.

Gem::Version.name: Gem::Version
Gem::Version.comment:
The Version class processes string versions into comparable values. A version
string should normally be a series of numbers separated by periods. Each part
(digits separated by periods) is considered its own number, and these are used
for sorting. So for instance, 3.10 sorts higher than 3.2 because ten is
greater than two.

If any part contains letters (currently only a-z are supported) then that
version is considered prerelease. Versions with a prerelease part in the Nth
part sort less than versions with N-1 parts. Prerelease parts are sorted
alphabetically using the normal Ruby string sorting rules. If a prerelease
part contains both letters and numbers, it will be broken into multiple parts
to provide expected sort behavior (1.0.a10 becomes 1.0.a.10, and is greater
than 1.0.a9).

Prereleases sort between real releases (newest to oldest):

1. 1.0
2. 1.0.b1
3. 1.0.a.2
4. 0.9

If you want to specify a version restriction that includes both prereleases
and regular releases of 1.x or later versions:

  s.add_dependency 'example', '>= 1.0.0.a'

== How Software Changes

Libraries generally change in 3 ways:

1. The change is an implementation detail, bug fix, security fix, or
   optimization, and has no behavioral effect on the software using it.

2. The change adds new features, and software using those new features is not
   compatible with previous versions of the library, but software using
   previous versions of the library is compatible with the change.

3. The change modifies the public interface of some part of the library in
   such a way that software that uses that part of the library must be
   modified to work.

== RubyGems Rational Versioning (the recommended approach)

* Versions shall be represented by three non-negative integers, separated by
  periods (e.g. 3.1.4).  The first integer is the "major" version number, the
  second integer is the "minor" version number, and the third integer is the
  "patch" version number.

* A category 1 change (implementation detail, bug fix, or security fix) will
  increment the patch number.

* A category 2 change (backwards compatible) will increment the minor version
  number and reset the patch number.

* A category 3 change (incompatible) will increment the major version number
  and reset the minor and patch numbers.

* Any "public" release of a gem should have a different version.

== Optimistic Vs. Pessimistic Dependency Versioning

Users expect to be able to specify a version constraint that gives them a
reasonable expectation that new versions of a library will work with their
software if the version constraint is true, and not work with their software
if the version constraint is false.  In other words, the perfect system will
accept all compatible versions of the library and reject all incompatible
versions. Unfortunately, there is no perfect system, as you cannot predict the
future. You can never know whether a future version of a library will contain
which type of change.

There are two common outlooks on dependency versioning:

1. Optimistic. This does not set an upper bound on a dependency. It is
   possible that a future version of a dependency will break the software, and
   in that case, the dependency version will need to be updated and changes
   will need to be made.

2. Pessimistic. This assumes all major version changes of a dependency will
   break the software, and that patch or minor changes of a dependency will
   not break the software. If there is a major version of a dependency
   released, the dependency version must be updated in order to use it, even
   if no code changes are actually needed.

In general, optimistic versioning is superior to pessimistic versioning.
Pessimistic versioning is often wrong in both directions. Dependencies can
release patch or minor versions that contain incompatibilities. One common
reason is that a security fix may require a backwards-incompatible API change.
In this case, even though pessimistic versioning was used, it didn't even save
effort, as you still need to make code changes and adjust dependency versions.
Similarly, for all but the smallest dependencies, just because the dependency
made a backwards incompatible change to one interface doesn't mean the
dependency made a backwards incompatible change to an interface that the
software is using. It is a common problem that a dependency will release a new
major version and the software does not require any changes in order to use
it. In this case, being pessimistic results in additional work for no benefit.

When a library uses pessimistic versioning of dependencies, it causes
significant problems if that library is not diligent about updating dependency
versions and any library is depending on that library. For example:

* Library A is currently on release 1.2.3.

* Library B is at version 2.3.4 and has a pessimistic dependency on library A,
  using ~> 1.0 (>= 1.0, < 2).

* Library C is at version 3.4.5 and has an optimistic dependency on library A,
  using >= 1.0.

* Library D has optimistic dependencies on both libraries B and C.

* Library A releases a new major version, 2.0.0, with new features, which is
  mostly backwards compatible, but does contain some backwards incompatible
  changes.

* Library B would work with A 2.0.0, but cannot use it due to pessimistic
  versioning.

* Library C wants to use the new features in the major release of library A to
  implement its own new features, so it does so, bumps the dependency version
  of A to >= 2.0, and releases version 3.5.0.

* Library D cannot upgrade to the new version of library C, because it depends
  on library B, which has a pessimistic dependency on library A.

* Library C releases a security fix patch version 3.5.1 to fix a vulnerability
  present in all previous versions.

* Library D is now in a terrible situation. It cannot upgrade to library C
  3.5.1, as that requires library A > 2.0, because it depends on library B,
  which requires library A > 1.0, < 2, even though library B would work fine
  with library A 2.0.0.

This type of situation brought on by pessimistic versioning is unfortunately
both common and serious in practice.

This is not to say that optimistic versioning never causes a problem. However,
with optimistic versioning, if there is a problem, it can be solved with the
addition of a single dependency. For example, continuing the previous example:

* Library A releases a new major version, 3.0.0, which makes backwards
  incompatible changes that break library C.

* Until library C releases an updated version with new changes, library D only
  needs to set a specific dependency on library A for > 2.0, < 3, until
  library C is updated to work with the new version of library A.

Both optimistic versioning and pessimistic versioning have problems in certain
cases. However, it's significantly easier to fix optimistic versioning
problems than to fix pessimistic versioning problems.

That is not to say that pessimistic versioning is never appropriate. If the
dependency is a library that adds a single method, where any change resulting
in a major version bump would probably break a library using it, then using
pessimistic versioning may be warranted. Additionally, if a dependency has
already announced or committed backwards incompatible changes that would break
a library's use of it, then having that library use a pessimistic version
constraint would likely be warranted. However, outside of specific situations,
you should avoid using pessimistic versioning, as the costs typically exceed
the benefits.

Hash.name: Hash
Hash.comment: A Hash object maps each of its unique keys to a specific value. A hash has certain similarities to an Array, but: * An array index is always an integer. * A hash key can be (almost) any object. === Hash Data Syntax The original syntax for a hash entry uses the "hash rocket," =>: h = {:foo => 0, :bar => 1, :baz => 2} h # => {foo: 0, bar: 1, baz: 2} Alternatively, but only for a key that's a symbol, you can use a newer JSON-style syntax, where each bareword becomes a symbol: h = {foo: 0, bar: 1, baz: 2} h # => {foo: 0, bar: 1, baz: 2} You can also use a string in place of a bareword: h = {'foo': 0, 'bar': 1, 'baz': 2} h # => {foo: 0, bar: 1, baz: 2} And you can mix the styles: h = {foo: 0, :bar => 1, 'baz': 2} h # => {foo: 0, bar: 1, baz: 2} But it's an error to try the JSON-style syntax for a key that's not a bareword or a string: # Raises SyntaxError (syntax error, unexpected ':', expecting =>): h = {0: 'zero'} The value can be omitted, meaning that value will be fetched from the context by the name of the key: x = 0 y = 100 h = {x:, y:} h # => {x: 0, y: 100} === Common Uses You can use a hash to give names to objects: person = {name: 'Matz', language: 'Ruby'} person # => {name: "Matz", language: "Ruby"} You can use a hash to give names to method arguments: def some_method(hash) p hash end some_method({foo: 0, bar: 1, baz: 2}) # => {foo: 0, bar: 1, baz: 2} Note: when the last argument in a method call is a hash, the curly braces may be omitted: some_method(foo: 0, bar: 1, baz: 2) # => {foo: 0, bar: 1, baz: 2} You can use a hash to initialize an object: class Dev attr_accessor :name, :language def initialize(hash) self.name = hash[:name] self.language = hash[:language] end end matz = Dev.new(name: 'Matz', language: 'Ruby') matz # => # === Creating a Hash You can create a Hash object explicitly with: * A {hash literal}[rdoc-ref:syntax/literals.rdoc@Hash+Literals]. You can convert certain objects to hashes with: * Method Kernel#Hash. You can create a hash by calling method Hash.new: # Create an empty hash. h = Hash.new h # => {} h.class # => Hash You can create a hash by calling method Hash.[]: # Create an empty hash. h = Hash[] h # => {} # Create a hash with initial entries. h = Hash[foo: 0, bar: 1, baz: 2] h # => {foo: 0, bar: 1, baz: 2} You can create a hash by using its literal form (curly braces): # Create an empty hash. h = {} h # => {} # Create a +Hash+ with initial entries. h = {foo: 0, bar: 1, baz: 2} h # => {foo: 0, bar: 1, baz: 2} === Hash Value Basics The simplest way to retrieve a hash value (instance method #[]): h = {foo: 0, bar: 1, baz: 2} h[:foo] # => 0 The simplest way to create or update a hash value (instance method #[]=): h = {foo: 0, bar: 1, baz: 2} h[:bat] = 3 # => 3 h # => {foo: 0, bar: 1, baz: 2, bat: 3} h[:foo] = 4 # => 4 h # => {foo: 4, bar: 1, baz: 2, bat: 3} The simplest way to delete a hash entry (instance method #delete): h = {foo: 0, bar: 1, baz: 2} h.delete(:bar) # => 1 h # => {foo: 0, baz: 2} === Entry Order A Hash object presents its entries in the order of their creation. This is seen in: * Iterative methods such as each, each_key, each_pair, each_value. * Other order-sensitive methods such as shift, keys, values. * The string returned by method inspect. A new hash has its initial ordering per the given entries: h = Hash[foo: 0, bar: 1] h # => {foo: 0, bar: 1} New entries are added at the end: h[:baz] = 2 h # => {foo: 0, bar: 1, baz: 2} Updating a value does not affect the order: h[:baz] = 3 h # => {foo: 0, bar: 1, baz: 3} But re-creating a deleted entry can affect the order: h.delete(:foo) h[:foo] = 5 h # => {bar: 1, baz: 3, foo: 5} === Hash Keys ==== Hash Key Equivalence Two objects are treated as the same hash key when their hash value is identical and the two objects are eql? to each other. ==== Modifying an Active Hash Key Modifying a Hash key while it is in use damages the hash's index. This Hash has keys that are Arrays: a0 = [ :foo, :bar ] a1 = [ :baz, :bat ] h = {a0 => 0, a1 => 1} h.include?(a0) # => true h[a0] # => 0 a0.hash # => 110002110 Modifying array element a0[0] changes its hash value: a0[0] = :bam a0.hash # => 1069447059 And damages the Hash index: h.include?(a0) # => false h[a0] # => nil You can repair the hash index using method rehash: h.rehash # => {[:bam, :bar]=>0, [:baz, :bat]=>1} h.include?(a0) # => true h[a0] # => 0 A String key is always safe. That's because an unfrozen String passed as a key will be replaced by a duplicated and frozen String: s = 'foo' s.frozen? # => false h = {s => 0} first_key = h.keys.first first_key.frozen? # => true ==== User-Defined Hash Keys To be usable as a Hash key, objects must implement the methods hash and eql?. Note: this requirement does not apply if the Hash uses #compare_by_identity since comparison will then rely on the keys' object id instead of hash and eql?. Object defines basic implementation for hash and eq? that makes each object a distinct key. Typically, user-defined classes will want to override these methods to provide meaningful behavior, or for example inherit Struct that has useful definitions for these. A typical implementation of hash is based on the object's data while eql? is usually aliased to the overridden == method: class Book attr_reader :author, :title def initialize(author, title) @author = author @title = title end def ==(other) self.class === other && other.author == @author && other.title == @title end alias eql? == def hash [self.class, @author, @title].hash end end book1 = Book.new 'matz', 'Ruby in a Nutshell' book2 = Book.new 'matz', 'Ruby in a Nutshell' reviews = {} reviews[book1] = 'Great reference!' reviews[book2] = 'Nice and compact!' reviews.length #=> 1 === Key Not Found? When a method tries to retrieve and return the value for a key and that key is found, the returned value is the value associated with the key. But what if the key is not found? In that case, certain methods will return a default value while other will raise a KeyError. ==== Nil Return Value If you want nil returned for a not-found key, you can call: * #[](key) (usually written as #[key]. * #assoc(key). * #dig(key, *identifiers). * #values_at(*keys). You can override these behaviors for #[], #dig, and #values_at (but not #assoc); see {Hash Default}[rdoc-ref:Hash@Hash+Default]. ==== KeyError If you want KeyError raised for a not-found key, you can call: * #fetch(key). * #fetch_values(*keys). ==== Hash Default For certain methods (#[], #dig, and #values_at), the return value for a not-found key is determined by two hash properties: * default value: returned by method #default. * default proc: returned by method #default_proc. In the simple case, both values are nil, and the methods return nil for a not-found key; see {Nil Return Value}[rdoc-ref:Hash@Nil+Return+Value] above. Note that this entire section ("Hash Default"): * Applies only to methods #[], #dig, and #values_at. * Does not apply to methods #assoc, #fetch, or #fetch_values, which are not affected by the default value or default proc. ===== Any-Key Default You can define an any-key default for a hash; that is, a value that will be returned for any not-found key: * The value of #default_proc must be nil. * The value of #default (which may be any object, including nil) will be returned for a not-found key. You can set the default value when the hash is created with Hash.new and option default_value, or later with method #default=. Note: although the value of #default may be any object, it may not be a good idea to use a mutable object. ===== Per-Key Defaults You can define a per-key default for a hash; that is, a Proc that will return a value based on the key itself. You can set the default proc when the hash is created with Hash.new and a block, or later with method #default_proc=. Note that the proc can modify self, but modifying self in this way is not thread-safe; multiple threads can concurrently call into the default proc for the same key. ==== Method Default For two methods, you can specify a default value for a not-found key that has effect only for a single method call (and not for any subsequent calls): * For method #fetch, you can specify an any-key default: * For either method #fetch or method #fetch_values, you can specify a per-key default via a block. === What's Here First, what's elsewhere. Class Hash: * Inherits from {class Object}[rdoc-ref:Object@Whats+Here]. * Includes {module Enumerable}[rdoc-ref:Enumerable@Whats+Here], which provides dozens of additional methods. Here, class Hash provides methods that are useful for: * {Creating a Hash}[rdoc-ref:Hash@Methods+for+Creating+a+Hash] * {Setting Hash State}[rdoc-ref:Hash@Methods+for+Setting+Hash+State] * {Querying}[rdoc-ref:Hash@Methods+for+Querying] * {Comparing}[rdoc-ref:Hash@Methods+for+Comparing] * {Fetching}[rdoc-ref:Hash@Methods+for+Fetching] * {Assigning}[rdoc-ref:Hash@Methods+for+Assigning] * {Deleting}[rdoc-ref:Hash@Methods+for+Deleting] * {Iterating}[rdoc-ref:Hash@Methods+for+Iterating] * {Converting}[rdoc-ref:Hash@Methods+for+Converting] * {Transforming Keys and Values}[rdoc-ref:Hash@Methods+for+Transforming+Keys+and+Values] Class Hash also includes methods from module Enumerable. ==== Methods for Creating a Hash * ::[]: Returns a new hash populated with given objects. * ::new: Returns a new empty hash. * ::try_convert: Returns a new hash created from a given object. ==== Methods for Setting Hash State * #compare_by_identity: Sets self to consider only identity in comparing keys. * #default=: Sets the default to a given value. * #default_proc=: Sets the default proc to a given proc. * #rehash: Rebuilds the hash table by recomputing the hash index for each key. ==== Methods for Querying * #any?: Returns whether any element satisfies a given criterion. * #compare_by_identity?: Returns whether the hash considers only identity when comparing keys. * #default: Returns the default value, or the default value for a given key. * #default_proc: Returns the default proc. * #empty?: Returns whether there are no entries. * #eql?: Returns whether a given object is equal to self. * #hash: Returns the integer hash code. * #has_value? (aliased as #value?): Returns whether a given object is a value in self. * #include?
