Note: this method is obsolete, please use TracePoint instead. proc takes up to six parameters: * an event name string * a filename string * a line number * a method name symbol, or nil * a binding, or nil * the class, module, or nil proc is invoked whenever an event occurs. Events are: "c-call": call a C-language routine "c-return": return from a C-language routine "call": call a Ruby method "class": start a class or module definition "end": finish a class or module definition "line": execute code on a new line "raise": raise an exception "return": return from a Ruby method Tracing is disabled within the context of proc. class Test def test a = 1 b = 2 end end set_trace_func proc { |event, file, line, id, binding, class_or_module| printf "%8s %s:%-2d %16p %14p\n", event, file, line, id, class_or_module } t = Test.new t.test Produces: c-return prog.rb:8 :set_trace_func Kernel line prog.rb:11 nil nil c-call prog.rb:11 :new Class c-call prog.rb:11 :initialize BasicObject c-return prog.rb:11 :initialize BasicObject c-return prog.rb:11 :new Class line prog.rb:12 nil nil call prog.rb:2 :test Test line prog.rb:3 :test Test line prog.rb:4 :test Test return prog.rb:5 :test Test

Kernel#sleep.name: sleep
Kernel#sleep.comment:
Suspends execution of the current thread for the number of seconds specified
by numeric argument <tt>secs</tt>, or forever if <tt>secs</tt> is
<tt>nil</tt>; returns the integer number of seconds suspended (rounded).

  Time.new  # => 2008-03-08 19:56:19 +0900
  sleep 1.2 # => 1
  Time.new  # => 2008-03-08 19:56:20 +0900
  sleep 1.9 # => 2
  Time.new  # => 2008-03-08 19:56:22 +0900

Kernel#spawn.name: spawn
Kernel#spawn.call_seq:
spawn([env, ] command_line, options = {}) -> pid
spawn([env, ] exe_path, *args, options  = {}) -> pid
Kernel#spawn.comment: Creates a new child process by doing one of the following in that process: * Passing string command_line to the shell. * Invoking the executable at exe_path. This method has potential security vulnerabilities if called with untrusted input; see {Command Injection}[rdoc-ref:security/command_injection.rdoc]. Returns the process ID (pid) of the new process, without waiting for it to complete. To avoid zombie processes, the parent process should call either: * Process.wait, to collect the termination statuses of its children. * Process.detach, to register disinterest in their status. The new process is created using the {exec system call}[https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799.2018edition/functions/e xecve.html]; it may inherit some of its environment from the calling program (possibly including open file descriptors). Argument env, if given, is a hash that affects ENV for the new process; see {Execution Environment}[rdoc-ref:Process@Execution+Environment]. Argument options is a hash of options for the new process; see {Execution Options}[rdoc-ref:Process@Execution+Options]. The first required argument is one of the following: * command_line if it is a string, and if it begins with a shell reserved word or special built-in, or if it contains one or more meta characters. * exe_path otherwise. Argument command_line String argument command_line is a command line to be passed to a shell; it must begin with a shell reserved word, begin with a special built-in, or contain meta characters: spawn('if true; then echo "Foo"; fi') # => 798847 # Shell reserved word. Process.wait # => 798847 spawn('exit') # => 798848 # Built-in. Process.wait # => 798848 spawn('date > /tmp/date.tmp') # => 798879 # Contains meta character. Process.wait # => 798849 spawn('date > /nop/date.tmp') # => 798882 # Issues error message. Process.wait # => 798882 The command line may also contain arguments and options for the command: spawn('echo "Foo"') # => 799031 Process.wait # => 799031 Output: Foo See {Execution Shell}[rdoc-ref:Process@Execution+Shell] for details about the shell. Raises an exception if the new process could not execute. Argument exe_path Argument exe_path is one of the following: * The string path to an executable to be called. * A 2-element array containing the path to an executable to be called, and the string to be used as the name of the executing process. spawn('/usr/bin/date') # Path to date on Unix-style system. Process.wait Output: Mon Aug 28 11:43:10 AM CDT 2023 Ruby invokes the executable directly. This form does not use the shell; see {Arguments args}[rdoc-ref:Process@Arguments+args] for caveats. If one or more args is given, each is an argument or option to be passed to the executable: spawn('echo', 'C*') # => 799392 Process.wait # => 799392 spawn('echo', 'hello', 'world') # => 799393 Process.wait # => 799393 Output: C* hello world Raises an exception if the new process could not execute.

Kernel#sprintf.name: sprintf
Kernel#sprintf.comment:
Returns the string resulting from formatting <tt>objects</tt> into
<tt>format_string</tt>.

For details on <tt>format_string</tt>, see {Format
Specifications}[rdoc-ref:language/format_specifications.rdoc].

Kernel#srand.name: srand
Kernel#srand.comment:
Seeds the system pseudo-random number generator, with <tt>number</tt>. The
previous seed value is returned.

If <tt>number</tt> is omitted, seeds the generator using a source of entropy
provided by the operating system, if available (/dev/urandom on Unix systems
or the RSA cryptographic provider on Windows), which is then combined with the
time, the process id, and a sequence number.

srand may be used to ensure repeatable sequences of pseudo-random numbers
between different runs of the program. By setting the seed to a known value,
programs can be made deterministic during testing.

  srand 1234               # => 268519324636777531569100071560086917274
  [ rand, rand ]           # => [0.1915194503788923, 0.6221087710398319]
  [ rand(10), rand(1000) ] # => [4, 664]
  srand 1234               # => 1234
  [ rand, rand ]           # => [0.1915194503788923, 0.6221087710398319]

Kernel#sub.name: sub
Kernel#sub.comment: Equivalent to $_.sub(args), except that $_ will be updated if substitution occurs. Available only when -p/-n command line option specified.

Kernel#syscall.name: syscall
Kernel#syscall.comment:
Invokes Posix system call
{syscall(2)}[https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/syscall.2.html], which
calls a specified function.

Calls the operating system function identified by <tt>integer_callno</tt>;
returns the result of the function or raises SystemCallError if it failed. The
effect of the call is platform-dependent. The arguments and returned value are
platform-dependent.

For each of <tt>arguments</tt>: if it is an integer, it is passed directly; if
it is a string, it is interpreted as a binary sequence of bytes. There may be
as many as nine such arguments.

Arguments <tt>integer_callno</tt> and <tt>argument</tt>, as well as the
returned value, are platform-dependent.

Note: Method <tt>syscall</tt> is essentially unsafe and unportable. The DL
(Fiddle) library is preferred for safer and a bit more portable programming.

Not implemented on all platforms.

Kernel#system.name: system
Kernel#system.call_seq:
system([env, ] command_line, options = {}, exception: false) -> true, false, or nil
system([env, ] exe_path, *args, options  = {}, exception: false) -> true, false, or nil
Kernel#system.comment: Creates a new child process by doing one of the following in that process: * Passing string command_line to the shell. * Invoking the executable at exe_path. This method has potential security vulnerabilities if called with untrusted input; see {Command Injection}[rdoc-ref:security/command_injection.rdoc]. Returns: * true if the command exits with status zero. * false if the exit status is a non-zero integer. * nil if the command could not execute. Raises an exception (instead of returning false or nil) if keyword argument exception is set to true. Assigns the command's error status to $?. The new process is created using the {system system call}[https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799.2018edition/functions/s ystem.html]; it may inherit some of its environment from the calling program (possibly including open file descriptors). Argument env, if given, is a hash that affects ENV for the new process; see {Execution Environment}[rdoc-ref:Process@Execution+Environment]. Argument options is a hash of options for the new process; see {Execution Options}[rdoc-ref:Process@Execution+Options]. The first required argument is one of the following: * command_line if it is a string, and if it begins with a shell reserved word or special built-in, or if it contains one or more meta characters. * exe_path otherwise. Argument command_line String argument command_line is a command line to be passed to a shell; it must begin with a shell reserved word, begin with a special built-in, or contain meta characters: system('if true; then echo "Foo"; fi') # => true # Shell reserved word. system('exit') # => true # Built-in. system('date > /tmp/date.tmp') # => true # Contains meta character. system('date > /nop/date.tmp') # => false system('date > /nop/date.tmp', exception: true) # Raises RuntimeError. Assigns the command's error status to $?: system('exit') # => true # Built-in. $? # => # system('date > /nop/date.tmp') # => false $? # => # The command line may also contain arguments and options for the command: system('echo "Foo"') # => true Output: Foo See {Execution Shell}[rdoc-ref:Process@Execution+Shell] for details about the shell. Argument exe_path Argument exe_path is one of the following: * The string path to an executable to be called. * A 2-element array containing the path to an executable and the string to be used as the name of the executing process. Example: system('/usr/bin/date') # => true # Path to date on Unix-style system. system('foo') # => nil # Command failed. Output: Mon Aug 28 11:43:10 AM CDT 2023 Assigns the command's error status to $?: system('/usr/bin/date') # => true $? # => # system('foo') # => nil $? # => # Ruby invokes the executable directly. This form does not use the shell; see {Arguments args}[rdoc-ref:Process@Arguments+args] for caveats. system('doesnt_exist') # => nil If one or more args is given, each is an argument or option to be passed to the executable: system('echo', 'C*') # => true system('echo', 'hello', 'world') # => true Output: C* hello world

Kernel#tap.name: tap

Kernel#test.name: test
Kernel#test.comment: Performs a test on one or both of the filesystem entities at the given paths path0 and path1: * Each path path0 or path1 points to a file, directory, device, pipe, etc. * Character char selects a specific test. The tests: * Each of these tests operates only on the entity at path0, and returns true or false; for a non-existent entity, returns false (does not raise exception): Character |Test ------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------- 'b'|Whether the entity is a block device. 'c'|Whether the entity is a character device. 'd'|Whether the entity is a directory. 'e'|Whether the entity is an existing entity. 'f'|Whether the entity is an existing regular file. 'g'|Whether the entity's setgid bit is set. 'G'|Whether the entity's group ownership is equal to the caller's. 'k'|Whether the entity's sticky bit is set. 'l'|Whether the entity is a symbolic link. 'o'|Whether the entity is owned by the caller's effective uid. 'O'|Like 'o', but uses the real uid (not the effective uid). 'p'|Whether the entity is a FIFO device (named pipe). 'r'|Whether the entity is readable by the caller's effective uid/gid. 'R'|Like 'r', but uses the real uid/gid (not the effective uid/gid). 'S'|Whether the entity is a socket. 'u'|Whether the entity's setuid bit is set. 'w'|Whether the entity is writable by the caller's effective uid/gid. 'W'|Like 'w', but uses the real uid/gid (not the effective uid/gid). 'x'|Whether the entity is executable by the caller's effective uid/gid. 'X'|Like 'x', but uses the real uid/gid (not the effective uid/git). 'z'|Whether the entity exists and is of length zero. * This test operates only on the entity at path0, and returns an integer size or nil: Character |Test ------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 's'|Returns positive integer size if the entity exists and has non-zero length, `nil` otherwise. * Each of these tests operates only on the entity at path0, and returns a Time object; raises an exception if the entity does not exist: Character |Test ------------|-------------------------------------- 'A'|Last access time for the entity. 'C'|Last change time for the entity. 'M'|Last modification time for the entity. * Each of these tests operates on the modification time (mtime) of each of the entities at path0 and path1, and returns a true or false; returns false if either entity does not exist: Character |Test ------------|--------------------------------------------------------------- '<'|Whether the `mtime` at `path0` is less than that at `path1`. '='|Whether the `mtime` at `path0` is equal to that at `path1`. '>'|Whether the `mtime` at `path0` is greater than that at `path1`. * This test operates on the content of each of the entities at path0 and path1, and returns a true or false; returns false if either entity does not exist: Character |Test ------------|--------------------------------------------- '-'|Whether the entities exist and are identical.

Kernel#then.name: then
Kernel#then.comment:
Yields self to the block and returns the result of the block.

  3.next.then {|x| x**x }.to_s             #=> "256"

A good use of <tt>then</tt> is value piping in method chains:

  require 'open-uri'
  require 'json'

  construct_url(arguments)
    .then {|url| URI(url).read }
    .then {|response| JSON.parse(response) }

When called without a block, the method returns an <tt>Enumerator</tt>, which
can be used, for example, for conditional circuit-breaking:

  # Meets condition, no-op
  1.then.detect(&:odd?)            # => 1
  # Does not meet condition, drop value
  2.then.detect(&:odd?)            # => nil

Kernel#throw.name: throw
Kernel#throw.comment: Transfers control to the end of the active catch block waiting for tag. Raises UncaughtThrowError if there is no catch block for the tag. The optional second parameter supplies a return value for the catch block, which otherwise defaults to nil. For examples, see Kernel::catch.

Kernel#trace_var.name: trace_var
Kernel#trace_var.call_seq:
trace_var(symbol, cmd )             -> nil
trace_var(symbol) {|val| block }    -> nil
Kernel#trace_var.comment: Controls tracing of assignments to global variables. The parameter symbol identifies the variable (as either a string name or a symbol identifier). cmd (which may be a string or a Proc object) or block is executed whenever the variable is assigned. The block or Proc object receives the variable's new value as a parameter. Also see #untrace_var. trace_var :$_, proc {|v| puts "$_ is now '#{v}'" } $_ = "hello" $_ = ' there' produces: $_ is now 'hello' $_ is now ' there'

Kernel#trap.name: trap
Kernel#trap.comment:
Specifies the handling of signals. Returns the previous handler for the given
signal.

Argument <tt>signal</tt> is a signal name (a string or symbol such as
<tt>SIGALRM</tt> or <tt>SIGUSR1</tt>) or an integer signal number. When
<tt>signal</tt> is a string or symbol, the leading characters <tt>SIG</tt> may
be omitted.

Argument <tt>command</tt> or block provided specifies code to be run when the
signal is raised.

Argument <tt>command</tt> may also be a string or symbol with the following
special values:

* <tt>IGNORE</tt>, <tt>SIG_IGN</tt>: the signal will be ignored.
* <tt>DEFAULT</tt>, <tt>SIG_DFL</tt>: Ruby's default handler will be invoked.
* <tt>EXIT</tt>: the process will be terminated by the signal.
* <tt>SYSTEM_DEFAULT</tt>: the operating system's default handler will be
  invoked.

The special signal name <tt>EXIT</tt> or signal number zero will be invoked
just prior to program termination:

  Signal.trap(0, proc { puts "Terminating: #{$$}" })
  Signal.trap("CLD")  { puts "Child died" }
  fork && Process.wait

Outputs:

  Terminating: 27461
  Child died
  Terminating: 27460

Kernel#untrace_var.name: untrace_var
Kernel#untrace_var.comment:
Removes tracing for the specified command on the given global variable and
returns <tt>nil</tt>. If no command is specified, removes all tracing for that
variable and returns an array containing the commands actually removed.

Kernel#warn.name: warn
Kernel#warn.call_seq: warn(*msgs, uplevel: nil, category: nil)   -> nil
Kernel#warn.comment: If warnings have been disabled (for example with the -W0 flag), does nothing. Otherwise, converts each of the messages to strings, appends a newline character to the string if the string does not end in a newline, and calls Warning.warn with the string. warn("warning 1", "warning 2") produces: warning 1 warning 2 If the uplevel keyword argument is given, the string will be prepended with information for the given caller frame in the same format used by the rb_warn C function. # In baz.rb def foo warn("invalid call to foo", uplevel: 1) end def bar foo end bar produces: baz.rb:6: warning: invalid call to foo If category keyword argument is given, passes the category to Warning.warn. The category given must be one of the following categories: :deprecated: Used for warning for deprecated functionality that may be removed in the future. :experimental: Used for experimental features that may change in future releases. :performance: Used for warning about APIs or pattern that have negative performance impact

Kernel#JSON.name: JSON
Kernel#JSON.comment: If object is string-like, parse the string and return the parsed result as a Ruby data structure. Otherwise, generate a JSON text from the Ruby data structure object and return it. The opts argument is passed through to generate/parse respectively. See generate and parse for their documentation.

Kernel#URI.name: URI
Kernel#URI.comment:
Returns a URI object derived from the given <tt>uri</tt>, which may be a URI
string or an existing URI object:

  require 'uri'
  # Returns a new URI.
  uri = URI('http://github.com/ruby/ruby')
  # => #<URI::HTTP http://github.com/ruby/ruby>
  # Returns the given URI.
  URI(uri)
  # => #<URI::HTTP http://github.com/ruby/ruby>

You must require 'uri' to use this method.

Kernel#gem.name: gem
Kernel#gem.comment: Use Kernel#gem to activate a specific version of gem_name. requirements is a list of version requirements that the specified gem must match, most commonly "= example.version.number". See Gem::Requirement for how to specify a version requirement. If you will be activating the latest version of a gem, there is no need to call Kernel#gem, Kernel#require will do the right thing for you. Kernel#gem returns true if the gem was activated, otherwise false. If the gem could not be found, didn't match the version requirements, or a different version was already activated, an exception will be raised. Kernel#gem should be called before any require statements (otherwise RubyGems may load a conflicting library version). Kernel#gem only loads prerelease versions when prerelease requirements are given: gem 'rake', '>= 1.1.a', '< 2' In older RubyGems versions, the environment variable GEM_SKIP could be used to skip activation of specified gems, for example to test out changes that haven't been installed yet. Now RubyGems defers to -I and the RUBYLIB environment variable to skip activation of a gem. Example: GEM_SKIP=libA:libB ruby -I../libA -I../libB ./mycode.rb

Kernel#pp.name: pp
Kernel#pp.comment:
prints arguments in pretty form.

<tt>#pp</tt> returns argument(s).

Kernel#require.name: require
Kernel#require.comment:
When RubyGems is required, Kernel#require is replaced with our own which is
capable of loading gems on demand.

When you call <tt>require 'x'</tt>, this is what happens:
* If the file can be loaded from the existing Ruby loadpath, it is.
* Otherwise, installed gems are searched for a file that matches. If it's
  found in gem 'y', that gem is activated (added to the loadpath).

The normal <tt>require</tt> functionality of returning false if that file has
already been loaded is preserved.

Kernel#y.name: y
Kernel#y.comment: An alias for Psych.dump_stream meant to be used with IRB.

KeyError.name: KeyError
KeyError.comment:
Raised when the specified key is not found. It is a subclass of IndexError.

  h = {"foo" => :bar}
  h.fetch("foo") #=> :bar
  h.fetch("baz") #=> KeyError: key not found: "baz"

KeyError::new.name: new
KeyError::new.call_seq: KeyError.new(message=nil, receiver: nil, key: nil) -> key_error
KeyError::new.comment:
Construct a new <tt>KeyError</tt> exception with the given message, receiver
and key.

KeyError#key.name: key
KeyError#key.comment: Return the key caused this KeyError exception.

KeyError#receiver.name: receiver
KeyError#receiver.comment: Return the receiver associated with this KeyError exception.

LoadError.name: LoadError
LoadError.comment: Raised when a file required (a Ruby script, extension library, ...) fails to load. require 'this/file/does/not/exist' raises the exception: LoadError: no such file to load -- this/file/does/not/exist for RubyGems without Bundler environment. If loading library is not part of the default gems and the bundled gems, warn it.

LocalJumpError.name: LocalJumpError
LocalJumpError.comment: Raised when Ruby can't yield as requested. A typical scenario is attempting to yield when no block is given: def call_block yield 42 end call_block raises the exception: LocalJumpError: no block given (yield) A more subtle example: def get_me_a_return Proc.new { return 42 } end get_me_a_return.call raises the exception: LocalJumpError: unexpected return

LocalJumpError#exit_value.name: exit_value
LocalJumpError#exit_value.comment: Returns the exit value associated with this <tt>LocalJumpError</tt>.

LocalJumpError#reason.name: reason
LocalJumpError#reason.comment:
The reason this block was terminated: :break, :redo, :retry, :next, :return,
or :noreason.

MakeMakefile.name: MakeMakefile
MakeMakefile.comment:
Module MakeMakefile is used by Ruby C extensions to generate a Makefile which
will correctly compile and link the C extension to Ruby and a third-party
library.
Namespace for <tt>mkmf</tt> extension-building helpers.

MakeMakefile#append_cflags.name: append_cflags
MakeMakefile#append_cflags.comment:
Check whether each given C compiler flag is acceptable and append it to
<tt>$CFLAGS</tt> if so.

<tt>flags</tt>:
  a C compiler flag as a <tt>String</tt> or an <tt>Array</tt> of them

MakeMakefile#append_ldflags.name: append_ldflags
MakeMakefile#append_ldflags.comment:
Check whether each given linker flag is acceptable and append it to
<tt>$LDFLAGS</tt> if so.

<tt>flags</tt>:
  a linker flag as a <tt>String</tt> or an <tt>Array</tt> of them

MakeMakefile#check_signedness.name: check_signedness
MakeMakefile#check_signedness.comment:
Returns the signedness of the given <tt>type</tt>.  You may optionally specify
additional <tt>headers</tt> to search in for the <tt>type</tt>.

If the <tt>type</tt> is found and is a numeric type, a macro is passed as a
preprocessor constant to the compiler using the <tt>type</tt> name, in
uppercase, prepended with <tt>SIGNEDNESS_OF_</tt>, followed by the
<tt>type</tt> name, followed by <tt>=X</tt> where "X" is positive integer if
the <tt>type</tt> is unsigned and a negative integer if the <tt>type</tt> is
signed.

For example, if <tt>size_t</tt> is defined as unsigned, then
<tt>check_signedness('size_t')</tt> would return +1 and the
<tt>SIGNEDNESS_OF_SIZE_T=+1</tt> preprocessor macro would be passed to the
compiler.  The <tt>SIGNEDNESS_OF_INT=-1</tt> macro would be set for
<tt>check_signedness('int')</tt>

MakeMakefile#check_sizeof.name: check_sizeof
MakeMakefile#check_sizeof.comment:
Returns the size of the given <tt>type</tt>.  You may optionally specify
additional <tt>headers</tt> to search in for the <tt>type</tt>.

If found, a macro is passed as a preprocessor constant to the compiler using
the type name, in uppercase, prepended with <tt>SIZEOF_</tt>, followed by the
type name, followed by <tt>=X</tt> where "X" is the actual size.

For example, if <tt>check_sizeof('mystruct')</tt> returned 12, then the
<tt>SIZEOF_MYSTRUCT=12</tt> preprocessor macro would be passed to the
compiler.

MakeMakefile#conftest_source.name: conftest_source
MakeMakefile#conftest_source.comment: Returns the language-dependent source file name for configuration checks.

MakeMakefile#convertible_int.name: convertible_int
MakeMakefile#convertible_int.comment: Returns the convertible integer type of the given type. You may optionally specify additional headers to search in for the type. convertible means actually the same type, or typedef'd from the same type. If the type is an integer type and the convertible type is found, the following macros are passed as preprocessor constants to the compiler using the type name, in uppercase. * TYPEOF_, followed by the type name, followed by =X where "X" is the found convertible type name. * TYP2NUM and NUM2TYP, where TYP is the type name in uppercase with replacing an _t suffix with "T", followed by =X where "X" is the macro name to convert type to an Integer object, and vice versa. For example, if foobar_t is defined as unsigned long, then convertible_int("foobar_t") would return "unsigned long", and define these macros: #define TYPEOF_FOOBAR_T unsigned long #define FOOBART2NUM ULONG2NUM #define NUM2FOOBART NUM2ULONG

MakeMakefile#create_header.name: create_header
MakeMakefile#create_header.comment:
Generates a header file consisting of the various macro definitions generated
by other methods such as have_func and have_header. These are then wrapped in
a custom <tt>#ifndef</tt> based on the <tt>header</tt> file name, which
defaults to "extconf.h".

For example:

  # extconf.rb
  require 'mkmf'
  have_func('realpath')
  have_header('sys/utime.h')
  create_header
  create_makefile('foo')

The above script would generate the following extconf.h file:

  #ifndef EXTCONF_H
  #define EXTCONF_H
  #define HAVE_REALPATH 1
  #define HAVE_SYS_UTIME_H 1
  #endif

Given that the create_header method generates a file based on definitions set
earlier in your extconf.rb file, you will probably want to make this one of
the last methods you call in your script.

MakeMakefile#create_makefile.name: create_makefile
MakeMakefile#create_makefile.comment:
Generates the Makefile for your extension, passing along any options and
preprocessor constants that you may have generated through other methods.

The <tt>target</tt> name should correspond the name of the global function
name defined within your C extension, minus the <tt>Init_</tt>.  For example,
if your C extension is defined as <tt>Init_foo</tt>, then your target would
simply be "foo".

If any "/" characters are present in the target name, only the last name is
interpreted as the target name, and the rest are considered toplevel directory
names, and the generated Makefile will be altered accordingly to follow that
directory structure.

For example, if you pass "test/foo" as a target name, your extension will be
installed under the "test" directory.  This means that in order to load the
file within a Ruby program later, that directory structure will have to be
followed, e.g. <tt>require 'test/foo'</tt>.

The <tt>srcprefix</tt> should be used when your source files are not in the
same directory as your build script. This will not only eliminate the need for
you to manually copy the source files into the same directory as your build
script, but it also sets the proper <tt>target_prefix</tt> in the generated
Makefile.

Setting the <tt>target_prefix</tt> will, in turn, install the generated binary
in a directory under your <tt>RbConfig::CONFIG['sitearchdir']</tt> that mimics
your local filesystem when you run <tt>make install</tt>.

For example, given the following file tree:

  ext/
    extconf.rb
    test/
      foo.c

And given the following code:

  create_makefile('test/foo', 'test')

That will set the <tt>target_prefix</tt> in the generated Makefile to "test".
That, in turn, will create the following file tree when installed via the
<tt>make install</tt> command:

  /path/to/ruby/sitearchdir/test/foo.so

It is recommended that you use this approach to generate your makefiles,
instead of copying files around manually, because some third party libraries
may depend on the <tt>target_prefix</tt> being set properly.

The <tt>srcprefix</tt> argument can be used to override the default source
directory, i.e. the current directory.  It is included as part of the
<tt>VPATH</tt> and added to the list of <tt>INCFLAGS</tt>.

Yields the configuration part of the makefile to be generated, as an array of
strings, if the block is given.  The returned value will be used the new
configuration part.

  create_makefile('foo') {|conf|
    [
      *conf,
      "MACRO_YOU_NEED = something",
    ]
  }

If "depend" file exist in the source directory, that content will be included
in the generated makefile, with formatted by depend_rules method.

With <tt>--update-depend</tt>, the autogenerated section in "depend" is
updated from the sources and objects found by this method.  The source tree
root is detected from ".git", or can be specified with
<tt>--depend-root=DIR</tt>.  An existing autogenerated section is required.

MakeMakefile#create_tmpsrc.name: create_tmpsrc
MakeMakefile#create_tmpsrc.comment: Creats temporary source file from COMMON_HEADERS and src. Yields the created source string and uses the returned string as the source code, if the block is given.

MakeMakefile#depend_rules.name: depend_rules
MakeMakefile#depend_rules.comment:
Processes the data contents of the "depend" file.  Each line of this file is
expected to be a file name.

Returns the output of findings, in Makefile format.

MakeMakefile#dir_config.name: dir_config
MakeMakefile#dir_config.call_seq:
dir_config(target)
dir_config(target, prefix)
dir_config(target, idefault, ldefault)
MakeMakefile#dir_config.comment:
Sets a <tt>target</tt> name that the user can then use to configure various
"with" options with on the command line by using that name.  For example, if
the target is set to "foo", then the user could use the
<tt>--with-foo-dir=prefix</tt>, <tt>--with-foo-include=dir</tt> and
<tt>--with-foo-lib=dir</tt> command line options to tell where to search for
header/library files.

You may pass along additional parameters to specify default values.  If one is
given it is taken as default <tt>prefix</tt>, and if two are given they are
taken as "include" and "lib" defaults in that order.

In any case, the return value will be an array of determined "include" and
"lib" directories, either of which can be nil if no corresponding command line
option is given when no default value is specified.

Note that dir_config only adds to the list of places to search for libraries
and include files.  It does not link the libraries into your application.

MakeMakefile#egrep_cpp.name: egrep_cpp
MakeMakefile#egrep_cpp.comment:
Returns whether or not the <tt>src</tt> can be preprocessed with the C
preprocessor and matches with <tt>pat</tt>.

If a block given, it is called with the source before compilation. You can
modify the source in the block.

<tt>pat</tt>:
  a Regexp or a String

<tt>src</tt>:
  a String which contains a C source

<tt>opt</tt>:
  a String which contains preprocessor options

NOTE: When pat is a Regexp the matching will be checked in process, otherwise
egrep(1) will be invoked to check it.

MakeMakefile#enable_config.name: enable_config
MakeMakefile#enable_config.comment: Tests for the presence of an --enable-config or --disable-config option. Returns true if the enable option is given, false if the disable option is given, and the default value otherwise. This can be useful for adding custom definitions, such as debug information. Example: if enable_config("debug") $defs.push("-DOSSL_DEBUG") unless $defs.include? "-DOSSL_DEBUG" end

MakeMakefile#find_header.name: find_header
MakeMakefile#find_header.comment:
Instructs mkmf to search for the given <tt>header</tt> in any of the
<tt>paths</tt> provided, and returns whether or not it was found in those
paths.

If the header is found then the path it was found on is added to the list of
included directories that are sent to the compiler (via the <tt>-I</tt>
switch).

MakeMakefile#find_library.name: find_library
MakeMakefile#find_library.comment:
Returns whether or not the entry point <tt>func</tt> can be found within the
library <tt>lib</tt> in one of the <tt>paths</tt> specified, where
<tt>paths</tt> is an array of strings.  If <tt>func</tt> is <tt>nil</tt> ,
then the <tt>main()</tt> function is used as the entry point.

If <tt>lib</tt> is found, then the path it was found on is added to the list
of library paths searched and linked against.

MakeMakefile#have_const.name: have_const
MakeMakefile#have_const.comment:
Returns whether or not the constant <tt>const</tt> is defined.  You may
optionally pass the <tt>type</tt> of <tt>const</tt> as <tt>[const, type]</tt>,
such as:

  have_const(%w[PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER pthread_mutex_t], "pthread.h")

You may also pass additional <tt>headers</tt> to check against in addition to
the common header files, and additional flags to <tt>opt</tt> which are then
passed along to the compiler.

If found, a macro is passed as a preprocessor constant to the compiler using
the type name, in uppercase, prepended with <tt>HAVE_CONST_</tt>.

For example, if <tt>have_const('foo')</tt> returned true, then the
<tt>HAVE_CONST_FOO</tt> preprocessor macro would be passed to the compiler.

MakeMakefile#have_framework.name: have_framework
MakeMakefile#have_framework.comment:
Returns whether or not the given <tt>framework</tt> can be found on your
system. If found, a macro is passed as a preprocessor constant to the compiler
using the framework name, in uppercase, prepended with
<tt>HAVE_FRAMEWORK_</tt>.

For example, if <tt>have_framework('Ruby')</tt> returned true, then the
<tt>HAVE_FRAMEWORK_RUBY</tt> preprocessor macro would be passed to the
compiler.

If <tt>fw</tt> is a pair of the framework name and its header file name that
header file is checked, instead of the normally used header file which is
named same as the framework.

MakeMakefile#have_func.name: have_func
MakeMakefile#have_func.comment:
Returns whether or not the function <tt>func</tt> can be found in the common
header files, or within any <tt>headers</tt> that you provide.  If found, a
macro is passed as a preprocessor constant to the compiler using the function
name, in uppercase, prepended with <tt>HAVE_</tt>.

To check functions in an additional library, you need to check that library
first using <tt>have_library()</tt>.  The <tt>func</tt> shall be either mere
function name or function name with arguments.

For example, if <tt>have_func('foo')</tt> returned <tt>true</tt>, then the
<tt>HAVE_FOO</tt> preprocessor macro would be passed to the compiler.

MakeMakefile#have_header.name: have_header
MakeMakefile#have_header.comment:
Returns whether or not the given <tt>header</tt> file can be found on your
system. If found, a macro is passed as a preprocessor constant to the compiler
using the header file name, in uppercase, prepended with <tt>HAVE_</tt>.

For example, if <tt>have_header('foo.h')</tt> returned true, then the
<tt>HAVE_FOO_H</tt> preprocessor macro would be passed to the compiler.

MakeMakefile#have_library.name: have_library
MakeMakefile#have_library.comment:
Returns whether or not the given entry point <tt>func</tt> can be found within
<tt>lib</tt>.  If <tt>func</tt> is <tt>nil</tt>, the <tt>main()</tt> entry
point is used by default.  If found, it adds the library to list of libraries
to be used when linking your extension.

If <tt>headers</tt> are provided, it will include those header files as the
header files it looks in when searching for <tt>func</tt>.

The real name of the library to be linked can be altered by
<tt>--with-FOOlib</tt> configuration option.

MakeMakefile#have_macro.name: have_macro
MakeMakefile#have_macro.comment:
Returns whether or not <tt>macro</tt> is defined either in the common header
files or within any <tt>headers</tt> you provide.

Any options you pass to <tt>opt</tt> are passed along to the compiler.

MakeMakefile#have_struct_member.name: have_struct_member
MakeMakefile#have_struct_member.comment:
Returns whether or not the struct of type <tt>type</tt> contains
<tt>member</tt>.  If it does not, or the struct type can't be found, then
false is returned. You may optionally specify additional <tt>headers</tt> in
which to look for the struct (in addition to the common header files).

If found, a macro is passed as a preprocessor constant to the compiler using
the type name and the member name, in uppercase, prepended with
<tt>HAVE_</tt>.

For example, if <tt>have_struct_member('struct foo', 'bar')</tt> returned
true, then the <tt>HAVE_STRUCT_FOO_BAR</tt> preprocessor macro would be passed
to the compiler.

<tt>HAVE_ST_BAR</tt> is also defined for backward compatibility.

MakeMakefile#have_var.name: have_var
MakeMakefile#have_var.comment:
Returns whether or not the variable <tt>var</tt> can be found in the common
header files, or within any <tt>headers</tt> that you provide.  If found, a
macro is passed as a preprocessor constant to the compiler using the variable
name, in uppercase, prepended with <tt>HAVE_</tt>.

To check variables in an additional library, you need to check that library
first using <tt>have_library()</tt>.

For example, if <tt>have_var('foo')</tt> returned true, then the
<tt>HAVE_FOO</tt> preprocessor macro would be passed to the compiler.

MakeMakefile#modified?.name: modified?
MakeMakefile#modified?.comment:
Returns time stamp of the <tt>target</tt> file if it exists and is newer than
or equal to all of <tt>times</tt>.

MakeMakefile#pkg_config.name: pkg_config
MakeMakefile#pkg_config.comment:
Returns compile/link information about an installed library in a tuple of
<tt>[cflags, ldflags, libs]</tt>, by using the command found first in the
following commands:

1. If <tt>--with-{pkg}-config={command}</tt> is given via command line option:
   <tt>{command} {options}</tt>

2. <tt>{pkg}-config {options}</tt>

3. <tt>pkg-config {options} {pkg}</tt>

Where <tt>options</tt> is the option name without dashes, for instance
<tt>"cflags"</tt> for the <tt>--cflags</tt> flag.

The values obtained are appended to <tt>$INCFLAGS</tt>, <tt>$CFLAGS</tt>,
<tt>$LDFLAGS</tt> and <tt>$libs</tt>.

If one or more <tt>options</tt> argument is given, the config command is
invoked with the options and a stripped output string is returned without
modifying any of the global values mentioned above.

MakeMakefile#what_type?.name: what_type?
MakeMakefile#what_type?.comment: Returns a string represents the type of type, or member of type if member is not nil.

MakeMakefile#with_config.name: with_config
MakeMakefile#with_config.comment: Tests for the presence of a --with-config or --without-config option. Returns true if the with option is given, false if the without option is given, and the default value otherwise. This can be useful for adding custom definitions, such as debug information. Example: if with_config("debug") $defs.push("-DOSSL_DEBUG") unless $defs.include? "-DOSSL_DEBUG" end

MakeMakefile#with_cppflags.name: with_cppflags
MakeMakefile#with_cppflags.comment: Sets $CPPFLAGS to flags and yields. If the block returns a falsy value, $CPPFLAGS is reset to its previous value, remains set to flags otherwise. flags: a C preprocessor flag as a String

MakeMakefile#xpopen.name: xpopen
MakeMakefile#xpopen.comment: Executes command similarly to xsystem, but yields opened pipe.

MakeMakefile#xsystem.name: xsystem
MakeMakefile#xsystem.call_seq: xsystem(command, werror: false)   -> true or false
MakeMakefile#xsystem.comment: Executes command with expanding variables, and returns the exit status like as Kernel#system. If werror is true and the error output is not empty, returns false. The output will logged.

MakeMakefile::Depend.name: MakeMakefile::Depend
MakeMakefile::Depend.comment:
Generates dependency rules for Ruby and C extension sources.

An extension project can update the autogenerated section of its
<tt>depend</tt> file while running <tt>extconf.rb</tt>:

  ruby extconf.rb --update-depend

The <tt>depend</tt> file must contain these markers:

  # AUTOGENERATED DEPENDENCIES START
  # AUTOGENERATED DEPENDENCIES END

MakeMakefile::Depend scans each source and the headers it includes without
invoking a compiler.  When updating an extension project, files outside the
project tree, such as system and installed Ruby headers, are omitted.  Use
<tt>--depend-root=DIR</tt> when the project root cannot be detected from a
<tt>.git</tt> directory.

MakeMakefile::Depend::find_root.name: find_root
MakeMakefile::Depend::find_root.comment:
Finds the nearest ancestor of <tt>path</tt> containing <tt>.git</tt>.

Returns <tt>path</tt> itself when no repository root can be found.

MakeMakefile::Depend::main.name: main
MakeMakefile::Depend::main.comment:
Runs the command-line interface with <tt>argv</tt>.

Returns whether the requested update or check succeeded.

MakeMakefile::Depend::execute.name: execute
MakeMakefile::Depend::execute.comment: Creates an updater and runs it with the parsed command-line options.

MakeMakefile::Depend::parse_options.name: parse_options
MakeMakefile::Depend::parse_options.comment: Parses command-line arguments into runner options and input paths.

MakeMakefile::Depend#run.name: run
MakeMakefile::Depend#run.params: (inputs = ARGV, out: $stdout, err: $stderr, mode: :stdout, output: nil, make_variables: {}, nmake: false, sources: false, scope: nil, thread_model: nil, verbose: false)
MakeMakefile::Depend#run.comment:
Processes dependency <tt>inputs</tt> according to the selected update
<tt>mode</tt>.

<tt>make_variables</tt> supplies values for Make variables in declarations.
<tt>thread_model</tt> is a shortcut for its <tt>THREAD_MODEL</tt> entry.

Returns <tt>false</tt> only when check mode finds an outdated dependency file.

MakeMakefile::Depend#update_extension.name: update_extension
MakeMakefile::Depend#update_extension.params: (input, source_map, make_variables: {}, nmake: false, verbose: false)
MakeMakefile::Depend#update_extension.comment:
Updates the marked dependency section in extension file <tt>input</tt>.

<tt>source_map</tt> maps object targets to source paths.
<tt>make_variables</tt> supplies values of Make variables used by manual
dependency rules. Returns <tt>true</tt> when the file changed and
<tt>false</tt> when its dependencies were already current.

MakeMakefile::Depend#compact_dependencie.name: compact_dependencies
MakeMakefile::Depend#compact_dependencie.comment:
Sorts and deduplicates <tt>rules</tt>, optionally grouping targets by
dependency.

MakeMakefile::Depend#declaration.name: declaration
MakeMakefile::Depend#declaration.comment:
Finds the declaration for <tt>name</tt>, accounting for an input-relative
name.

MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_cache_si.name: dependency_cache_signature
MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_cache_si.comment: Returns the cache signature for options affecting generated dependencies.

MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_declarat.name: dependency_declarations
MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_declarat.comment: Returns merged global and file-local declarations for an input or source.

MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_file_con.name: dependency_file_content
MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_file_con.comment: Reads and caches a dependency file, or caches supplied <tt>content</tt>.

MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_files.name: dependency_files
MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_files.comment: Returns marked dependency files selected by <tt>scope</tt>.

MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_input.name: dependency_input
MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_input.comment: Returns the dependency file that governs <tt>source</tt>.

MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_output_f.name: dependency_output_fresh?
MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_output_f.comment:
Returns whether <tt>destination</tt> and all recorded scan inputs are
unchanged.

MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_scanner.name: dependency_scanner
MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_scanner.comment: Builds a Scanner configured by the declarations governing <tt>src</tt>.

MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_source?.name: dependency_source?
MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_source?.comment:
Returns whether <tt>source</tt> is declared as generated or otherwise
resolvable.

MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_source_m.name: dependency_source_map
MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_source_m.comment: Returns an object-target to source-path mapping extracted from <tt>rules</tt>.

MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_source_r.name: dependency_source_rules
MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_source_r.comment: Extracts the best source rule for each object target in <tt>rules</tt>.

MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_sources.name: dependency_sources
MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_sources.comment: Returns the source paths identified by <tt>rules</tt>.

MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_stat.name: dependency_stat
MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_stat.comment:
Returns cached stat information, or <tt>false</tt> when <tt>path</tt> does not
exist.

MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_target.name: dependency_target
MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_target.comment: Finds the declared target matching <tt>name</tt> in <tt>input</tt>.

MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_targets.name: dependency_targets
MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_targets.comment:
Returns generated targets declared outside the marked section of
<tt>input</tt>.

MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_vpath.name: dependency_vpath
MakeMakefile::Depend#dependency_vpath.comment: Returns the VPATH prefix used for dependencies of <tt>source</tt>.

MakeMakefile::Depend#depends.name: depends
MakeMakefile::Depend#depends.params: (files, vpath, source: nil, input: nil, declarations: nil, project: false)
MakeMakefile::Depend#depends.comment:
Converts scanned <tt>files</tt> into sorted Make dependencies for
<tt>source</tt>.

MakeMakefile::Depend#expand_dependency_v.name: expand_dependency_variables
MakeMakefile::Depend#expand_dependency_v.comment: Expands known Make variables that stand for dependency lists.

MakeMakefile::Depend#expand_make_variabl.name: expand_make_variables
MakeMakefile::Depend#expand_make_variabl.comment: Expands known Make variables embedded in <tt>value</tt>.

MakeMakefile::Depend#expand_scan_declara.name: expand_scan_declaration
MakeMakefile::Depend#expand_scan_declara.comment:
Expands matching wildcards in a <tt>scan</tt> declaration.

Returns a generated-name to source-path mapping.

MakeMakefile::Depend#extension_dependenc.name: extension_dependency
MakeMakefile::Depend#extension_dependenc.comment: Converts an extension dependency to the Make variable path it requires.

MakeMakefile::Depend#makedepend.name: makedepend
MakeMakefile::Depend#makedepend.params: (src, out = [], target: nil, input: nil, project: false, accessed: nil)
MakeMakefile::Depend#makedepend.comment:
Appends Make dependency rules for <tt>src</tt> to <tt>out</tt> and returns
<tt>out</tt>.

MakeMakefile::Depend#minimize_deps.name: minimize_deps
MakeMakefile::Depend#minimize_deps.comment: Reduces <tt>rules</tt> to source mappings needed to regenerate dependencies.

MakeMakefile::Depend#normalize_dependenc.name: normalize_dependency_rules
MakeMakefile::Depend#normalize_dependenc.comment: Removes VPATH markers that are unnecessary in build-directory output.

MakeMakefile::Depend#object_name.name: object_name
MakeMakefile::Depend#object_name.comment: Returns the Make object name for source path <tt>src</tt>.

MakeMakefile::Depend#parse_dependency_de.name: parse_dependency_declarations
MakeMakefile::Depend#parse_dependency_de.comment:
Parses <tt>mkdepend</tt> declarations from <tt>path</tt> or the supplied
<tt>content</tt>.

MakeMakefile::Depend#project_dependency.name: project_dependency
MakeMakefile::Depend#project_dependency.comment: Converts a standalone project's file to a dependency relative to its source.

MakeMakefile::Depend#relative_dependency.name: relative_dependency
MakeMakefile::Depend#relative_dependency.comment:
Makes <tt>path</tt> relative to #root, keeping a relative name that does not
refer to a source-tree file as-is: generated dependencies such as
builtin_binary.rbbin must keep the name their Make rules use.

MakeMakefile::Depend#relative_source.name: relative_source
MakeMakefile::Depend#relative_source.comment:
Makes <tt>path</tt> relative to #root when it refers to a source-tree file.

A relative name is resolved against #root, not the current directory: a build
directory nested inside the source tree holds generated files under
source-tree names, and those must not be taken for the sources they are
generated from.  Only a name reaching outside #root is resolved against the
current directory, where the tool may also be run.

MakeMakefile::Depend#replace_file.name: replace_file
MakeMakefile::Depend#replace_file.comment:
Atomically replaces <tt>path</tt> with <tt>content</tt>, preserving its file
mode.

MakeMakefile::Depend#report_outdated_dep.name: report_outdated_dependencies
MakeMakefile::Depend#report_outdated_dep.comment: Reports how dependency rules in <tt>input</tt> differ from <tt>expected</tt>.

MakeMakefile::Depend#resolve_dependency_.name: resolve_dependency_source
MakeMakefile::Depend#resolve_dependency_.comment:
Resolves <tt>src</tt> to an existing, missing-library, or declared source
path.

MakeMakefile::Depend#same_dependency_rul.name: same_dependency_rules?
MakeMakefile::Depend#same_dependency_rul.comment: Returns whether two rule sets differ only by removable VPATH markers.

MakeMakefile::Depend#select_make_variabl.name: select_make_variables
MakeMakefile::Depend#select_make_variabl.comment: Selects known Make variable values used during dependency generation.

MakeMakefile::Depend#update_deps.name: update_deps
MakeMakefile::Depend#update_deps.params: (rules, input, group: true, verbose: false, accessed: nil)
MakeMakefile::Depend#update_deps.comment:
Regenerates dependency <tt>rules</tt> for the sources identified in
<tt>input</tt>.

MakeMakefile::Depend#write_dependency_ca.name: write_dependency_cache
MakeMakefile::Depend#write_dependency_ca.comment: Records scan inputs used to produce <tt>destination</tt>.

Marshal.name: Marshal
Marshal.comment:
The marshaling library converts collections of Ruby objects into a byte
stream, allowing them to be stored outside the currently active script. This
data may subsequently be read and the original objects reconstituted.

Marshaled data has major and minor version numbers stored along with the
object information. In normal use, marshaling can only load data written with
the same major version number and an equal or lower minor version number. If
Ruby's ``verbose'' flag is set (normally using -d, -v, -w, or --verbose) the
major and minor numbers must match exactly. Marshal versioning is independent
of Ruby's version numbers. You can extract the version by reading the first
two bytes of marshaled data.

  str = Marshal.dump("thing")
  RUBY_VERSION   #=> "1.9.0"
  str[0].ord     #=> 4
  str[1].ord     #=> 8

Some objects cannot be dumped: if the objects to be dumped include bindings,
procedure or method objects, instances of class IO, or singleton objects, a
TypeError will be raised.

If your class has special serialization needs (for example, if you want to
serialize in some specific format), or if it contains objects that would
otherwise not be serializable, you can implement your own serialization
strategy.

There are two methods of doing this, your object can define either
marshal_dump and marshal_load or _dump and _load.  marshal_dump will take
precedence over _dump if both are defined.  marshal_dump may result in smaller
Marshal strings.

== Security considerations

By design, Marshal.load can deserialize almost any class loaded into the Ruby
process. In many cases this can lead to remote code execution if the Marshal
data is loaded from an untrusted source.

As a result, Marshal.load is not suitable as a general purpose serialization
format and you should never unmarshal user supplied input or other untrusted
data.

If you need to deserialize untrusted data, use JSON or another serialization
format that is only able to load simple, 'primitive' types such as String,
Array, Hash, etc. Never allow user input to specify arbitrary types to
deserialize into.

== marshal_dump and marshal_load

When dumping an object the method marshal_dump will be called. marshal_dump
must return a result containing the information necessary for marshal_load to
reconstitute the object.  The result can be any object.

When loading an object dumped using marshal_dump the object is first allocated
then marshal_load is called with the result from marshal_dump. marshal_load
must recreate the object from the information in the result.

Example:

  class MyObj
    def initialize name, version, data
      @name    = name
      @version = version
      @data    = data
    end

    def marshal_dump
      [@name, @version]
    end

    def marshal_load array
      @name, @version = array
    end
  end

== _dump and _load

Use _dump and _load when you need to allocate the object you're restoring
yourself.

When dumping an object the instance method _dump is called with an Integer
which indicates the maximum depth of objects to dump (a value of -1 implies
that you should disable depth checking).  _dump must return a String
containing the information necessary to reconstitute the object.

The class method _load should take a String and use it to return an object of
the same class.

Example:

  class MyObj
    def initialize name, version, data
      @name    = name
      @version = version
      @data    = data
    end

    def _dump level
      [@name, @version].join ':'
    end

    def self._load args
      new(*args.split(':'))
    end
  end

Since Marshal.dump outputs a string you can have _dump return a Marshal string
which is Marshal.loaded in _load for complex objects.

Marshal::dump.name: dump
Marshal::dump.comment:
Serializes obj and all descendant objects. If anIO is specified, the
serialized data will be written to it, otherwise the data will be returned as
a String. If limit is specified, the traversal of subobjects will be limited
to that depth. If limit is negative, no checking of depth will be performed.

  class Klass
    def initialize(str)
      @str = str
    end
    def say_hello
      @str
    end
  end

(produces no output)

  o = Klass.new("hello\n")
  data = Marshal.dump(o)
  obj = Marshal.load(data)
  obj.say_hello  #=> "hello\n"

Marshal can't dump following objects:
* anonymous Class/Module.
* objects which are related to system (ex: Dir, File::Stat, IO, File, Socket
  and so on)
* an instance of MatchData, Method, UnboundMethod, Proc, Thread, ThreadGroup,
  Continuation
* objects which define singleton methods

Marshal::load.name: load
Marshal::load.call_seq: load(source, proc = nil, freeze: false) -> obj
Marshal::load.comment:
Returns the result of converting the serialized data in source into a Ruby
object (possibly with associated subordinate objects). source may be either an
instance of IO or an object that responds to to_str. If proc is specified,
each object will be passed to the proc, as the object is being deserialized.

Never pass untrusted data (including user supplied input) to this method.
Please see the overview for further details.

If the <tt>freeze: true</tt> argument is passed, deserialized object would be
deeply frozen. Note that it may lead to more efficient memory usage due to
frozen strings deduplication:

  serialized = Marshal.dump(['value1', 'value2', 'value1', 'value2'])

  deserialized = Marshal.load(serialized)
  deserialized.map(&:frozen?)
  # => [false, false, false, false]
  deserialized.map(&:object_id)
  # => [1023900, 1023920, 1023940, 1023960] -- 4 different objects

  deserialized = Marshal.load(serialized, freeze: true)
  deserialized.map(&:frozen?)
  # => [true, true, true, true]
  deserialized.map(&:object_id)
  # => [1039360, 1039380, 1039360, 1039380] -- only 2 different objects, object_ids repeating

MatchData.name: MatchData
MatchData.comment:
MatchData encapsulates the result of matching a Regexp against string. It is
returned by Regexp#match and String#match, and also stored in a global
variable returned by Regexp.last_match.

Usage:

  url = 'https://docs.ruby-lang.org/en/2.5.0/MatchData.html'
  m = url.match(/(\d\.?)+/)   # => #<MatchData "2.5.0" 1:"0">
  m.string                    # => "https://docs.ruby-lang.org/en/2.5.0/MatchData.html"
  m.regexp                    # => /(\d\.?)+/
  # entire matched substring:
  m[0]                        # => "2.5.0"

  # Working with unnamed captures
  m = url.match(%r{([^/]+)/([^/]+)\.html$})
  m.captures                  # => ["2.5.0", "MatchData"]
  m[1]                        # => "2.5.0"
  m.values_at(1, 2)           # => ["2.5.0", "MatchData"]

  # Working with named captures
  m = url.match(%r{(?<version>[^/]+)/(?<module>[^/]+)\.html$})
  m.captures                  # => ["2.5.0", "MatchData"]
  m.named_captures            # => {"version"=>"2.5.0", "module"=>"MatchData"}
  m[:version]                 # => "2.5.0"
  m.values_at(:version, :module)
                              # => ["2.5.0", "MatchData"]
  # Numerical indexes are working, too
  m[1]                        # => "2.5.0"
  m.values_at(1, 2)           # => ["2.5.0", "MatchData"]

== Global variables equivalence

Parts of last MatchData (returned by Regexp.last_match) are also aliased as
global variables:

* <tt>$~</tt> is Regexp.last_match;
* <tt>$&</tt> is Regexp.last_match<tt>[ 0 ]</tt>;
* <tt>$1</tt>, <tt>$2</tt>, and so on are Regexp.last_match<tt>[ i ]</tt>
  (captures by number);
* <tt>$`</tt> is Regexp.last_match<tt>.pre_match</tt>;
* <tt>$'</tt> is Regexp.last_match<tt>.post_match</tt>;
* <tt>$+</tt> is Regexp.last_match<tt>[ -1 ]</tt> (the last capture).

See also Regexp@Global+Variables.

MatchData#==.comment:
Returns whether <tt>other</tt> is another MatchData object whose target
string, regexp, match, and captures are the same as <tt>self</tt>.

MatchData#[].call_seq:
self[offset] -> string or nil
self[offset, size] -> array
self[range] -> array
self[name] -> string or nil
MatchData#[].comment:
When arguments <tt>offset</tt>, <tt>offset</tt> and <tt>size</tt>, or
<tt>range</tt> are given, returns match and captures in the style of Array#[]:

  m = /(.)(.)(\d+)(\d)/.match("THX1138.")
  # => #<MatchData "HX1138" 1:"H" 2:"X" 3:"113" 4:"8">
  m[0] # => "HX1138"
  m[1, 2]  # => ["H", "X"]
  m[1..3]  # => ["H", "X", "113"]
  m[-3, 2] # => ["X", "113"]

When string or symbol argument <tt>name</tt> is given, returns the matched
substring for the given name:

  m = /(?<foo>.)(.)(?<bar>.+)/.match("hoge")
  # => #<MatchData "hoge" foo:"h" bar:"ge">
  m['foo'] # => "h"
  m[:bar]  # => "ge"

If multiple captures have the same name, returns the last matched substring.

  m = /(?<foo>.)(?<foo>.+)/.match("hoge")
  # => #<MatchData "hoge" foo:"h" foo:"oge">
  m[:foo] #=> "oge"

  m = /\W(?<foo>.+)|\w(?<foo>.+)|(?<foo>.+)/.match("hoge")
  #<MatchData "hoge" foo:nil foo:"oge" foo:nil>
  m[:foo] #=> "oge"

MatchData#begin.name: begin
MatchData#begin.comment:
Returns the offset (in characters) of the beginning of the specified match.

When non-negative integer argument <tt>n</tt> is given, returns the offset of
the beginning of the <tt>n</tt>th match:

  m = /(.)(.)(\d+)(\d)/.match("THX1138.")
  # => #<MatchData "HX1138" 1:"H" 2:"X" 3:"113" 4:"8">
  m[0]       # => "HX1138"
  m.begin(0) # => 1
  m[3]       # => "113"
  m.begin(3) # => 3

  m = /(ん)(に)(ち)/.match('こんにちは')
  # => #<MatchData "んにち" 1:"ん" 2:"に" 3:"ち">
  m[0]       # => "んにち"
  m.begin(0) # => 1
  m[3]       # => "ち"
  m.begin(3) # => 3

When string or symbol argument <tt>name</tt> is given, returns the offset of
the beginning for the named match:

  m = /(?<foo>.)(.)(?<bar>.)/.match("hoge")
  # => #<MatchData "hog" foo:"h" bar:"g">
  m[:foo]        # => "h"
  m.begin('foo') # => 0
  m[:bar]        # => "g"
  m.begin(:bar)  # => 2

Related: MatchData#end, MatchData#offset, MatchData#byteoffset.

MatchData#bytebegin.name: bytebegin
MatchData#bytebegin.comment:
Returns the offset (in bytes) of the beginning of the specified match.

When non-negative integer argument <tt>n</tt> is given, returns the offset of
the beginning of the <tt>n</tt>th match:

  m = /(.)(.)(\d+)(\d)/.match("THX1138.")
  # => #<MatchData "HX1138" 1:"H" 2:"X" 3:"113" 4:"8">
  m[0]       # => "HX1138"
  m.bytebegin(0) # => 1
  m[3]       # => "113"
  m.bytebegin(3) # => 3

  m = /(ん)(に)(ち)/.match('こんにちは')
  # => #<MatchData "んにち" 1:"ん" 2:"に" 3:"ち">
  m[0]           # => "んにち"
  m.bytebegin(0) # => 3
  m[3]           # => "ち"
  m.bytebegin(3) # => 9

When string or symbol argument <tt>name</tt> is given, returns the offset of
the beginning for the named match:

  m = /(?<foo>.)(.)(?<bar>.)/.match("hoge")
  # => #<MatchData "hog" foo:"h" bar:"g">
  m[:foo]        # => "h"
  m.bytebegin('foo') # => 0
  m[:bar]        # => "g"
  m.bytebegin(:bar)  # => 2

Related: MatchData#byteend, MatchData#byteoffset.

MatchData#byteend.name: byteend
MatchData#byteend.comment:
Returns the offset (in bytes) of the end of the specified match.

When non-negative integer argument <tt>n</tt> is given, returns the offset of
the end of the <tt>n</tt>th match:

  m = /(.)(.)(\d+)(\d)/.match("THX1138.")
  # => #<MatchData "HX1138" 1:"H" 2:"X" 3:"113" 4:"8">
  m[0]     # => "HX1138"
  m.byteend(0) # => 7
  m[3]     # => "113"
  m.byteend(3) # => 6

  m = /(ん)(に)(ち)/.match('こんにちは')
  # => #<MatchData "んにち" 1:"ん" 2:"に" 3:"ち">
  m[0]         # => "んにち"
  m.byteend(0) # => 12
  m[3]         # => "ち"
  m.byteend(3) # => 12

When string or symbol argument <tt>name</tt> is given, returns the offset of
the end for the named match:

  m = /(?<foo>.)(.)(?<bar>.)/.match("hoge")
  # => #<MatchData "hog" foo:"h" bar:"g">
  m[:foo]      # => "h"
  m.byteend('foo') # => 1
  m[:bar]      # => "g"
  m.byteend(:bar)  # => 3

Related: MatchData#bytebegin, MatchData#byteoffset.

MatchData#byteoffset.name: byteoffset
MatchData#byteoffset.comment: Returns a two-element array containing the beginning and ending byte-based offsets of the nth match. n can be a string or symbol to reference a named capture. m = /(.)(.)(\d+)(\d)/.match("THX1138.") m.byteoffset(0) #=> [1, 7] m.byteoffset(4) #=> [6, 7] m = /(?.)(.)(?.)/.match("hoge") p m.byteoffset(:foo) #=> [0, 1] p m.byteoffset(:bar) #=> [2, 3]

MatchData#captures.name: captures
MatchData#captures.comment:
Returns the array of captures, which are all matches except <tt>m[0]</tt>:

  m = /(.)(.)(\d+)(\d)/.match("THX1138.")
  # => #<MatchData "HX1138" 1:"H" 2:"X" 3:"113" 4:"8">
  m[0]       # => "HX1138"
  m.captures # => ["H", "X", "113", "8"]

Related: MatchData.to_a.

MatchData#deconstruct.name: deconstruct
MatchData#deconstruct.comment:
Returns the array of captures, which are all matches except <tt>m[0]</tt>:

  m = /(.)(.)(\d+)(\d)/.match("THX1138.")
  # => #<MatchData "HX1138" 1:"H" 2:"X" 3:"113" 4:"8">
  m[0]       # => "HX1138"
  m.captures # => ["H", "X", "113", "8"]

Related: MatchData.to_a.

MatchData#deconstruct_keys.name: deconstruct_keys

MatchData#end.name: end
MatchData#end.comment:
Returns the offset (in characters) of the end of the specified match.

When non-negative integer argument <tt>n</tt> is given, returns the offset of
the end of the <tt>n</tt>th match:

  m = /(.)(.)(\d+)(\d)/.match("THX1138.")
  # => #<MatchData "HX1138" 1:"H" 2:"X" 3:"113" 4:"8">
  m[0]     # => "HX1138"
  m.end(0) # => 7
  m[3]     # => "113"
  m.end(3) # => 6

  m = /(ん)(に)(ち)/.match('こんにちは')
  # => #<MatchData "んにち" 1:"ん" 2:"に" 3:"ち">
  m[0]     # => "んにち"
  m.end(0) # => 4
  m[3]     # => "ち"
  m.end(3) # => 4

When string or symbol argument <tt>name</tt> is given, returns the offset of
the end for the named match:

  m = /(?<foo>.)(.)(?<bar>.)/.match("hoge")
  # => #<MatchData "hog" foo:"h" bar:"g">
  m[:foo]      # => "h"
  m.end('foo') # => 1
  m[:bar]      # => "g"
  m.end(:bar)  # => 3

Related: MatchData#begin, MatchData#offset, MatchData#byteoffset.

MatchData#eql?.name: eql?
MatchData#eql?.comment:
Returns whether <tt>other</tt> is another MatchData object whose target
string, regexp, match, and captures are the same as <tt>self</tt>.

MatchData#hash.name: hash
MatchData#hash.comment:
Returns the integer hash value for <tt>self</tt>, based on the target string,
regexp, match, and captures.

See also Object#hash.

MatchData#inspect.name: inspect
MatchData#inspect.comment:
Returns a string representation of <tt>self</tt>:

  m = /.$/.match("foo")
  # => #<MatchData "o">
  m.inspect # => "#<MatchData \"o\">"

  m = /(.)(.)(.)/.match("foo")
  # => #<MatchData "foo" 1:"f" 2:"o" 3:"o">
  m.inspect # => "#<MatchData \"foo\" 1:\"f\" 2:\"o\

  m = /(.)(.)?(.)/.match("fo")
  # => #<MatchData "fo" 1:"f" 2:nil 3:"o">
  m.inspect # => "#<MatchData \"fo\" 1:\"f\" 2:nil 3:\"o\">"

Related: MatchData#to_s.

MatchData#integer_at.name: integer_at
MatchData#integer_at.call_seq:
integer_at(index, base = 10) -> integer or nil
integer_at(name, base = 10) -> integer or nil
MatchData#integer_at.comment:
Converts the matched substring to integer and return the result.
+$~.integer_at(N)+ is equivalent to +$N&.to_i+.

  m = /(\d+{4})(\d+{2})(\d+{2})/.match("20260308")
  # => #<MatchData "20260308" 1:"2026" 2:"03" 3:"08">
  m.integer_at(0)     # => 20260308
  m.integer_at(1)     # => 2026
  m.integer_at(2)     # => 3
  m.integer_at(3)     # => 8

  m = /(?<y>\d+{4})(?<m>\d+{2})(?<d>\d+{2})/.match("20260308")
  m.integer_at("y")   # => 2026
  m.integer_at("m")   # => 3
  m.integer_at("d")   # => 8

If the substring does not match, returns <tt>nil</tt>.

  re = /(\d+)?/
  re.match("123").integer_at(1) #=> 123
  re.match("abc").integer_at(1) #=> nil

The string is converted in decimal by default.

  /\d+/.match("011").integer_at(0)     #=> 10
  /\d+/.match("011").integer_at(0, 12) #=> 13
  /\d+/.match("011").integer_at(0, 0)  #=> 9

See also MatchData#[], String#to_i.

MatchData#length.name: length
MatchData#length.comment:
Returns size of the match array:

  m = /(.)(.)(\d+)(\d)/.match("THX1138.")
  # => #<MatchData "HX1138" 1:"H" 2:"X" 3:"113" 4:"8">
  m.size # => 5

MatchData#match.name: match
MatchData#match.call_seq:
match(n) -> string or nil
match(name) -> string or nil
MatchData#match.comment:
Returns the matched substring corresponding to the given argument.

When non-negative argument <tt>n</tt> is given, returns the matched substring
for the <tt>n</tt>th match:

  m = /(.)(.)(\d+)(\d)(\w)?/.match("THX1138.")
  # => #<MatchData "HX1138" 1:"H" 2:"X" 3:"113" 4:"8" 5:nil>
  m.match(0) # => "HX1138"
  m.match(4) # => "8"
  m.match(5) # => nil

When string or symbol argument <tt>name</tt> is given, returns the matched
substring for the given name:

  m = /(?<foo>.)(.)(?<bar>.+)/.match("hoge")
  # => #<MatchData "hoge" foo:"h" bar:"ge">
  m.match('foo') # => "h"
  m.match(:bar)  # => "ge"

MatchData#match_length.name: match_length
MatchData#match_length.call_seq:
match_length(n) -> integer or nil
match_length(name) -> integer or nil
MatchData#match_length.comment:
Returns the length (in characters) of the matched substring corresponding to
the given argument.

When non-negative argument <tt>n</tt> is given, returns the length of the
matched substring for the <tt>n</tt>th match:

  m = /(.)(.)(\d+)(\d)(\w)?/.match("THX1138.")
  # => #<MatchData "HX1138" 1:"H" 2:"X" 3:"113" 4:"8" 5:nil>
  m.match_length(0) # => 6
  m.match_length(4) # => 1
  m.match_length(5) # => nil

When string or symbol argument <tt>name</tt> is given, returns the length of
the matched substring for the named match:

  m = /(?<foo>.)(.)(?<bar>.+)/.match("hoge")
  # => #<MatchData "hoge" foo:"h" bar:"ge">
  m.match_length('foo') # => 1
  m.match_length(:bar)  # => 2

MatchData#named_captures.name: named_captures
MatchData#named_captures.comment:
Returns a hash of the named captures; each key is a capture name; each value
is its captured string or <tt>nil</tt>:

  m = /(?<foo>.)(.)(?<bar>.+)/.match("hoge")
  # => #<MatchData "hoge" foo:"h" bar:"ge">
  m.named_captures # => {"foo"=>"h", "bar"=>"ge"}

  m = /(?<a>.)(?<b>.)/.match("01")
  # => #<MatchData "01" a:"0" b:"1">
  m.named_captures #=> {"a" => "0", "b" => "1"}

  m = /(?<a>.)(?<b>.)?/.match("0")
  # => #<MatchData "0" a:"0" b:nil>
  m.named_captures #=> {"a" => "0", "b" => nil}

  m = /(?<a>.)(?<a>.)/.match("01")
  # => #<MatchData "01" a:"0" a:"1">
  m.named_captures #=> {"a" => "1"}

If keyword argument <tt>symbolize_names</tt> is given a true value, the keys
in the resulting hash are Symbols:

  m = /(?<a>.)(?<a>.)/.match("01")
  # => #<MatchData "01" a:"0" a:"1">
  m.named_captures(symbolize_names: true) #=> {:a => "1"}

MatchData#names.name: names
MatchData#names.comment:
Returns an array of the capture names (see {Named
Captures}[rdoc-ref:Regexp@Named+Captures]):

  m = /(?<foo>.)(?<bar>.)(?<baz>.)/.match("hoge")
  # => #<MatchData "hog" foo:"h" bar:"o" baz:"g">
  m.names # => ["foo", "bar", "baz"]

  m = /foo/.match('foo') # => #<MatchData "foo">
  m.names # => [] # No named captures.

Equivalent to:

  m = /(?<foo>.)(?<bar>.)(?<baz>.)/.match("hoge")
  m.regexp.names # => ["foo", "bar", "baz"]

MatchData#offset.name: offset
MatchData#offset.comment:
Returns a 2-element array containing the beginning and ending offsets (in
characters) of the specified match.

When non-negative integer argument <tt>n</tt> is given, returns the starting
and ending offsets of the <tt>n</tt>th match:

  m = /(.)(.)(\d+)(\d)/.match("THX1138.")
  # => #<MatchData "HX1138" 1:"H" 2:"X" 3:"113" 4:"8">
  m[0]        # => "HX1138"
  m.offset(0) # => [1, 7]
  m[3]        # => "113"
  m.offset(3) # => [3, 6]

  m = /(ん)(に)(ち)/.match('こんにちは')
  # => #<MatchData "んにち" 1:"ん" 2:"に" 3:"ち">
  m[0]        # => "んにち"
  m.offset(0) # => [1, 4]
  m[3]        # => "ち"
  m.offset(3) # => [3, 4]

When string or symbol argument <tt>name</tt> is given, returns the starting
and ending offsets for the named match:

  m = /(?<foo>.)(.)(?<bar>.)/.match("hoge")
  # => #<MatchData "hog" foo:"h" bar:"g">
  m[:foo]         # => "h"
  m.offset('foo') # => [0, 1]
  m[:bar]         # => "g"
  m.offset(:bar)  # => [2, 3]

Related: MatchData#byteoffset, MatchData#begin, MatchData#end.

MatchData#post_match.name: post_match
MatchData#post_match.comment:
Returns the substring of the target string from the end of the first match in
<tt>self</tt> (that is, <tt>self[0]</tt>) to the end of the string; equivalent
to regexp global variable <tt>$'</tt>:

  m = /(.)(.)(\d+)(\d)/.match("THX1138: The Movie")
  # => #<MatchData "HX1138" 1:"H" 2:"X" 3:"113" 4:"8">
  m[0]         # => "HX1138"
  m.post_match # => ": The Movie"\

Related: MatchData.pre_match.

MatchData#pre_match.name: pre_match
MatchData#pre_match.comment:
Returns the substring of the target string from its beginning up to the first
match in <tt>self</tt> (that is, <tt>self[0]</tt>); equivalent to regexp
global variable <tt>$`</tt>:

  m = /(.)(.)(\d+)(\d)/.match("THX1138.")
  # => #<MatchData "HX1138" 1:"H" 2:"X" 3:"113" 4:"8">
  m[0]        # => "HX1138"
  m.pre_match # => "T"

Related: MatchData#post_match.

MatchData#regexp.name: regexp
MatchData#regexp.comment:
Returns the regexp that produced the match:

  m = /a.*b/.match("abc") # => #<MatchData "ab">
  m.regexp                # => /a.*b/

MatchData#size.name: size
MatchData#size.comment:
Returns size of the match array:

  m = /(.)(.)(\d+)(\d)/.match("THX1138.")
  # => #<MatchData "HX1138" 1:"H" 2:"X" 3:"113" 4:"8">
  m.size # => 5

MatchData#string.name: string
MatchData#string.comment:
Returns the target string if it was frozen; otherwise, returns a frozen copy
of the target string:

  m = /(.)(.)(\d+)(\d)/.match("THX1138.")
  # => #<MatchData "HX1138" 1:"H" 2:"X" 3:"113" 4:"8">
  m.string # => "THX1138."

MatchData#to_a.name: to_a
MatchData#to_a.comment:
Returns the array of matches:

  m = /(.)(.)(\d+)(\d)/.match("THX1138.")
  # => #<MatchData "HX1138" 1:"H" 2:"X" 3:"113" 4:"8">
  m.to_a # => ["HX1138", "H", "X", "113", "8"]

Related: MatchData#captures.

MatchData#to_s.name: to_s
MatchData#to_s.comment:
Returns the matched string:

  m = /(.)(.)(\d+)(\d)/.match("THX1138.")
  # => #<MatchData "HX1138" 1:"H" 2:"X" 3:"113" 4:"8">
  m.to_s # => "HX1138"

  m = /(?<foo>.)(.)(?<bar>.+)/.match("hoge")
  # => #<MatchData "hoge" foo:"h" bar:"ge">
  m.to_s # => "hoge"

Related: MatchData.inspect.

MatchData#values_at.name: values_at
MatchData#values_at.comment:
Returns match and captures at the given <tt>indexes</tt>, which may include
any mixture of:

* Integers.
* Ranges.
* Names (strings and symbols).

Examples:

  m = /(.)(.)(\d+)(\d)/.match("THX1138: The Movie")
  # => #<MatchData "HX1138" 1:"H" 2:"X" 3:"113" 4:"8">
  m.values_at(0, 2, -2) # => ["HX1138", "X", "113"]
  m.values_at(1..2, -1) # => ["H", "X", "8"]

  m = /(?<a>\d+) *(?<op>[+\-*\/]) *(?<b>\d+)/.match("1 + 2")
  # => #<MatchData "1 + 2" a:"1" op:"+" b:"2">
  m.values_at(0, 1..2, :a, :b, :op)
  # => ["1 + 2", "1", "+", "1", "2", "+"]

Math.name: Math
Math.comment: Module Math provides methods for basic trigonometric, logarithmic, and transcendental functions, and for extracting roots. You can write its constants and method calls thus: Math::PI # => 3.141592653589793 Math::E # => 2.718281828459045 Math.sin(0.0) # => 0.0 Math.cos(0.0) # => 1.0 If you include module Math, you can write simpler forms: include Math PI # => 3.141592653589793 E # => 2.718281828459045 sin(0.0) # => 0.0 cos(0.0) # => 1.0 For simplicity, the examples here assume: include Math INFINITY = Float::INFINITY The domains and ranges for the methods are denoted by open or closed intervals, using, respectively, parentheses or square brackets: * An open interval does not include the endpoints: (-INFINITY, INFINITY) * A closed interval includes the endpoints: [-1.0, 1.0] * A half-open interval includes one endpoint, but not the other: [1.0, INFINITY) Many values returned by Math methods are numerical approximations. This is because many such values are, in mathematics, of infinite precision, while in numerical computation the precision is finite. Thus, in mathematics, cos(π/2) is exactly zero, but in our computation cos(PI/2) is a number very close to zero: cos(PI/2) # => 6.123031769111886e-17 For very large and very small returned values, we have added formatted numbers for clarity: tan(PI/2) # => 1.633123935319537e+16 # 16331239353195370.0 tan(PI) # => -1.2246467991473532e-16 # -0.0000000000000001 See class Float for the constants that affect Ruby's floating-point arithmetic. === What's Here ==== Trigonometric Functions * ::cos: Returns the cosine of the given argument. * ::sin: Returns the sine of the given argument. * ::tan: Returns the tangent of the given argument. ==== Inverse Trigonometric Functions * ::acos: Returns the arc cosine of the given argument. * ::asin: Returns the arc sine of the given argument. * ::atan: Returns the arc tangent of the given argument. * ::atan2: Returns the arg tangent of two given arguments. ==== Hyperbolic Trigonometric Functions * ::cosh: Returns the hyperbolic cosine of the given argument. * ::sinh: Returns the hyperbolic sine of the given argument. * ::tanh: Returns the hyperbolic tangent of the given argument. ==== Inverse Hyperbolic Trigonometric Functions * ::acosh: Returns the inverse hyperbolic cosine of the given argument. * ::asinh: Returns the inverse hyperbolic sine of the given argument. * ::atanh: Returns the inverse hyperbolic tangent of the given argument. ==== Exponentiation and Logarithmic Functions * ::exp: Returns the value of a given value raised to a given power. * ::log: Returns the logarithm of a given value in a given base. * ::log10: Returns the base 10 logarithm of the given argument. * ::log2: Returns the base 2 logarithm of the given argument. ==== Fraction and Exponent Functions * ::frexp: Returns the fraction and exponent of the given argument. * ::ldexp: Returns the value for a given fraction and exponent. ==== Root Functions * ::cbrt: Returns the cube root of the given argument. * ::sqrt: Returns the square root of the given argument. ==== Error Functions * ::erf: Returns the value of the Gauss error function for the given argument. * ::erfc: Returns the value of the complementary error function for the given argument. ==== Gamma Functions * ::gamma: Returns the value of the gamma function for the given argument. * ::lgamma: Returns the value of the logarithmic gamma function for the given argument. ==== Hypotenuse Function * ::hypot: Returns sqrt(a**2 + b**2) for the given a and b.

Math::acos.name: acos
Math::acos.comment:
Returns the {arc
cosine}[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_trigonometric_functions] of
<tt>x</tt>.

* Domain: <tt>[-1, 1]</tt>.
* Range: <tt>[0, PI]</tt>.

Examples:

  acos(-1.0) # => 3.141592653589793  # PI
  acos(0.0)  # => 1.5707963267948966 # PI/2
  acos(1.0)  # => 0.0

Math::acosh.name: acosh
Math::acosh.comment:
Returns the {inverse hyperbolic
cosine}[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_hyperbolic_functions] of
<tt>x</tt>.

* Domain: <tt>[1, INFINITY]</tt>.
* Range: <tt>[0, INFINITY]</tt>.

Examples:

  acosh(1.0)      # => 0.0
  acosh(INFINITY) # => Infinity

Math::asin.name: asin
Math::asin.comment:
Returns the {arc
sine}[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_trigonometric_functions] of
<tt>x</tt>.

* Domain: <tt>[-1, -1]</tt>.
* Range: <tt>[-PI/2, PI/2]</tt>.

Examples:

  asin(-1.0) # => -1.5707963267948966 # -PI/2
  asin(0.0)  # => 0.0
  asin(1.0)  # => 1.5707963267948966  # PI/2

Math::asinh.name: asinh
Math::asinh.comment:
Returns the {inverse hyperbolic
sine}[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_hyperbolic_functions] of
<tt>x</tt>.

* Domain: <tt>[-INFINITY, INFINITY]</tt>.
* Range: <tt>[-INFINITY, INFINITY]</tt>.

Examples:

  asinh(-INFINITY) # => -Infinity
  asinh(0.0)       # => 0.0
  asinh(INFINITY)  # => Infinity

Math::atan.name: atan
Math::atan.comment:
Returns the {arc
tangent}[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_trigonometric_functions] of
<tt>x</tt>.

* Domain: <tt>[-INFINITY, INFINITY]</tt>.
* Range: <tt>[-PI/2, PI/2]  </tt>.

Examples:

  atan(-INFINITY) # => -1.5707963267948966 # -PI2
  atan(-PI)       # => -1.2626272556789115
  atan(-PI/2)     # => -1.0038848218538872
  atan(0.0)       # => 0.0
  atan(PI/2)      # => 1.0038848218538872
  atan(PI)        # => 1.2626272556789115
  atan(INFINITY)  # => 1.5707963267948966  # PI/2

Math::atan2.name: atan2
Math::atan2.comment:
Returns the {arc tangent}[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atan2] of <tt>y</tt>
and <tt>x</tt> in
{radians}[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometric_functions#Radians_versus
_degrees].

* Domain of <tt>y</tt>: <tt>[-INFINITY, INFINITY]</tt>.
* Domain of <tt>x</tt>: <tt>[-INFINITY, INFINITY]</tt>.
* Range: <tt>[-PI, PI]</tt>.

Examples:

  atan2(-1.0, -1.0) # => -2.356194490192345  # -3*PI/4
  atan2(-1.0, 0.0)  # => -1.5707963267948966 # -PI/2
  atan2(-1.0, 1.0)  # => -0.7853981633974483 # -PI/4
  atan2(0.0, -1.0)  # => 3.141592653589793   # PI

Math::atanh.name: atanh
Math::atanh.comment:
Returns the {inverse hyperbolic
tangent}[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_hyperbolic_functions] of
<tt>x</tt>.

* Domain: <tt>[-1, 1]</tt>.
* Range: <tt>[-INFINITY, INFINITY]</tt>.

Examples:

  atanh(-1.0) # => -Infinity
  atanh(0.0)  # => 0.0
  atanh(1.0)  # => Infinity

Math::cbrt.name: cbrt
Math::cbrt.comment:
Returns the {cube root}[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cube_root] of
<tt>x</tt>.

* Domain: <tt>[-INFINITY, INFINITY]</tt>.
* Range: <tt>[-INFINITY, INFINITY]</tt>.

Examples:
