OpenSSL::PKey::PKey#raw_private_key.comment: See the OpenSSL documentation for EVP_PKEY_get_raw_private_key()

OpenSSL::PKey::PKey#raw_public_key.name: raw_public_key
OpenSSL::PKey::PKey#raw_public_key.comment: See the OpenSSL documentation for EVP_PKEY_get_raw_public_key()

OpenSSL::PKey::PKey#sign.name: sign
OpenSSL::PKey::PKey#sign.comment:
Hashes and signs the <tt>data</tt> using a message digest algorithm
<tt>digest</tt> and a private key <tt>pkey</tt>.

See #verify for the verification operation.

See also the man page EVP_DigestSign(3).

<tt>digest</tt>:
  A String that represents the message digest algorithm name, or <tt>nil</tt>
  if the PKey type requires no digest algorithm. For backwards compatibility,
  this can be an instance of OpenSSL::Digest. Its state will not affect the
  signature.

<tt>data</tt>:
  A String. The data to be hashed and signed.

<tt>options</tt>:
  A Hash that contains algorithm specific control operations to OpenSSL. See
  OpenSSL's man page EVP_PKEY_CTX_ctrl_str(3) for details. <tt>options</tt>
  parameter was added in version 3.0.

Example:
  data = "Sign me!"
  pkey = OpenSSL::PKey.generate_key("RSA", rsa_keygen_bits: 2048)
  signopts = { rsa_padding_mode: "pss" }
  signature = pkey.sign("SHA256", data, signopts)

  # Creates a copy of the RSA key pkey, but without the private components
  pub_key = OpenSSL::PKey.read(pkey.public_to_der)
  puts pub_key.verify("SHA256", signature, data, signopts) # => true

OpenSSL::PKey::PKey#sign_raw.name: sign_raw
OpenSSL::PKey::PKey#sign_raw.comment:
Signs <tt>data</tt> using a private key <tt>pkey</tt>. Unlike #sign,
<tt>data</tt> will not be hashed by <tt>digest</tt> automatically.

See #verify_raw for the verification operation.

Added in version 3.0. See also the man page EVP_PKEY_sign(3).

<tt>digest</tt>:
  A String that represents the message digest algorithm name, or <tt>nil</tt>
  if the PKey type requires no digest algorithm. Although this method will not
  hash <tt>data</tt> with it, this parameter may still be required depending
  on the signature algorithm.

<tt>data</tt>:
  A String. The data to be signed.

<tt>options</tt>:
  A Hash that contains algorithm specific control operations to OpenSSL. See
  OpenSSL's man page EVP_PKEY_CTX_ctrl_str(3) for details.

Example:
  data = "Sign me!"
  hash = OpenSSL::Digest.digest("SHA256", data)
  pkey = OpenSSL::PKey.generate_key("RSA", rsa_keygen_bits: 2048)
  signopts = { rsa_padding_mode: "pss" }
  signature = pkey.sign_raw("SHA256", hash, signopts)

  # Creates a copy of the RSA key pkey, but without the private components
  pub_key = OpenSSL::PKey.read(pkey.public_to_der)
  puts pub_key.verify_raw("SHA256", signature, hash, signopts) # => true

OpenSSL::PKey::PKey#to_text.name: to_text
OpenSSL::PKey::PKey#to_text.comment:
Dumps key parameters, public key, and private key components contained in the
key into a human-readable text.

This is intended for debugging purpose.

See also the man page EVP_PKEY_print_private(3).

OpenSSL::PKey::PKey#verify.name: verify
OpenSSL::PKey::PKey#verify.call_seq: pkey.verify(digest, signature, data [, options]) -> true or false
OpenSSL::PKey::PKey#verify.comment:
Verifies the <tt>signature</tt> for the <tt>data</tt> using a message digest
algorithm <tt>digest</tt> and a public key <tt>pkey</tt>.

Returns <tt>true</tt> if the signature is successfully verified,
<tt>false</tt> otherwise. The caller must check the return value.

See #sign for the signing operation and an example.

See also the man page EVP_DigestVerify(3).

<tt>digest</tt>:
  See #sign.

<tt>signature</tt>:
  A String containing the signature to be verified.

<tt>data</tt>:
  See #sign.

<tt>options</tt>:
  See #sign. <tt>options</tt> parameter was added in version 3.0.

OpenSSL::PKey::PKey#verify_raw.name: verify_raw
OpenSSL::PKey::PKey#verify_raw.call_seq: pkey.verify_raw(digest, signature, data [, options]) -> true or false
OpenSSL::PKey::PKey#verify_raw.comment:
Verifies the <tt>signature</tt> for the <tt>data</tt> using a public key
<tt>pkey</tt>. Unlike #verify, this method will not hash <tt>data</tt> with
<tt>digest</tt> automatically.

Returns <tt>true</tt> if the signature is successfully verified,
<tt>false</tt> otherwise. The caller must check the return value.

See #sign_raw for the signing operation and an example code.

Added in version 3.0. See also the man page EVP_PKEY_verify(3).

<tt>signature</tt>:
  A String containing the signature to be verified.

OpenSSL::PKey::PKey#verify_recover.name: verify_recover
OpenSSL::PKey::PKey#verify_recover.comment:
Recovers the signed data from <tt>signature</tt> using a public key
<tt>pkey</tt>. Not all signature algorithms support this operation.

Added in version 3.0. See also the man page EVP_PKEY_verify_recover(3).

<tt>signature</tt>:
  A String containing the signature to be verified.

OpenSSL::PKey::PKeyError.name: OpenSSL::PKey::PKeyError
OpenSSL::PKey::PKeyError.comment:
Raised when errors occur during PKey#sign or PKey#verify.

Before version 4.0.0, OpenSSL::PKey::PKeyError had the following subclasses.
These subclasses have been removed and the constants are now defined as
aliases of OpenSSL::PKey::PKeyError.

* OpenSSL::PKey::DHError
* OpenSSL::PKey::DSAError
* OpenSSL::PKey::ECError
* OpenSSL::PKey::RSAError

OpenSSL::PKey::RSA.name: OpenSSL::PKey::RSA
OpenSSL::PKey::RSA.comment:
RSA is an asymmetric public key algorithm that has been formalized in RFC
3447. It is in widespread use in public key infrastructures (PKI) where
certificates (cf. OpenSSL::X509::Certificate) often are issued on the basis of
a public/private RSA key pair. RSA is used in a wide field of applications
such as secure (symmetric) key exchange, e.g. when establishing a secure
TLS/SSL connection. It is also used in various digital signature schemes.

OpenSSL::PKey::RSA::generate.name: generate
OpenSSL::PKey::RSA::generate.comment:
Generates an RSA keypair.

See also OpenSSL::PKey.generate_key.

<tt>size</tt>:
  The desired key size in bits.

<tt>exponent</tt>:
  An odd Integer, normally 3, 17, or 65537.

OpenSSL::PKey::RSA::new.name: new
OpenSSL::PKey::RSA::new.call_seq:
RSA.new -> rsa
RSA.new(encoded_key [, password ]) -> rsa
RSA.new(encoded_key) { password } -> rsa
RSA.new(size [, exponent]) -> rsa
OpenSSL::PKey::RSA::new.comment: Generates or loads an RSA keypair. If called without arguments, creates a new instance with no key components set. They can be set individually by #set_key, #set_factors, and #set_crt_params. This form is not compatible with OpenSSL 3.0 or later. If called with a String, tries to parse as DER or PEM encoding of an RSA key. Note that if password is not specified, but the key is encrypted with a password, OpenSSL will prompt for it. See also OpenSSL::PKey.read which can parse keys of any kind. If called with a number, generates a new key pair. This form works as an alias of RSA.generate. Examples: OpenSSL::PKey::RSA.new 2048 OpenSSL::PKey::RSA.new File.read 'rsa.pem' OpenSSL::PKey::RSA.new File.read('rsa.pem'), 'my password'

OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#export.name: export
OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#export.comment: Serializes a private or public key to a PEM-encoding. When the key contains public components only: Serializes it into an X.509 SubjectPublicKeyInfo. The parameters cipher and password are ignored. A PEM-encoded key will look like: -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- [...] -----END PUBLIC KEY----- Consider using #public_to_pem instead. This serializes the key into an X.509 SubjectPublicKeyInfo regardless of whether the key is a public key or a private key. When the key contains private components, and no parameters are given: Serializes it into a PKCS #1 RSAPrivateKey. A PEM-encoded key will look like: -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY----- [...] -----END RSA PRIVATE KEY----- When the key contains private components, and cipher and password are given: Serializes it into a PKCS #1 RSAPrivateKey and encrypts it in OpenSSL's traditional PEM encryption format. cipher must be a cipher name understood by OpenSSL::Cipher.new or an instance of OpenSSL::Cipher. An encrypted PEM-encoded key will look like: -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY----- Proc-Type: 4,ENCRYPTED DEK-Info: AES-128-CBC,733F5302505B34701FC41F5C0746E4C0 [...] -----END RSA PRIVATE KEY----- Note that this format uses MD5 to derive the encryption key, and hence will not be available on FIPS-compliant systems. This method is kept for compatibility. This should only be used when the PKCS #1 RSAPrivateKey format is required. Consider using #public_to_pem (X.509 SubjectPublicKeyInfo) or #private_to_pem (PKCS #8 PrivateKeyInfo or EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo) instead.

OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#params.name: params
OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#params.comment:
Stores all parameters of key to a Hash.

The hash has keys 'n', 'e', 'd', 'p', 'q', 'dmp1', 'dmq1', and 'iqmp'.

OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#private?.name: private?
OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#private?.comment: Does this keypair contain a private key?

OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#private_decrypt.name: private_decrypt
OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#private_decrypt.comment: Decrypt string, which has been encrypted with the public key, with the private key. padding defaults to PKCS1_PADDING, which is known to be insecure but is kept for backwards compatibility. Deprecated in version 3.0. Consider using PKey::PKey#encrypt and PKey::PKey#decrypt instead.

OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#private_encrypt.name: private_encrypt
OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#private_encrypt.comment: Encrypt string with the private key. padding defaults to PKCS1_PADDING, which is known to be insecure but is kept for backwards compatibility. The encrypted string output can be decrypted using #public_decrypt. Deprecated in version 3.0. Consider using PKey::PKey#sign_raw and PKey::PKey#verify_raw, and PKey::PKey#verify_recover instead.

OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#public?.name: public?
OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#public?.comment:
The return value is always <tt>true</tt> since every private key is also a
public key.

OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#public_decrypt.name: public_decrypt
OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#public_decrypt.comment: Decrypt string, which has been encrypted with the private key, with the public key. padding defaults to PKCS1_PADDING which is known to be insecure but is kept for backwards compatibility. Deprecated in version 3.0. Consider using PKey::PKey#sign_raw and PKey::PKey#verify_raw, and PKey::PKey#verify_recover instead.

OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#public_encrypt.name: public_encrypt
OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#public_encrypt.comment: Encrypt string with the public key. padding defaults to PKCS1_PADDING, which is known to be insecure but is kept for backwards compatibility. The encrypted string output can be decrypted using #private_decrypt. Deprecated in version 3.0. Consider using PKey::PKey#encrypt and PKey::PKey#decrypt instead.

OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#public_key.name: public_key
OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#public_key.comment:
Returns a new RSA instance that carries just the public key components.

This method is provided for backwards compatibility. In most cases, there is
no need to call this method.

For the purpose of serializing the public key, to PEM or DER encoding of X.509
SubjectPublicKeyInfo format, check PKey#public_to_pem and PKey#public_to_der.

OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#set_crt_params.name: set_crt_params
OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#set_crt_params.comment: Sets dmp1, dmq1, iqmp for the RSA instance. They are calculated by d mod (p - 1), d mod (q - 1) and q^(-1) mod p respectively.

OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#sign_pss.name: sign_pss
OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#sign_pss.comment: Signs data using the Probabilistic Signature Scheme (RSA-PSS) and returns the calculated signature. PKeyError will be raised if an error occurs. See #verify_pss for the verification operation. === Parameters digest: A String containing the message digest algorithm name. data: A String. The data to be signed. salt_length: The length in octets of the salt. Two special values are reserved: :digest means the digest length, and :max means the maximum possible length for the combination of the private key and the selected message digest algorithm. mgf1_hash: The hash algorithm used in MGF1 (the currently supported mask generation function (MGF)). === Example data = "Sign me!" pkey = OpenSSL::PKey::RSA.new(2048) signature = pkey.sign_pss("SHA256", data, salt_length: :max, mgf1_hash: "SHA256") pub_key = OpenSSL::PKey.read(pkey.public_to_der) puts pub_key.verify_pss("SHA256", signature, data, salt_length: :auto, mgf1_hash: "SHA256") # => true

OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#to_der.name: to_der
OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#to_der.comment: Serializes a private or public key to a DER-encoding. See #to_pem for details. This method is kept for compatibility. This should only be used when the PKCS #1 RSAPrivateKey format is required. Consider using #public_to_der or #private_to_der instead.

OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#to_pem.name: to_pem
OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#to_pem.comment: Serializes a private or public key to a PEM-encoding. When the key contains public components only: Serializes it into an X.509 SubjectPublicKeyInfo. The parameters cipher and password are ignored. A PEM-encoded key will look like: -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- [...] -----END PUBLIC KEY----- Consider using #public_to_pem instead. This serializes the key into an X.509 SubjectPublicKeyInfo regardless of whether the key is a public key or a private key. When the key contains private components, and no parameters are given: Serializes it into a PKCS #1 RSAPrivateKey. A PEM-encoded key will look like: -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY----- [...] -----END RSA PRIVATE KEY----- When the key contains private components, and cipher and password are given: Serializes it into a PKCS #1 RSAPrivateKey and encrypts it in OpenSSL's traditional PEM encryption format. cipher must be a cipher name understood by OpenSSL::Cipher.new or an instance of OpenSSL::Cipher. An encrypted PEM-encoded key will look like: -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY----- Proc-Type: 4,ENCRYPTED DEK-Info: AES-128-CBC,733F5302505B34701FC41F5C0746E4C0 [...] -----END RSA PRIVATE KEY----- Note that this format uses MD5 to derive the encryption key, and hence will not be available on FIPS-compliant systems. This method is kept for compatibility. This should only be used when the PKCS #1 RSAPrivateKey format is required. Consider using #public_to_pem (X.509 SubjectPublicKeyInfo) or #private_to_pem (PKCS #8 PrivateKeyInfo or EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo) instead.

OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#to_s.name: to_s
OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#to_s.comment: Serializes a private or public key to a PEM-encoding. When the key contains public components only: Serializes it into an X.509 SubjectPublicKeyInfo. The parameters cipher and password are ignored. A PEM-encoded key will look like: -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- [...] -----END PUBLIC KEY----- Consider using #public_to_pem instead. This serializes the key into an X.509 SubjectPublicKeyInfo regardless of whether the key is a public key or a private key. When the key contains private components, and no parameters are given: Serializes it into a PKCS #1 RSAPrivateKey. A PEM-encoded key will look like: -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY----- [...] -----END RSA PRIVATE KEY----- When the key contains private components, and cipher and password are given: Serializes it into a PKCS #1 RSAPrivateKey and encrypts it in OpenSSL's traditional PEM encryption format. cipher must be a cipher name understood by OpenSSL::Cipher.new or an instance of OpenSSL::Cipher. An encrypted PEM-encoded key will look like: -----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY----- Proc-Type: 4,ENCRYPTED DEK-Info: AES-128-CBC,733F5302505B34701FC41F5C0746E4C0 [...] -----END RSA PRIVATE KEY----- Note that this format uses MD5 to derive the encryption key, and hence will not be available on FIPS-compliant systems. This method is kept for compatibility. This should only be used when the PKCS #1 RSAPrivateKey format is required. Consider using #public_to_pem (X.509 SubjectPublicKeyInfo) or #private_to_pem (PKCS #8 PrivateKeyInfo or EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo) instead.

OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#verify_pss.name: verify_pss
OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#verify_pss.call_seq: rsa.verify_pss(digest, signature, data, salt_length:, mgf1_hash:) -> true | false
OpenSSL::PKey::RSA#verify_pss.comment: Verifies data using the Probabilistic Signature Scheme (RSA-PSS). The return value is true if the signature is valid, false otherwise. PKeyError will be raised if an error occurs. See #sign_pss for the signing operation and an example code. === Parameters digest: A String containing the message digest algorithm name. data: A String. The data to be signed. salt_length: The length in octets of the salt. Two special values are reserved: :digest means the digest length, and :auto means automatically determining the length based on the signature. mgf1_hash: The hash algorithm used in MGF1.

OpenSSL::PKey::RSAError.name: OpenSSL::PKey::RSAError
OpenSSL::PKey::RSAError.comment:
Raised when errors occur during PKey#sign or PKey#verify.

Before version 4.0.0, OpenSSL::PKey::PKeyError had the following subclasses.
These subclasses have been removed and the constants are now defined as
aliases of OpenSSL::PKey::PKeyError.

* OpenSSL::PKey::DHError
* OpenSSL::PKey::DSAError
* OpenSSL::PKey::ECError
* OpenSSL::PKey::RSAError

OpenSSL::Random::egd.name: egd
OpenSSL::Random::egd.comment: Same as ::egd_bytes but queries 255 bytes by default.

OpenSSL::Random::egd_bytes.name: egd_bytes
OpenSSL::Random::egd_bytes.comment: Queries the entropy gathering daemon EGD on socket path given by filename. Fetches length number of bytes and uses ::add to seed the OpenSSL built-in PRNG.

OpenSSL::Random::load_random_file.name: load_random_file
OpenSSL::Random::load_random_file.comment: Reads bytes from filename and adds them to the PRNG.

OpenSSL::Random::random_add.name: random_add
OpenSSL::Random::random_add.comment: Mixes the bytes from str into the Pseudo Random Number Generator(PRNG) state. Thus, if the data from str are unpredictable to an adversary, this increases the uncertainty about the state and makes the PRNG output less predictable. The entropy argument is (the lower bound of) an estimate of how much randomness is contained in str, measured in bytes. === Example pid = $$ now = Time.now ary = [now.to_i, now.nsec, 1000, pid] OpenSSL::Random.add(ary.join, 0.0) OpenSSL::Random.seed(ary.join)

OpenSSL::Random::random_bytes.name: random_bytes
OpenSSL::Random::random_bytes.comment: Generates a String with length number of cryptographically strong pseudo-random bytes. === Example OpenSSL::Random.random_bytes(12) #=> "..."

OpenSSL::Random::seed.name: seed
OpenSSL::Random::seed.comment: ::seed is equivalent to ::add where entropy is length of str.

OpenSSL::Random::status?.name: status?
OpenSSL::Random::status?.comment:
Return <tt>true</tt> if the PRNG has been seeded with enough data,
<tt>false</tt> otherwise.

OpenSSL::Random::write_random_file.name: write_random_file
OpenSSL::Random::write_random_file.comment: Writes a number of random generated bytes (currently 1024) to filename which can be used to initialize the PRNG by calling ::load_random_file in a later session.

OpenSSL::SSL.name: OpenSSL::SSL
OpenSSL::SSL.comment:
Use SSLContext to set up the parameters for a TLS (former SSL) connection.
Both client and server TLS connections are supported. SSLSocket may be used in
conjunction with a TCPServer and an instance of SSLContext to set up
connections.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext.name: OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext.comment:
An SSLContext is used to set various options regarding certificates,
algorithms, verification, session caching, etc.  The SSLContext is used to
create an SSLSocket.

All attributes must be set before creating an SSLSocket as the SSLContext will
be frozen afterward.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext::new.name: new
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext::new.call_seq:
SSLContext.new           -> ctx
SSLContext.new(:TLSv1)   -> ctx
SSLContext.new("SSLv23") -> ctx
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext::new.comment:
Creates a new SSL context.

If an argument is given, #ssl_version= is called with the value. Note that
this form is deprecated. New applications should use #min_version= and
#max_version= as necessary.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#add_certificate.name: add_certificate
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#add_certificate.comment: Adds a certificate to the context. pkey must be a corresponding private key with certificate. Multiple certificates with different public key type can be added by repeated calls of this method, and OpenSSL will choose the most appropriate certificate during the handshake. #cert=, #key=, and #extra_chain_cert= are old accessor methods for setting certificate and internally call this method. === Parameters certificate: A certificate. An instance of OpenSSL::X509::Certificate. pkey: The private key for certificate. An instance of OpenSSL::PKey::PKey. extra_certs: Optional. An array of OpenSSL::X509::Certificate. When sending a certificate chain, the certificates specified by this are sent following certificate, in the order in the array. === Example rsa_cert = OpenSSL::X509::Certificate.new(...) rsa_pkey = OpenSSL::PKey.read(...) ca_intermediate_cert = OpenSSL::X509::Certificate.new(...) ctx.add_certificate(rsa_cert, rsa_pkey, [ca_intermediate_cert]) ecdsa_cert = ... ecdsa_pkey = ... another_ca_cert = ... ctx.add_certificate(ecdsa_cert, ecdsa_pkey, [another_ca_cert])

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#ciphers.name: ciphers
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#ciphers.comment: The list of cipher suites configured for this context.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#ciphers=.name: ciphers=
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#ciphers=.call_seq:
ctx.ciphers = "cipher1:cipher2:..."
ctx.ciphers = [name, ...]
ctx.ciphers = [[name, version, bits, alg_bits], ...]
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#ciphers=.comment:
Sets the list of available cipher suites for TLS 1.2 and below for this
context.

Note in a server context some ciphers require the appropriate certificates.
For example, an RSA cipher suite can only be chosen when an RSA certificate is
available.

This method does not affect TLS 1.3 connections. See also #ciphersuites=.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#ciphersuites=.name: ciphersuites=
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#ciphersuites=.comment: Sets the list of available TLS 1.3 cipher suites for this context.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#client_sigalgs=.name: client_sigalgs=
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#client_sigalgs=.comment:
Sets the list of "supported signature algorithms" for client authentication
for this context.

For a TLS server, the list is sent to the client as part of the
CertificateRequest message.

See also #sigalgs= for the server authentication equivalent.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#ecdh_curves=.name: ecdh_curves=
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#ecdh_curves=.comment:
Sets the list of supported groups for key agreement for this context.

For a TLS client, the list is directly used in the "supported_groups"
extension. For a server, the list is used by OpenSSL to determine the set of
shared supported groups. OpenSSL will pick the most appropriate one from it.

#ecdh_curves= is a deprecated alias for #groups=.

See also the man page SSL_CTX_set1_groups_list(3).

=== Example
  ctx1 = OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext.new
  ctx1.groups = "X25519:P-256"
  Thread.new {
    ssl = OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket.new(tcp_svr.accept, ctx1)
    ssl.accept
  }

  ctx2 = OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext.new
  ctx2.groups = "P-256"
  cli = OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket.new(tcp_sock, ctx2)
  cli.connect

  p cli.tmp_key.group.curve_name
  # => "prime256v1" (is an alias for NIST P-256)

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#enable_fallback.name: enable_fallback_scsv
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#enable_fallback.comment: Activate TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV for this context. See RFC 7507.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#flush_sessions.name: flush_sessions
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#flush_sessions.comment: Removes sessions in the internal cache that have expired at time.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#freeze.name: freeze
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#freeze.comment:
This method is called automatically when a new SSLSocket is created. However,
it is not thread-safe and must be called before creating SSLSocket objects in
a multi-threaded program.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#groups=.name: groups=
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#groups=.comment:
Sets the list of supported groups for key agreement for this context.

For a TLS client, the list is directly used in the "supported_groups"
extension. For a server, the list is used by OpenSSL to determine the set of
shared supported groups. OpenSSL will pick the most appropriate one from it.

#ecdh_curves= is a deprecated alias for #groups=.

See also the man page SSL_CTX_set1_groups_list(3).

=== Example
  ctx1 = OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext.new
  ctx1.groups = "X25519:P-256"
  Thread.new {
    ssl = OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket.new(tcp_svr.accept, ctx1)
    ssl.accept
  }

  ctx2 = OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext.new
  ctx2.groups = "P-256"
  cli = OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket.new(tcp_sock, ctx2)
  cli.connect

  p cli.tmp_key.group.curve_name
  # => "prime256v1" (is an alias for NIST P-256)

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#max_version=.name: max_version=
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#max_version=.call_seq:
ctx.max_version = OpenSSL::SSL::TLS1_2_VERSION
ctx.max_version = :TLS1_2
ctx.max_version = 0
ctx.max_version = nil
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#max_version=.comment:
Sets the upper bound of the supported SSL/TLS protocol version range. See
#min_version= for the possible values.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#min_version=.name: min_version=
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#min_version=.call_seq:
ctx.min_version = OpenSSL::SSL::TLS1_2_VERSION
ctx.min_version = :TLS1_2
ctx.min_version = 0
ctx.min_version = nil
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#min_version=.comment:
Sets the lower bound of the supported SSL/TLS protocol version range. The
version may be specified by an integer constant named OpenSSL::SSL::*_VERSION
or a Symbol. A value of <tt>0</tt> or <tt>nil</tt> leaves the lower bound
unspecified.

See also #security_level=, which may further restrict the available protocol
versions.

=== Example
  ctx = OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext.new
  ctx.min_version = OpenSSL::SSL::TLS1_1_VERSION
  ctx.max_version = OpenSSL::SSL::TLS1_2_VERSION

  sock = OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket.new(tcp_sock, ctx)
  sock.connect # Initiates a connection using either TLS 1.1 or TLS 1.2

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#options=.name: options=
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#options=.comment:
Sets various OpenSSL options. The options are a bit field and can be combined
with the bitwise OR operator (<tt>|</tt>). Available options are defined as
constants in OpenSSL::SSL that begin with <tt>OP_</tt>.

For backwards compatibility, passing <tt>nil</tt> has the same effect as
passing OpenSSL::SSL::OP_ALL.

See also man page SSL_CTX_set_options(3).

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#security_level.name: security_level
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#security_level.comment:
Returns the security level for the context.

See also OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#security_level=.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#security_level=.name: security_level=
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#security_level=.comment:
Sets the security level for the context. OpenSSL limits parameters according
to the level. The "parameters" include: ciphersuites, curves, key sizes,
certificate signature algorithms, protocol version and so on. For example,
level 1 rejects parameters offering below 80 bits of security, such as
ciphersuites using MD5 for the MAC or RSA keys shorter than 1024 bits.

Note that attempts to set such parameters with insufficient security are also
blocked. You need to lower the level first.

This feature is not supported in OpenSSL < 1.1.0, and setting the level to
other than 0 will raise NotImplementedError. Level 0 means everything is
permitted, the same behavior as previous versions of OpenSSL.

See the manpage of SSL_CTX_set_security_level(3) for details.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#session_cache_m.name: session_cache_mode=
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#session_cache_m.comment:
Sets the SSL session cache mode.  Bitwise-or together the desired
SESSION_CACHE_* constants to set.  See SSL_CTX_set_session_cache_mode(3) for
details.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#session_cache_s.name: session_cache_size
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#session_cache_s.comment:
Returns the current session cache size.  Zero is used to represent an
unlimited cache size.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#session_cache_s.name: session_cache_size=
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#session_cache_s.comment:
Sets the session cache size.  Returns the previously valid session cache size.
 Zero is used to represent an unlimited session cache size.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#session_cache_s.name: session_cache_stats
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#session_cache_s.comment:
Returns a Hash containing the following keys:

:accept:
  Number of started SSL/TLS handshakes in server mode

:accept_good:
  Number of established SSL/TLS sessions in server mode

:accept_renegotiate:
  Number of start renegotiations in server mode

:cache_full:
  Number of sessions that were removed due to cache overflow

:cache_hits:
  Number of successfully reused connections

:cache_misses:
  Number of sessions proposed by clients that were not found in the cache

:cache_num:
  Number of sessions in the internal session cache

:cb_hits:
  Number of sessions retrieved from the external cache in server mode

:connect:
  Number of started SSL/TLS handshakes in client mode

:connect_good:
  Number of established SSL/TLS sessions in client mode

:connect_renegotiate:
  Number of start renegotiations in client mode

:timeouts:
  Number of sessions proposed by clients that were found in the cache but had
  expired due to timeouts

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#set_params.name: set_params
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#set_params.comment: Sets saner defaults optimized for the use with HTTP-like protocols. If a Hash params is given, the parameters are overridden with it. The keys in params must be assignment methods on SSLContext. If the verify_mode is not VERIFY_NONE and ca_file, ca_path and cert_store are not set then the system default certificate store is used.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#setup.name: setup
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#setup.call_seq:
ctx.setup => Qtrue # first time
ctx.setup => nil # thereafter
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#setup.comment:
This method is called automatically when a new SSLSocket is created. However,
it is not thread-safe and must be called before creating SSLSocket objects in
a multi-threaded program.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#sigalgs=.name: sigalgs=
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#sigalgs=.comment:
Sets the list of "supported signature algorithms" for this context.

For a TLS client, the list is used in the "signature_algorithms" extension in
the ClientHello message. For a server, the list is used by OpenSSL to
determine the set of shared signature algorithms. OpenSSL will pick the most
appropriate one from it.

See also #client_sigalgs= for the client authentication equivalent.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#ssl_version=.name: ssl_version=
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#ssl_version=.comment:
Sets the SSL/TLS protocol version for the context. This forces connections to
use only the specified protocol version. This is deprecated and only provided
for backwards compatibility. Use #min_version= and #max_version= instead.

=== History
As the name hints, this used to call the SSL_CTX_set_ssl_version() function
which sets the SSL method used for connections created from the context. As of
Ruby/OpenSSL 2.1, this accessor method is implemented to call #min_version=
and #max_version= instead.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#tmp_dh=.name: tmp_dh=
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext#tmp_dh=.comment:
Sets DH parameters used for ephemeral DH key exchange. This is relevant for
servers only.

<tt>pkey</tt> is an instance of OpenSSL::PKey::DH. Note that key components
contained in the key object, if any, are ignored. The server will always
generate a new key pair for each handshake.

Added in version 3.0. See also the man page SSL_CTX_set0_tmp_dh_pkey(3).

=== Example
  ctx = OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext.new
  ctx.tmp_dh = OpenSSL::PKey::DH.generate(2048)
  Thread.new {
    ssl = OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket.new(tcp_svr.accept, ctx)
    ssl.accept
  }

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError.name: OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLError.comment: Generic error class raised by SSLSocket and SSLContext.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLServer.name: OpenSSL::SSL::SSLServer
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLServer.comment: SSLServer represents a TCP/IP server socket with Secure Sockets Layer. Deprecated. Use TCPServer or Socket to accept a TCP connection, and then wrap it with OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket. See also OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#accept.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLServer::new.name: new
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLServer::new.comment: Creates a new instance of SSLServer. * srv is an instance of TCPServer. * ctx is an instance of OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLServer#accept.name: accept
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLServer#accept.comment: Works similar to TCPServer#accept. NOTE: SSLServer is deprecated. See #start_immediately for details.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLServer#to_io.name: to_io
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLServer#to_io.comment: Returns the TCPServer passed to the SSLServer when initialized.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket::new.name: new
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket::new.call_seq:
SSLSocket.new(io) => aSSLSocket
SSLSocket.new(io, ctx) => aSSLSocket
SSLSocket.new(io, ctx, sync_close:) => aSSLSocket
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket::new.comment: Creates a new SSL socket from io which must be a real IO object (not an IO-like object that responds to read/write). If ctx is provided the SSL Sockets initial params will be taken from the context. The optional sync_close keyword parameter sets the sync_close instance variable. Setting this to true will cause the underlying socket to be closed when the SSL/TLS connection is shut down. The OpenSSL::Buffering module provides additional IO methods. This method will freeze the SSLContext if one is provided; however, session management is still allowed in the frozen SSLContext.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket::open.name: open
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket::open.call_seq: open(remote_host, remote_port, local_host=nil, local_port=nil, context: nil)
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket::open.comment: Creates a new instance of SSLSocket. remotehost_ and remoteport_ are used to open TCPSocket. If localhost_ and localport_ are specified, then those parameters are used on the local end to establish the connection. If context is provided, the SSL Sockets initial params will be taken from the context. === Examples sock = OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket.open('localhost', 443) sock.connect # Initiates a connection to localhost:443 with SSLContext: ctx = OpenSSL::SSL::SSLContext.new sock = OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket.open('localhost', 443, context: ctx) sock.connect # Initiates a connection to localhost:443 with SSLContext

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#accept.name: accept
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#accept.comment: Waits for a SSL/TLS client to initiate a handshake.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#accept_nonblock.name: accept_nonblock
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#accept_nonblock.comment: Initiates the SSL/TLS handshake as a server in non-blocking manner. # emulates blocking accept begin ssl.accept_nonblock rescue IO::WaitReadable IO.select([s2]) retry rescue IO::WaitWritable IO.select(nil, [s2]) retry end By specifying a keyword argument exception to false, you can indicate that accept_nonblock should not raise an IO::WaitReadable or IO::WaitWritable exception, but return the symbol :wait_readable or :wait_writable instead.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#alpn_protocol.name: alpn_protocol
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#alpn_protocol.comment:
Returns the ALPN protocol string that was finally selected by the server
during the handshake.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#cert.name: cert
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#cert.comment: The X509 certificate for this socket endpoint.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#cipher.name: cipher
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#cipher.call_seq: ssl.cipher -> nil or [name, version, bits, alg_bits]
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#cipher.comment:
Returns the cipher suite actually used in the current session, or nil if no
session has been established.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#client_ca.name: client_ca
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#client_ca.comment:
Returns the list of client CAs. Please note that in contrast to
SSLContext#client_ca= no array of X509::Certificate is returned but X509::Name
instances of the CA's subject distinguished name.

In server mode, returns the list set by SSLContext#client_ca=. In client mode,
returns the list of client CAs sent from the server.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#close_read.name: close_read
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#close_read.comment:
Close the stream for reading. This method is ignored by OpenSSL as there is no
reasonable way to implement it, but exists for compatibility with IO.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#close_write.name: close_write
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#close_write.comment:
Closes the stream for writing. The behavior of this method depends on the
version of OpenSSL and the TLS protocol in use.

* Sends a 'close_notify' alert to the peer.
* Does not wait for the peer's 'close_notify' alert in response.

In TLS 1.2 and earlier:
* On receipt of a 'close_notify' alert, responds with a 'close_notify' alert
  of its own and close down the connection immediately, discarding any pending
  writes.

Therefore, on TLS 1.2, this method will cause the connection to be completely
shut down. On TLS 1.3, the connection will remain open for reading only.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#connect.name: connect
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#connect.comment: Initiates an SSL/TLS handshake with a server.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#connect_nonblock.name: connect_nonblock
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#connect_nonblock.comment: Initiates the SSL/TLS handshake as a client in non-blocking manner. # emulates blocking connect begin ssl.connect_nonblock rescue IO::WaitReadable IO.select([s2]) retry rescue IO::WaitWritable IO.select(nil, [s2]) retry end By specifying a keyword argument exception to false, you can indicate that connect_nonblock should not raise an IO::WaitReadable or IO::WaitWritable exception, but return the symbol :wait_readable or :wait_writable instead.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#export_keying_ma.name: export_keying_material
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#export_keying_ma.comment: Enables use of shared session key material in accordance with RFC 5705.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#finished_message.name: finished_message
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#finished_message.comment: Returns the contents of the last <tt>Finished</tt> message sent to the peer.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#group.name: group
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#group.comment:
Returns the name of the group that was used for the key agreement of the
current TLS session establishment.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#hostname=.name: hostname=
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#hostname=.comment:
Sets the server hostname used for SNI. This needs to be set before
SSLSocket#connect.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#npn_protocol.name: npn_protocol
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#npn_protocol.comment:
Returns the protocol string that was finally selected by the client during the
handshake.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#peer_cert.name: peer_cert
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#peer_cert.comment: The X509 certificate for this socket's peer.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#peer_cert_chain.name: peer_cert_chain
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#peer_cert_chain.comment: The X509 certificate chain for this socket's peer.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#peer_finished_me.name: peer_finished_message
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#peer_finished_me.comment:
Returns the contents of the last <tt>Finished</tt> message expected to be sent
by the peer.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#peer_sigalg.name: peer_sigalg
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#peer_sigalg.comment:
Returns the signature algorithm name, the IANA name of the signature scheme
used by the peer to sign the TLS handshake.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#pending.name: pending
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#pending.comment:
Returns the number of bytes buffered by the OpenSSL library and immediately
available for reading with #sysread.

This does not include data read ahead and buffered by SSLSocket. It may
therefore return 0 even when data is available for reading with methods that
are aware of the SSLSocket buffer, such as #read or #gets.

See also the man page SSL_pending(3).

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#post_connection_.name: post_connection_check
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#post_connection_.comment:
Perform hostname verification following RFC 6125.

This method MUST be called after calling #connect to ensure that the hostname
of a remote peer has been verified.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#session.name: session
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#session.comment:
Returns the SSLSession object currently used, or nil if the session is not
established.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#session=.name: session=
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#session=.comment: Sets the Session to be used when the connection is established.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#session_reused?.name: session_reused?
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#session_reused?.comment: Returns <tt>true</tt> if a reused session was negotiated during the handshake.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#sigalg.name: sigalg
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#sigalg.comment:
Returns the signature algorithm name, the IANA name of the signature scheme
used by the local to sign the TLS handshake.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#ssl_version.name: ssl_version
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#ssl_version.comment:
Returns a String representing the SSL/TLS version that was negotiated for the
connection, for example "TLSv1.2".

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#state.name: state
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#state.comment:
A description of the current connection state. This is for diagnostic purposes
only.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#sysclose.name: sysclose
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#sysclose.comment:
Sends "close notify" to the peer and tries to shut down the SSL connection
gracefully.

If sync_close is set to <tt>true</tt>, the underlying IO is also closed.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#sysread.name: sysread
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#sysread.comment: Reads length bytes from the SSL connection. If a pre-allocated buffer is provided the data will be written into it.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#tmp_key.name: tmp_key
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#tmp_key.comment: Returns the ephemeral key used in case of forward secrecy cipher.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#verify_result.name: verify_result
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#verify_result.comment:
Returns the result of the peer certificates verification.  See verify(1) for
error values and descriptions.

If no peer certificate was presented X509_V_OK is returned.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#stop.name: stop
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#stop.comment:
Sends "close notify" to the peer and tries to shut down the SSL connection
gracefully.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#sysread_nonblock.name: sysread_nonblock
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#sysread_nonblock.call_seq:
ssl.sysread_nonblock(length) => string
ssl.sysread_nonblock(length, buffer) => buffer
ssl.sysread_nonblock(length[, buffer [, opts]) => buffer
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#sysread_nonblock.comment: A non-blocking version of #sysread. Raises an SSLError if reading would block. If "exception: false" is passed, this method returns a symbol of :wait_readable, :wait_writable, or nil, rather than raising an exception. Reads length bytes from the SSL connection. If a pre-allocated buffer is provided the data will be written into it.

OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#syswrite_nonbloc.name: syswrite_nonblock
OpenSSL::SSL::SSLSocket#syswrite_nonbloc.comment: Writes string to the SSL connection in a non-blocking manner. Raises an SSLError if writing would block. If "exception: false" is passed, this method returns a symbol of :wait_readable or :wait_writable, rather than raising an exception.

OpenSSL::SSL::Session::new.name: new
OpenSSL::SSL::Session::new.comment:
Creates a new Session object from an instance of SSLSocket or DER/PEM encoded
String.

OpenSSL::SSL::Session#==.comment: Returns <tt>true</tt> if the two Session is the same, <tt>false</tt> if not.

OpenSSL::SSL::Session#time.name: time
OpenSSL::SSL::Session#time.comment: Returns the time at which the session was established.

OpenSSL::SSL::Session#time=.name: time=
OpenSSL::SSL::Session#time=.comment: Sets start time of the session. Time resolution is in seconds.

OpenSSL::SSL::Session#timeout.name: timeout
OpenSSL::SSL::Session#timeout.comment:
Returns the timeout value set for the session, in seconds from the established
time.

OpenSSL::SSL::Session#timeout=.name: timeout=
OpenSSL::SSL::Session#timeout=.comment: Sets how long until the session expires in seconds.

OpenSSL::SSL::Session#to_der.name: to_der
OpenSSL::SSL::Session#to_der.comment: Returns an ASN1 encoded String that contains the Session object.

OpenSSL::SSL::Session#to_pem.name: to_pem
OpenSSL::SSL::Session#to_pem.comment: Returns a PEM encoded String that contains the Session object.

OpenSSL::SSL::Session#to_text.name: to_text
OpenSSL::SSL::Session#to_text.comment: Shows everything in the Session object. This is for diagnostic purposes.

OpenSSL::SSL::SocketForwarder#fileno.name: fileno
OpenSSL::SSL::SocketForwarder#fileno.comment: The file descriptor for the socket.

OpenSSL::SSL::SocketForwarder#wait.name: wait
OpenSSL::SSL::SocketForwarder#wait.comment:
Calls IO#wait on the underlying socket.

Note that this method may block even when there is data immediately available
to read, unlike IO#wait_readable.

OpenSSL::SSL::SocketForwarder#wait_reada.name: wait_readable
OpenSSL::SSL::SocketForwarder#wait_reada.comment:
Calls IO#wait_readable on the underlying socket.

Note that this method may block even when there is data immediately available
to read, unlike IO#wait_readable.

OpenSSL::SSL::SocketForwarder#wait_writa.name: wait_writable
OpenSSL::SSL::SocketForwarder#wait_writa.comment: Calls IO#wait_writable on the underlying socket.

OpenSSL::Timestamp.name: OpenSSL::Timestamp
OpenSSL::Timestamp.comment:
Provides classes and methods to request, create and validate
{RFC3161-compliant}[http://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc3161.txt] timestamps. Request
may be used to either create requests from scratch or to parse existing
requests that again can be used to request timestamps from a timestamp server,
e.g. via the net/http. The resulting timestamp response may be parsed using
Response.

Please note that Response is read-only and immutable. To create a Response, an
instance of Factory as well as a valid Request are needed.

=== Create a Response:
  #Assumes ts.p12 is a PKCS#12-compatible file with a private key
  #and a certificate that has an extended key usage of 'timeStamping'
  p12 = OpenSSL::PKCS12.new(File.binread('ts.p12'), 'pwd')
  md = OpenSSL::Digest.new('SHA1')
  hash = md.digest(data) #some binary data to be timestamped
  req = OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request.new
  req.algorithm = 'SHA1'
  req.message_imprint = hash
  req.policy_id = "1.2.3.4.5"
  req.nonce = 42
  fac = OpenSSL::Timestamp::Factory.new
  fac.gen_time = Time.now
  fac.serial_number = 1
  timestamp = fac.create_timestamp(p12.key, p12.certificate, req)

=== Verify a timestamp response:
  #Assume we have a timestamp token in a file called ts.der
  ts = OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response.new(File.binread('ts.der'))
  #Assume we have the Request for this token in a file called req.der
  req = OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request.new(File.binread('req.der'))
  # Assume the associated root CA certificate is contained in a
  # DER-encoded file named root.cer
  root = OpenSSL::X509::Certificate.new(File.binread('root.cer'))
  # get the necessary intermediate certificates, available in
  # DER-encoded form in inter1.cer and inter2.cer
  inter1 = OpenSSL::X509::Certificate.new(File.binread('inter1.cer'))
  inter2 = OpenSSL::X509::Certificate.new(File.binread('inter2.cer'))
  ts.verify(req, root, inter1, inter2) -> ts or raises an exception if validation fails

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Factory.name: OpenSSL::Timestamp::Factory
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Factory.comment:
Used to generate a Response from scratch.

Please bear in mind that the implementation will always apply and prefer the
policy object identifier given in the request over the default policy id
specified in the Factory. As a consequence, <tt>default_policy_id</tt> will
only be applied if no Request#policy_id was given. But this also means that
one needs to check the policy identifier in the request manually before
creating the Response, e.g. to check whether it complies to a specific set of
acceptable policies.

There exists also the possibility to add certificates (instances of
OpenSSL::X509::Certificate) besides the timestamping certificate that will be
included in the resulting timestamp token if Request#cert_requested? is
<tt>true</tt>. Ideally, one would also include any intermediate certificates
(the root certificate can be left out - in order to trust it any verifying
party will have to be in its possession anyway). This simplifies validation of
the timestamp since these intermediate certificates are "already there" and
need not be passed as external parameters to Response#verify anymore, thus
minimizing external resources needed for verification.

=== Example: Inclusion of (untrusted) intermediate certificates

Assume we received a timestamp request that has set Request#policy_id to
<tt>nil</tt> and Request#cert_requested? to true. The raw request bytes are
stored in a variable called <tt>req_raw</tt>. We'd still like to integrate the
necessary intermediate certificates (in <tt>inter1.cer</tt> and
<tt>inter2.cer</tt>) to simplify validation of the resulting Response.
<tt>ts.p12</tt> is a PKCS#12-compatible file including the private key and the
timestamping certificate.

  req = OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request.new(raw_bytes)
  p12 = OpenSSL::PKCS12.new(File.binread('ts.p12'), 'pwd')
  inter1 = OpenSSL::X509::Certificate.new(File.binread('inter1.cer'))
  inter2 = OpenSSL::X509::Certificate.new(File.binread('inter2.cer'))
  fac = OpenSSL::Timestamp::Factory.new
  fac.gen_time = Time.now
  fac.serial_number = 1
  fac.allowed_digests = ["sha256", "sha384", "sha512"]
  #needed because the Request contained no policy identifier
  fac.default_policy_id = '1.2.3.4.5'
  fac.additional_certificates = [ inter1, inter2 ]
  timestamp = fac.create_timestamp(p12.key, p12.certificate, req)

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Factory#create_times.name: create_timestamp
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Factory#create_times.comment:
Creates a Response with the help of an OpenSSL::PKey, an
OpenSSL::X509::Certificate and a Request.

Mandatory parameters for timestamp creation that need to be set in the
Request:

* Request#algorithm
* Request#message_imprint

Mandatory parameters that need to be set in the Factory:
* Factory#serial_number
* Factory#gen_time
* Factory#allowed_digests

In addition one of either Request#policy_id or Factory#default_policy_id must
be set.

Raises a TimestampError if creation fails, though successfully created error
responses may be returned.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request.name: OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request.comment:
Allows to create timestamp requests or parse existing ones. A Request is also
needed for creating timestamps from scratch with Factory. When created from
scratch, some default values are set:
* version is set to <tt>1</tt>
* cert_requested is set to <tt>true</tt>
* algorithm, message_imprint, policy_id, and nonce are set to <tt>false</tt>

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request::new.name: new
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request::new.call_seq:
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request.new(file)    -> request
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request.new(string)  -> request
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request.new          -> empty request
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request::new.comment:
When creating a Request with the <tt>File</tt> or <tt>string</tt> parameter,
the corresponding <tt>File</tt> or <tt>string</tt> must be DER-encoded.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request#algorithm.name: algorithm
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request#algorithm.comment:
Returns the 'short name' of the object identifier that represents the
algorithm that was used to create the message imprint digest.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request#algorithm=.name: algorithm=
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request#algorithm=.comment:
Allows to set the object identifier  or the 'short name' of the algorithm that
was used to create the message imprint digest.

=== Example:
  request.algorithm = "SHA1"

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request#cert_request.name: cert_requested=
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request#cert_request.comment:
Specify whether the response shall contain the timestamp authority's
certificate or not. The default value is <tt>true</tt>.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request#cert_request.name: cert_requested?
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request#cert_request.comment:
Indicates whether the response shall contain the timestamp authority's
certificate or not.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request#message_impr.name: message_imprint
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request#message_impr.comment: Returns the message imprint (digest) of the data to be timestamped.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request#nonce.name: nonce
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request#nonce.comment:
Returns the nonce (number used once) that the server shall include in its
response.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request#nonce=.name: nonce=
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request#nonce=.comment:
Sets the nonce (number used once) that the server shall include in its
response. If the nonce is set, the server must return the same nonce value in
a valid Response.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request#policy_id.name: policy_id
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request#policy_id.comment:
Returns the 'short name' of the object identifier that represents the
timestamp policy under which the server shall create the timestamp.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request#policy_id=.name: policy_id=
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request#policy_id=.comment:
Allows to set the object identifier that represents the timestamp policy under
which the server shall create the timestamp. This may be left <tt>nil</tt>,
implying that the timestamp server will issue the timestamp using some default
policy.

=== Example:
  request.policy_id = "1.2.3.4.5"

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request#version.name: version
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request#version.comment: Returns the version of this request. <tt>1</tt> is the default value.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request#version=.name: version=
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Request#version=.comment:
Sets the version number for this Request. This should be <tt>1</tt> for
compliant servers.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response.name: OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response.comment:
Immutable and read-only representation of a timestamp response returned from a
timestamp server after receiving an associated Request. Allows access to
specific information about the response but also allows to verify the
Response.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response::new.name: new
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response::new.comment:
Creates a Response from a <tt>File</tt> or <tt>string</tt> parameter, the
corresponding <tt>File</tt> or <tt>string</tt> must be DER-encoded. Please
note that Response is an immutable read-only class. If you'd like to create
timestamps please refer to Factory instead.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response#failure_inf.name: failure_info
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response#failure_inf.comment:
In cases no timestamp token has been created, this field contains further info
about the reason why response creation failed. The method returns either nil
(the request was successful and a timestamp token was created) or one of the
following:
* :BAD_ALG - Indicates that the timestamp server rejects the message imprint
  algorithm used in the Request
* :BAD_REQUEST - Indicates that the timestamp server was not able to process
  the Request properly
* :BAD_DATA_FORMAT - Indicates that the timestamp server was not able to parse
  certain data in the Request
* :TIME_NOT_AVAILABLE - Indicates that the server could not access its time
  source
* :UNACCEPTED_POLICY - Indicates that the requested policy identifier is not
  recognized or supported by the timestamp server
* :UNACCEPTED_EXTENSIION - Indicates that an extension in the Request is not
  supported by the timestamp server
* :ADD_INFO_NOT_AVAILABLE -Indicates that additional information requested is
  either not understood or currently not available
* :SYSTEM_FAILURE - Timestamp creation failed due to an internal error that
  occurred on the timestamp server

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response#status.name: status
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response#status.comment:
Returns one of GRANTED, GRANTED_WITH_MODS, REJECTION, WAITING,
REVOCATION_WARNING or REVOCATION_NOTIFICATION. A timestamp token has been
created only in case <tt>status</tt> is equal to GRANTED or GRANTED_WITH_MODS.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response#status_text.name: status_text
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response#status_text.call_seq: response.status_text -> Array of strings or nil
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response#status_text.comment:
In cases of failure this field may contain an array of strings further
describing the origin of the failure.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response#to_der.name: to_der
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response#to_der.comment: Returns the Response in DER-encoded form.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response#token.name: token
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response#token.comment:
If a timestamp token is present, this returns it in the form of a
OpenSSL::PKCS7.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response#token_info.name: token_info
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response#token_info.comment: Get the response's token info if present.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response#tsa_certifi.name: tsa_certificate
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response#tsa_certifi.comment:
If the Request specified to request the TSA certificate
(Request#cert_requested = true), then this field contains the certificate of
the timestamp authority.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response#verify.name: verify
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response#verify.call_seq:
response.verify(Request, root_store) -> Response
response.verify(Request, root_store, [intermediate_cert]) -> Response
OpenSSL::Timestamp::Response#verify.comment:
Verifies a timestamp token by checking the signature, validating the
certificate chain implied by tsa_certificate and by checking conformance to a
given Request. Mandatory parameters are the Request associated to this
Response, and an OpenSSL::X509::Store of trusted roots.

Intermediate certificates can optionally be supplied for creating the
certificate chain. These intermediate certificates must all be instances of
OpenSSL::X509::Certificate.

If validation fails, several kinds of exceptions can be raised:
* TypeError if types don't fit
* TimestampError if something is wrong with the timestamp token itself, if it
  is not conformant to the Request, or if validation of the timestamp
  certificate chain fails.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::TimestampError.comment: Generic exception class of the Timestamp module.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo.name: OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo
OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo.comment:
Immutable and read-only representation of a timestamp token info from a

OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo::new.name: new
OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo::new.comment:
Creates a TokenInfo from a <tt>File</tt> or <tt>string</tt> parameter, the
corresponding <tt>File</tt> or <tt>string</tt> must be DER-encoded. Please
note that TokenInfo is an immutable read-only class. If you'd like to create
timestamps please refer to Factory instead.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo#algorithm.name: algorithm
OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo#algorithm.comment:
Returns the 'short name' of the object identifier representing the algorithm
that was used to derive the message imprint digest. For valid timestamps, this
is the same value that was already given in the Request. If status is GRANTED
or GRANTED_WITH_MODS, this is never <tt>nil</tt>.

=== Example:
  algo = token_info.algorithm
  puts algo                -> "SHA1"

OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo#gen_time.name: gen_time
OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo#gen_time.comment:
Returns time when this timestamp token was created. If status is GRANTED or
GRANTED_WITH_MODS, this is never <tt>nil</tt>.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo#message_im.name: message_imprint
OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo#message_im.comment:
Returns the message imprint digest. For valid timestamps, this is the same
value that was already given in the Request. If status is GRANTED or
GRANTED_WITH_MODS, this is never <tt>nil</tt>.

=== Example:
  mi = token_info.msg_imprint
  puts mi                -> "DEADBEEF"

OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo#nonce.name: nonce
OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo#nonce.comment:
If the timestamp token is valid then this field contains the same nonce that
was passed to the timestamp server in the initial Request.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo#ordering.name: ordering
OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo#ordering.comment:
If the ordering field is missing, or if the ordering field is present and set
to false, then the genTime field only indicates the time at which the
time-stamp token has been created by the TSA.  In such a case, the ordering of
time-stamp tokens issued by the same TSA or different TSAs is only possible
when the difference between the genTime of the first time-stamp token and the
genTime of the second time-stamp token is greater than the sum of the
accuracies of the genTime for each time-stamp token.

If the ordering field is present and set to true, every time-stamp token from
the same TSA can always be ordered based on the genTime field, regardless of
the genTime accuracy.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo#policy_id.name: policy_id
OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo#policy_id.comment:
Returns the timestamp policy object identifier of the policy this timestamp
was created under. If status is GRANTED or GRANTED_WITH_MODS, this is never
<tt>nil</tt>.

=== Example:
  id = token_info.policy_id
  puts id                 -> "1.2.3.4.5"

OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo#serial_num.name: serial_number
OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo#serial_num.comment:
Returns serial number of the timestamp token. This value shall never be the
same for two timestamp tokens issued by a dedicated timestamp authority. If
status is GRANTED or GRANTED_WITH_MODS, this is never <tt>nil</tt>.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo#to_der.name: to_der
OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo#to_der.comment: Returns the TokenInfo in DER-encoded form.

OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo#version.name: version
OpenSSL::Timestamp::TokenInfo#version.comment:
Returns the version number of the token info. With compliant servers, this
value should be <tt>1</tt> if present. If status is GRANTED or
GRANTED_WITH_MODS.

OpenSSL::X509::CRL#by_serial.name: by_serial
OpenSSL::X509::CRL#by_serial.comment: Looks up the certificate serial (an Integer or OpenSSL::BN) in the CRL and returns the matching OpenSSL::X509::Revoked entry, or nil if that serial is not listed. Unlike iterating over #revoked, this does not instantiate the entire revocation list: it performs a sorted lookup (wrapping the OpenSSL function X509_CRL_get0_by_serial), which is significantly faster and uses far less memory for large CRLs. crl.by_serial(cert.serial) #=> # or nil crl.by_serial(cert.serial)&.time #=> revocation time, if revoked
